bullets: The new Quant-Arena benchmark evaluates an entire quantitative-trading research loop rather than isolated code or decisions. An agent develops features and stock-scoring code using feedback from 2022–2023 Chinese A-share market data, then freezes one strategy for assessment on a sealed 2024 holdout that was unavailable during development. Why it matters: If you are selecting agents for quantitative research, this design tests whether iterative improvements survive a genuinely withheld period rather than merely optimizing the visible research window. It makes holdout performance and the agent’s complete workflow more relevant than formula-level scores alone. Evidence: E004. High confidence.

The new VerifierBench tests whether agents can write executable verifiers—programs that decide whether a proposed solution is valid. Its 222 tasks include 4,993 hidden tests containing alternative correct solutions and attacks, while a six-check audit screens the benchmark’s own source verifiers and tests. Why it matters: If generated verifiers will filter synthetic training data or approve agent work, accepting one expected answer is insufficient. This benchmark lets model builders evaluate whether a verifier recognizes multiple valid solutions while rejecting adversarial invalid ones, and it also subjects the evaluation machinery itself to explicit checks. Evidence: E019. High confidence.

The new MOSAIC benchmark evaluates conversational memory across text, images, video, and audio using 923 questions over histories lasting 11–24 sessions. Its diagnostic protocol separates failures in representing evidence, retrieving it, delivering it to the model, and reading it; audio cases include annotated vocal cues such as tone and rhythm. Why it matters: If you are comparing memory systems for multimodal assistants, a single end-to-end accuracy score cannot identify which component needs improvement. MOSAIC supports decisions about storage, retrieval, context delivery, and model comprehension separately instead of treating every forgotten detail as the same failure. Evidence: E005. High confidence.

The new MicroPerf-Bench moves coding-agent evaluation from local code changes to performance optimization across microservices—applications composed of multiple interacting services. It targets cases where end-to-end speed depends on interactions among independently running components rather than one function or repository. Why it matters: If you are choosing coding agents for production performance work, success on function-level bug fixing does not establish that an agent can diagnose system-wide bottlenecks. This benchmark introduces a test aligned with distributed applications, where a locally sensible edit can fail to improve the complete service. Evidence: E011. High confidence.

A newly captured audit of the Safety Helmet Wearing Dataset reports that 2,288 of 7,581 images belong to near-duplicate clusters and that 421 of 1,517 official test images have a near-duplicate elsewhere in the dataset. The release adds controlled experiments and a duplicate-aware evaluation split. Why it matters: If you use this dataset to compare helmet detectors, the official split may reward recognition of repeated scenes rather than transfer to new scenes. The duplicate-aware split provides a more decision-relevant basis for model selection and illustrates why image-level random splits need explicit duplication checks. Evidence: E039. High confidence.

The new PCLA-Bridge tool runs unmodified autonomous-driving agents built for the CARLA simulator without an active CARLA server. It isolates dependencies and translates sensor tensors, routes, timing, and control outputs through a minimal interface for other datasets, simulators, or physical platforms. Why it matters: If you evaluate driving agents outside their original simulator, this tool reduces the need to rewrite each agent around different Application Programming Interfaces, sensors, and clocks. It enables a cleaner portability test: evaluators can preserve the original agent while changing the environment or sensor source. Evidence: E003. Medium confidence.

A new tourism-forecasting study compares three large-language-model families used as zero-shot forecasters against established statistical and machine-learning baselines across eight European source markets. Its out-of-sample checks include a stable pre-COVID period, an older-model condition, and a future period beyond model training cutoffs. Why it matters: If you are considering language models for forecasting, this design separates ordinary historical fit from performance after structural disruption and beyond likely training exposure. That makes it more useful for deciding whether apparent forecasting ability transfers to unseen time periods rather than reflecting familiarity with historical data. Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 Quant-Arena 基准评估的是完整的量化交易研究闭环，而非孤立的代码或决策。智能体利用 2022–2023 年中国 A 股市场数据的反馈来开发特征和股票评分代码，随后冻结一个策略，并在开发期间无法访问的密封 2024 年留出集上进行评估。Why it matters: 如果你正在为量化研究选择智能体，这种设计可检验迭代改进能否经受真正未见时期的考验，而非仅仅针对可见的研究窗口进行优化。与仅看公式层面的分数相比，它使留出集表现和智能体的完整工作流程更具参考价值。Evidence: E004. High confidence.

新发布的 VerifierBench 测试智能体能否编写可执行的验证器，即用于判定候选解是否有效的程序。其 222 项任务包含 4,993 个隐藏测试，其中涵盖替代性的正确解和攻击；同时，一项包含六项检查的审计会筛查该基准自身的源验证器和测试。Why it matters: 如果生成的验证器将用于筛选合成训练数据或批准智能体的工作，那么仅接受一个预期答案是不够的。该基准让模型开发者能够评估验证器是否可在拒绝对抗性无效解的同时识别多个有效解，并且还会对评估机制本身进行明确检查。Evidence: E019. High confidence.

新发布的 MOSAIC 基准使用跨越 11–24 个会话的历史记录和 923 个问题，评估文本、图像、视频及音频上的对话记忆。其诊断协议将以下环节的失败区分开来：表征证据、检索证据、向模型传递证据以及读取证据；音频案例还包括对语气和节奏等声音线索的标注。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较多模态助手的记忆系统，单一的端到端准确率分数无法确定哪个组件需要改进。MOSAIC 支持分别针对存储、检索、上下文传递和模型理解作出决策，而不是把每个被遗忘的细节都视为同一种失败。Evidence: E005. High confidence.

新发布的 MicroPerf-Bench 将编码智能体评估从局部代码修改扩展到跨微服务的性能优化；微服务应用由多个相互交互的服务组成。它针对的是端到端速度取决于多个独立运行组件之间交互的场景，而非取决于单个函数或代码仓库。Why it matters: 如果你正在为生产环境中的性能工作选择编码智能体，那么在函数级缺陷修复中取得成功，并不能证明智能体能够诊断全系统瓶颈。该基准引入了与分布式应用相匹配的测试；在这类应用中，局部看来合理的修改可能无法改善完整服务的性能。Evidence: E011. High confidence.

一项新近获取的 Safety Helmet Wearing Dataset 审计报告指出，在 7,581 张图像中，2,288 张属于近重复聚类；在 1,517 张官方测试图像中，421 张在该数据集的其他位置存在近重复图像。此次发布还增加了对照实验和一个考虑重复项的评估划分。Why it matters: 如果你使用该数据集比较安全帽检测器，官方划分可能会奖励对重复场景的识别，而非向新场景的迁移能力。考虑重复项的划分为模型选择提供了与决策更相关的依据，也说明了为何图像级随机划分需要进行明确的重复项检查。Evidence: E039. High confidence.

新发布的 PCLA-Bridge 工具无需运行中的 CARLA 服务器，即可运行专为 CARLA 模拟器构建且未经修改的自动驾驶智能体。它隔离依赖项，并通过一个面向其他数据集、模拟器或物理平台的最小化接口，转换传感器张量、路线、时序和控制输出。Why it matters: 如果你在原始模拟器之外评估驾驶智能体，该工具可以减少为适配不同的应用程序编程接口、传感器和时钟而重写每个智能体的需要。它支持更清晰的可移植性测试：评估者可以保留原始智能体，同时更换环境或传感器来源。Evidence: E003. Medium confidence.

一项新的旅游预测研究在八个欧洲客源市场中，将作为零样本预测器使用的三类大语言模型与成熟的统计和机器学习基线进行比较。其样本外检查包括稳定的 COVID 前时期、使用较旧模型的条件，以及超出模型训练截止时间的未来时期。Why it matters: 如果你正在考虑将语言模型用于预测，这种设计可将常规历史拟合与结构性扰动之后、以及超出可能训练数据覆盖范围后的表现区分开来。因此，它更有助于判断表面上的预测能力能否迁移到未见过的时间段，而不是反映模型对历史数据的熟悉程度。Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.
evidence_items.title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study aims to examine whether large language models (LLMs) can improve tourism demand forecasting accuracy compared to established statistical and machine learning approaches. Design/methodology/approach A systematic out-of-sample comparison is conducted using monthly tourism arrival data from Eurostat for eight European source markets. Benchmarks include optimized seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA), exponential smoothing (ETS), Prophet, Random Forest and seasonal naive models. Three LLM families are evaluated as zero-shot forecasters. Robustness is assessed across a pre-COVID stable period, a future period beyond LLM training cutoffs and an older model test. Findings LLM-based forecasts demonstrate consistent performance advantages over all benchmark models across countries and evaluation periods. In the main post-COVID period, LLMs achieve mean MASE values of 0.67–0.85 compared to 1.56 for ETS, 2.67 for SARIMA, 3.04 for Prophet and 4.32 for Random Forest. The LLM advantage persists in the pre-COVID stable period (LLM MASE 0.85–0.90 vs SARIMA 1.71 and ETS 1.31), indicating that the benefit extends beyond structural-break contexts. Robustness tests using an older LLM model and forecasts for a future period beyond LLM training data indicate that data contamination does not explain the observed performance patterns. Prompt ablation analysis reveals that providing contextual information (country identity and date labels) is the most beneficial design choice, while seasonal and shock hints offer no consistent improvement. Diebold–Mariano tests show directional evidence favoring LLMs in 31 of 32 pairwise comparisons, though limited test sample size (14–23 observations per country) precludes individual-country statistical significance at conventional levels. Research limitations/implications The analysis focuses on monthly national-level arrival data and zero-shot prompting.
evidence_items.title: Tourism demand forecasting in the artificial intelligence era using large language models

evidence_items.summary: Most high-performing end-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are developed for the CARLA Leaderboard, tightly coupling them to CARLA's APIs, sensor layouts, coordinate systems, and internal clock. Reusing these models on real datasets, alternative simulators, or physical platforms necessitates substantial manual re-engineering. We present PCLA-Bridge, a deployable tool that runs unmodified CARLA Leaderboard agents from any sensor source to any control destination without an active CARLA server. With PCLA-Bridge handling dependency isolation, tensor marshalling, routing, and synthetic timing, integrators only need to provide a minimal interface. We validate the tool across two operational paradigms: offline replay on in-domain CARLA recordings and real-world nuScenes logs, and live closed-loop control across three diverse simulation engines: MetaDrive, AWSIM, and AlpaSim. We analyze the lightweight integration requirements for each platform, highlighting output translation (such as converting agent actions into target trajectory formats) and coordinate-frame transformations, showing that integration requires minimal glue code rather than structural changes. All eight evaluated agents execute across all three simulators without modification, confirming the reliability of PCLA-Bridge and establishing a foundation for systematic sim-to-real, cross-sim, and security testing.
evidence_items.title: PCLA-Bridge: A Framework for Cross-Domain Deployment of CARLA Agents

evidence_items.summary: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022--2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.
evidence_items.title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research

evidence_items.summary: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
evidence_items.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents

evidence_items.summary: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6 times faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99 times median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark's RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.
evidence_items.title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
evidence_items.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?

evidence_items.summary: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
evidence_items.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are becoming an increasingly important paradigm for automating software engineering tasks. However, existing coding benchmarks primarily evaluate agents at the function or repository level, leaving their capabilities in more complex distributed software systems largely unexplored. In practice, many modern applications adopt microservice architectures, where end-to-end performance emerges from interactions among multiple independently running services, requiring agents to reason beyond local code changes. To study this capability, we introduce MicroPerf-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on end-to-end performance optimization in microservice systems. Constructing such a benchmark is challenging because reproducible system-level performance fixes are sparse and difficult to attribute. We address this challenge by injecting empirically grounded performance anti-patterns into real-world open-source systems while preserving functionality and ensuring measurable performance degradation. The resulting benchmark contains 65 optimization instances across seven systems and nine anti-patterns, each with an executable environment, functional tests, and mixed-workload evaluation. Across 1,755 runs covering nine agent-model configurations, the best configuration recovers only 42.0% of the injected performance degradation. The dominant failure is not invalid code, but functionally correct and constraint-compliant changes that fail to improve end-to-end performance, highlighting system-level bottleneck localization as a key challenge for current coding agents. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/zyzcjnb/microperf.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Coding Agents for System-Level Performance Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.
evidence_items.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
evidence_items.title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents

evidence_items.summary: Context: Reviewing a pull request requires verification evidence that addresses the proposed change. Coding agent benchmarks and studies of pull request outcomes do not directly assess this relationship. Objective: We test whether the V-Model's build and verify pairs can measure verification evidence in pull requests and support comparisons between agent-authored and human-authored changes. Method: VeeReview classifies four build and verify pairs using repository signals and a language-model judge. Three pairs use model judgements constrained by deterministic signals, and a rule over the diff and repository tree decides Module Design-Unit Test. We evaluated VeeReview against a 25-pull request reference set labelled by two raters and applied it to 1,454 matched pairs of agent and human pull requests from 741 repositories. Results: VeeReview assigned lower build-only rates to agent-authored pull requests on all four pairs, contrary to the preregistered hypothesis (mixed-effects odds ratios 0.52 to 0.86). Architecture-Integration was not significant. Standardization for linked issues, shipped tests and size reduced matched-rate differences by 34% to 60%, and the rule-decided pair's standardized interval included zero. The instrument did not meet its preregistered calibration criterion: agreement with adjudicated labels was 4% to 60% against a required 80%, and inter-rater agreement was weak (kappa = 0.154). Conclusions: The rule-decided pair shows that a process measure judged by a language model partly reflects how a pull request is presented rather than the verification work behind it. We report the cohort differences as observations made with this instrument, and we argue that such measures need a mechanically decided component and a validated human reference before they can support comparisons of verification practice.
evidence_items.title: VeeReview: Measuring Build-Verify Pairs in Agent-Authored Pull Requests from a V-Model Perspective

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
evidence_items.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

evidence_items.summary: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .
evidence_items.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

evidence_items.summary: Automated radiology report generation for multi-sequence brain MRI holds strong promise for alleviating radiologists' workload, yet it remains a demanding problem: brain MRI studies are inherently volumetric, each pulse sequence carries complementary diagnostic information, and annotated data are critically scarce for low-resource clinical languages. Existing brain MRI-report resources are still dominated by English reports, translated clinical text, or datasets adapted from task-specific imaging benchmarks, leaving routine low-resource clinical reporting and heterogeneous multi-sequence MRI protocols insufficiently represented. To bridge this gap, we introduce ViBMR, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multi-sequence brain MRI dataset paired with routine Vietnamese clinical reports, comprising 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series across T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences. Building on ViBMR, we establish a comprehensive evaluation setup for brain MRI report generation, covering representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies. The results provide key insights into dataset characteristics and model behavior, while demonstrating the necessity of native low-resource clinical datasets for reliable Vietnamese-origin brain MRI report generation. Our dataset and baseline models will be released for non-commercial research.
evidence_items.title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation

evidence_items.summary: Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes.

evidence_items.summary: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.
evidence_items.title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

evidence_items.summary: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions

evidence_items.summary: Through a tangle of real-world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. Across nine frontier LLMs, solving and authoring prove to be distinct skills: the strongest solvers are not the strongest authors, while smaller models learn more from how others played and write the hardest environments and the most useful hints. Beyond the scores, the pairwise interactions form a microcosm of how models affect one another. Head-to-head outcomes are transitive and so yield a stable ranking; independent authors converge on the same designs; and in a reinforcement-learning study with Qwen3.8-27B, the learner's hint lift on an author's environments tracks how much training on those environments improves it on held-out reasoning and agentic benchmarks, whether the environments are its own or another model's. Each of these patterns has a counterpart in how models shape one another outside the duel. By staging these interactions under controlled conditions, Environment Duels offers a window onto how LLMs teach, challenge and learn from one another. Code is available at https://github.com/LLM-Duels/EnvDuels.
evidence_items.title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill. To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).
evidence_items.title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation

evidence_items.summary: This paper describes our submission to the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. We adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA using organiser-provided data, EuroAlpaca, a multilingual instruction dataset created through task-preserving localisation, and CrossEuroAlpaca, a cross-lingual augmentation that assigns different source and target languages to instructions, contexts and responses. Our system targets open-ended question answering (QA-OEG) in ten shared-task languages represented in the auxiliary data. Under matched decoding, adaptation improves the mean Gemma-4 judge score on target-language QA-OEG by 7.8% relative to the base model. On an additional evaluation using the Aya Evaluation Suite across all shared-task languages, it yields relative gains of 41.5% in macro-averaged ROUGE-L and 2.9% in BERTScore-F1, with larger improvements in target languages. However, these gains are task- and language-specific. Gemma-4 scores improve for QA-OEG and summarisation in the target languages but decline for context-grounded QA there and across all three tasks in the non-target languages.
evidence_items.title: Task-Preserving Multilingual Instruction Tuning for Open-Ended QA in WMT 2026 MIST

evidence_items.summary: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.
evidence_items.title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents, yet it remains unclear how their foundational capabilities translate into agentic capabilities. End-to-end scores leave unresolved whether low benchmark capability or weak deployment drives a failure, limiting actionable diagnosis. We bridge foundational and agentic capabilities through an operation-level measurement framework. We represent each model with a foundational profile derived from capability benchmarks and an operation profile derived from interaction trajectories, and define capability realization gaps as deviations of observed operation performance from predictions based on foundational capabilities. Experiments on fifteen model services in $\tau^2$-Bench show that foundational profiles only partially predict agentic operations. Models with comparable profiles can differ substantially in execution, and these gaps remain consistent across task subsets. Operation profiles add information and substantially improve task-score prediction. The framework locates execution departures at the operation level to inform model development and agent evaluation. We will release our code and analysis artifacts.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Foundational and Agentic Capabilities of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
evidence_items.title: Melange: A Synthetic Visual Bias Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.
evidence_items.title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models

evidence_items.summary: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.
evidence_items.title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models

evidence_items.summary: The Gabriel graph is a proximity graph widely used in computational geometry and geometric machine learning, underlying large-margin classifiers and, as we show in this work, density-aware clustering methods. Its construction, however, has cubic time complexity $O(N^3)$ in the naive formulation, which severely limits its use on datasets beyond a few thousand samples. This paper presents a set of GPU parallelization strategies, implemented in CUDA, that make Gabriel graph construction practical at scale. We introduce (i) an implicit closed-form mapping from a linear thread index to the corresponding vertex pair $(i,j)$, which removes the need for an explicit $O(N^2)$ adjacency structure and lets every thread locate its pair in constant time and constant memory; (ii) a two-pass, bitmask-based, atomically-compacted edge-list construction that produces a dense edge array proportional only to the number of edges actually found; and (iii) a thread-coarsening strategy in which each thread evaluates several candidate pairs, trading launch and scheduling overhead against load balance. We evaluate these strategies on the acceleration of a Gabriel-graph-based large-margin classifier (NN-clas) and on a novel Gabriel-graph clustering algorithm that identifies connected components on a residual graph and performs GPU-parallel Union-Find with hierarchical edge-based merging. On 14 public benchmark datasets, the GPU implementation reduces Gabriel graph construction time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude relative to a sequential CPU baseline (up to 8484x), without loss of classification accuracy, and the proposed clustering method is statistically competitive with DBSCAN on the topological validity index Dunn while eliminating the need for an explicit density radius parameter.
evidence_items.title: GPU-Accelerated Construction of the Gabriel Graph: Parallelization Strategies and Applications to Large-Margin Classification and Graph-Based Clustering

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents operate in persistent collaborative environments involving multiple users, communities, memories, files, and tools. Community boundaries may remain fixed or evolve with changes in membership, roles, composition, and relationships. Agents must complete legitimate tasks and prevent unauthorized disclosure of protected information. Existing evaluations do not fully examine these risks in agent systems. We introduce \textbf{CoSec}, an executable benchmark for evaluating privacy and authorization enforcement in LLM agent systems operating within and across communities. CoSec contains 208 canonical scenarios spanning fixed and evolving boundaries, protected information belonging to the agent owner or other participants, and attacks through dialogue, environmental content, persistent memory, and composed workflows. CoSec executes complete agent systems with persistent sessions, memory, files and tools. It verifies information flows against the active authorization state using execution traces and artifacts. Across harness and model configurations, agents frequently complete benign tasks but violate privacy and authorization boundaries. Privacy behavior varies across harnesses, attack surfaces, and community states, revealing how memory, files, tools, and workflows can carry protected information beyond its authorized scope. These findings show that task utility does not imply privacy or authorization compliance and that authorization in community settings remains an unresolved security challenge for persistent LLM agents.
evidence_items.title: CoSec: Benchmarking Agent Security in Communities

evidence_items.summary: Caregivers seeking AI-mediated support express complex needs---information-seeking, emotional validation, and distress cues---that warrant careful evaluation of response safety and appropriateness. Existing AI evaluation frameworks, primarily focused on general risks (toxicity, hallucinations, policy violations, etc), may not adequately capture the nuanced risks of LLM-responses in caregiving-contexts. We introduce RubRIX (Rubric-based Risk Index), a theory-driven, clinician-validated framework for evaluating risks in LLM caregiving responses. Grounded in the Elements of an Ethic of Care, RubRIX operationalizes five empirically-derived risk dimensions: Inattention, Bias & Stigma, Information Inaccuracy, Uncritical Affirmation, and Epistemic Arrogance. We evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on over 20,000 caregiver queries from Reddit and ALZConnected. Rubric-guided refinement consistently reduced risk-components by 45-98% after one iteration across models. This work contributes a methodological approach for developing domain-sensitive, user-centered evaluation frameworks for high-burden contexts. Our findings highlight the importance of domain-sensitive, interactional risk evaluation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in caregiving support contexts. We release benchmark datasets to enable future research on contextual risk evaluation in AI-mediated support.
evidence_items.title: RubRIX: Rubric-Driven Risk Mitigation in Caregiver-AI Interactions

evidence_items.summary: Deploying LLMs for financial information retrieval demands accuracy, cost efficiency, and reproducibility, yet most approaches require expensive fine-tuning. PRISM is a training-free framework that composes three deployable modules (prompt engineering, in-context learning, and a candidate refinement module) with a boundary-condition study of multi-agent coordination for financial document retrieval. On FiQA-2018, stacked reranking and $k$-reciprocal encoding raise Recall@100 from 0.7783 to 0.8326. On FinAgentBench, a Cohere-refined top-50 pool yields a higher observed end-to-end NDCG@5, below this evaluation's minimum detectable effect, while cutting per-query cost by about 35%. Added complexity does not always pay off: $k$-reciprocal encoding stops helping once the upstream stage is already high-recall, and multi-agent coordination is not a default for fine-grained chunk ranking. Matched pairs that hold prompt, model, and exemplars fixed lose 0.0702 and 0.0681 combined NDCG@5 to their single-path controls, and the whole gap sits at the chunk stage. We release an expert-annotated FinAgentBench evaluation set, together with a label-robustness sweep over 16 alternative ground-truth constructions, restoring a reproducible evaluation path after the original evaluator went offline. Without fine-tuning, PRISM placed third on the official FinAgentBench private leaderboard (leaderboard basis, NDCG@5 0.71181), reaches NDCG@10 0.6197 on FiQA-2018, and 98% accuracy on FinanceBench. We report per-query latency, token, and dollar accounting across roughly 40 configurations, present the quality-cost-latency Pareto frontier, and introduce FACET, a transparent SLA-specific scalarization for choosing among non-dominated configurations. Code and dataset are released at https://bit.ly/prism-ailens.
evidence_items.title: PRISM: Prompt-Refined In-Context System Modelling for Financial Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types. Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector. We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target. AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers. It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus. Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings. A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.
evidence_items.title: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.
evidence_items.title: CAPSafe: A Benchmark for Contextual Action and Plan Safety Reasoning in Embodied Agents

evidence_items.summary: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which adversarial instructions are embedded in external data processed by a language model, pose a significant threat to the integrity of deployed LLM agents. Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) is a recently proposed white-box detection method that identifies prompt injection attacks by monitoring how a model's attention is distributed between user task tokens and data tokens, claiming dataset-agnostic detection via a scalar focus score threshold. In this paper, we provide the first evaluation of Attention Tracker in a realistic agentic IPI setting using the AgentDojo benchmark, finding that the dataset agnosticism claim does not hold. We find that in agentic environments, long structured tool outputs subvert the fundamental assumptions Attention Tracker makes about attention that the method depends on and produces near-chance detection on AgentDojo across most model families. We propose AttnDA, an extension replacing the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over the per-head focus score vector, and evaluate both methods in a cross-dataset setting spanning four benchmarks. AttnDA improves detection performance across agentic and tool-integrated benchmarks, though transfer to AgentDojo remains challenging regardless of classifier choice. A covariance ablation further shows that removing inter-head correlation structure substantially contributes to performance, with complex covariance assumptions causing significant degradation on cross-domain data. These results indicate that the attentional distraction signal underlying focus-score-based detection does not transfer reliably to agentic environments, and that learned linear classifiers over head-level attention features offer improved detection performance, provided training data from the target deployment domain is available.
evidence_items.title: Attention-based Classification for Indirect Prompt Injection

evidence_items.summary: Public benchmarks drive research on vision-based safety monitoring, and the Safety Helmet Wearing Dataset (SHWD) has become the de facto standard for helmet-wearing detection. This paper reports a systematic near-duplicate audit of SHWD and measures how the contamination it uncovers affects the accuracy reported on the benchmark. A two-stage matching procedure—64-bit perceptual hashing with complementary thumbnail-correlation verification—shows that 2288 of 7581 images (30.2%) belong to 193 near-duplicate clusters, the largest containing 802 frames from one fixed camera, and that 421 of the 1517 official test images (27.8%; 22–29% across matching thresholds) have a near-duplicate counterpart in the training split, and a blind manual rating of 350 pairs finds that 100% of accepted pairs are frames of the same fixed camera (28% strict near-duplicates). Controlled experiments with YOLOv8n, three seeds each, quantify the consequence. With the test data fixed, removing the 1534 contaminating training images lowers mAP@0.5 on the contaminated test subset by 4.4 points, and a size-matched random control shows that the difference is not a data-volume effect; on the full official test set the inflation is 1.92 points relative to the deduplicated model and 1.35 points relative to the control. A cluster-disjoint experiment that holds the domain composition of the training set fixed shows that frames from the same cameras and sessions as the test frames add a further 0.6 points on those frames, so that most of the gap under the official split reflects the classroom imagery that the contaminating images supply rather than recognition of specific frames. Tracing images to their source shows that 97.1% of the test images imported from the SCUT-HEAD classroom-video dataset are contaminated, against 3.0–5.5% of the genuine helmet imagery, and that the effect is confined to the imported subset (+8.1 points there, −0.4 on helmet imagery).
evidence_items.title: Near-Duplicate Contamination in a Widely Used Safety Helmet Detection Benchmark: Audit, Controlled Experiments, and a Duplicate-Aware Evaluation Split

evidence_items.summary: The reliability of quadcopters is becoming increasingly important. However, the field of quadcopter fault diagnosis lacks a standardized, reproducible benchmark for fair and comprehensive algorithm evaluation. To address this gap, this paper presents RflyBench-FD, a standardized, open benchmark for quadcopter fault diagnosis built upon the RflyMAD dataset, publicly accessible at https://www.rflybench.com/competitions/5/ . RflyBench-FD establishes a complete evaluation framework that covers eight representative fault types and provides standardized simulation/real dual-domain splits, a well-defined task formulated as eight parallel classification sub-tasks, publicly released scoring scripts, and a multi-dimensional metric system (accuracy, F1-score, and robustness under Gaussian noise at 8/4/2 dB SNR and physically motivated sensor degradations) aggregated into a weighted composite score whose ranking stability is verified by a sensitivity analysis. To validate the benchmark, we evaluate twelve baselines spanning classical machine learning, temporal deep learning, domain adaptation, transfer learning, and training-mode ablations, complemented by noise tests, physically motivated sensor-degradation tests, leakage-oriented checks, and paired significance tests; the results show that the benchmark produces stable and discriminative rankings across method families. The platform further supports daily submissions, a governed real-time leaderboard with anti-overfitting safeguards, full result traceability, and an LLMassisted analysis report. By providing a fair, reproducible, and insight-rich evaluation infrastructure, RflyBench-FD aims to support the development and real-world deployment of robust fault diagnosis solutions for autonomous quadcopters.
evidence_items.title: RflyBench-FD: The Benchmark for Quadcopter Fault Diagnosis

evidence_items.summary: SplitShiftLab v0.1.1 is an open-source Python research software package designed to support reproducible, auditable, and constraint-aware machine-learning data partitioning. The software supports random, group-based, temporal, and group-temporal splitting protocols. Its group-split feasibility preflight evaluates specified group-cardinality, minimum partition-size, and per-class support constraints, reporting feasible, infeasible, or undetermined outcomes as appropriate. It also provides machine-readable audit information, dataset fingerprints, and exploratory distribution-shift diagnostics. This reproducibility release includes independent feasibility verification using two real-world datasets. For UCI HAR, exhaustive analysis of 54,264 group allocations identified a maximum feasible minimum class support of 322 under the evaluated protocol. For MHEALTH, exhaustive analysis of 120 group allocations established a maximum feasible minimum class support of 3,174. The release also provides paired internal solver benchmarks, reproducible scikit-learn baseline experiments, dataset provenance metadata, independent verification scripts, and supporting documentation. The software passed 52 automated tests in the documented testing environments. The reported experimental findings apply to the specified datasets and constraints. They do not establish universal solver correctness, comprehensive semantic leakage prevention, superior predictive performance, or general superiority over alternative splitting tools. Raw benchmark datasets are not redistributed. Researchers should obtain the original datasets from their official sources and follow the preparation instructions in the repository. evidence_items.summary: Debate transcripts, drafted constitutions, extracted clauses and votes from 40 runs of a multi-agent large language model (LLM) experiment, accompanying the paper "Can AI agents make law? Evaluating AI legal relevance and creativity" (Ricaud & Galushko; preprint arXiv:2610.24661, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24661). In each run, a single LLM plays a panel of agents with distinct personas (Idealist, Pragmatist, Libertarian, Communitarian, Global Digital Rights Expert, a neutral Secretary and, in half the runs, an authoritarian Sovereign Architect). Through a five-phase protocol (independent proposals, blind reactions, final arguments, drafting, line-by-line vote), the agents draft a Bill of Rights for a community of AI agents. Six LLM families (DeepSeek V3.2, GPT-OSS-120B, Elephant Alpha, GLM-4.5-Air, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Mistral Small 3.2) were run in a 2 × 2 design: with or without the authoritarian agent, and with a virtual world that humans can or cannot access. The deposit contains: - every prompt and persona definition, the model list and a run inventory; - the full output of every run (proposals, reactions, arguments, drafted constitution, votes); - the 627 clauses extracted from the 40 drafted constitutions, coded into 11 themes and 50   subcategories, with a codebook; - the individual Phase 5 votes, recounted from the agents' vote files. The README describes the files and known data issues.
evidence_items.title: Multi-agent LLM constitutional assemblies: dataset for "Can AI agents make law?"

evidence_items.summary: The rapid evolution of cyber threats demands intelligent, adaptive  detection mechanisms beyond traditional rule-based systems. This paper reviews  artificial intelligence (AI) methods -- including deep learning (DL), transformer-based  architectures, federated learning (FL), and explainable AI (XAI) - applied to network  intrusion detection systems (IDS) between 2021 and 2026. Seven state-of-the-art  models are evaluated across modern benchmark datasets (CIC-IoT2023, BoT-IoT,  TON IoT, UNSW-NB15), achieving detection accuracies between 98.70% and  99.40% with False Alarm Rates (FAR) as low as 0.60%. Six core accuracy improvement strategies are systematically analyzed: feature selection, data  augmentation, attention mechanisms, federated training, explainability integration, and  hyperparameter optimization. The paper highlights that no single technique is  sufficient -- hybrid architectures combining temporal modeling, privacy-preserving  distributed training, and human-interpretable explanations consistently deliver the  highest real-world performance. The study concludes with open challenges including  adversarial robustness, regulatory compliance under the EU AI Act, and dataset  representativeness.
evidence_items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE METHODS FOR DETECTING ATTACKS  AND THE WAYS OF IMPROVING DETECTION ACCURACY

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS's pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question-answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22%-33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4%-22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.
evidence_items.title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with Aid of Operations Research Program

evidence_items.summary: Space-based missions such as CoRoT, , and TESS have revolutionised asteroseismology and strengthened its synergies with exoplanet science. With PLATO and ARIEL on the horizon, these synergies will play an even more central role. Kepler We revisit the characterisation of the nearby K dwarf HD 219134 using advanced seismic diagnostics. Our goals are to investigate the reported tension between asteroseismic and interferometric radii, update the fundamental parameters of the star, refine the properties of its planetary system, and investigate the coupled rotational, magnetic, and star–planet evolution of the system, including the atmospheric mass‑loss histories of its planets. The stellar characterisation is based on detailed asteroseismic forward modelling complemented by seismic inversions to quantify systematic uncertainties associated with non‑seismic constraints, assess the compatibility of radius measurements, and evaluate the impact of surface modelling on seismic inferences. The revised stellar properties were used as inputs for rotational evolution investigations, stellar wind modelling, and high‑energy irradiation histories. Seismic inversions rule out the most recent interferometric radius determination, whereas asteroseismic and spectroscopic results are compatible with the previous interferometric measurement from 2019. We derive revised stellar mass, radius, and age of 0.779 ± 0.015 ± 0.006 , M ⊙, 0.753 ± 0.005 ± 0.002 , R ⊙, and 8.92 ± 0.89 ± 0.19 Gyr, respectively. The quoted systematic uncertainties reflect contributions from the non-seismic observational constraints only. Literature values for combined uncertainties arising from physical inputs and surface-effect prescriptions are 0.007M ⊙, 0.002R ⊙, and 0.81 Gyr, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Detailed study of HD 219134: A benchmark K dwarf with a compact planetary system

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) based on Neuroevolution Potential (NEP) models were developed for the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate ([Emim][Ac]) using first-principles reference data generated with four density functionals: PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, optB88-vdW, and SCAN+rVV10. Using a unified training protocol, the resulting NEP models were systematically benchmarked against structural, thermophysical, transport, and hydrogen-bond-network properties, including radial distribution functions (RDFs), coordination numbers, neutron total scattering profiles, density, viscosity, ionic conductivity, and thermal conductivity. Spearman correlation analysis and weighted composite scoring were further used to establish a property-oriented evaluation framework for MLFF assessment and selection. The results reveal a pronounced dependence of NEP performance on the density functional used to generate the reference data. Although all four models reproduce the dominant local structural features of [Emim][Ac], appreciable differences emerge in medium-range structural ordering and transport properties. The PBE-D3-based NEP provides the most accurate overall description of structural properties, whereas the optB88-vdW-based NEP yields the closest agreement with experimental transport properties, particularly viscosity and ionic conductivity. Analysis of the hydrogen-bond network further reveals systematic relationships among hydrogen-bond populations, residence times, free-ion fractions, and ion transport. These results demonstrate that, for [Emim][Ac], the exchange–correlation functional used for reference-data generation influences the physical fidelity and property-specific performance of the resulting NEP models.
evidence_items.title:
Performance of
