Liquid [Emim][Ac]: A Systematic Benchmark of Four Density Functionals

evidence_items.summary: Hospital patient services (registration and appointment scheduling) often face fragmented systems, long handling times, and data-entry errors, while patients expect instant 24/7 digital interactions. This study uses Design Science Research to develop a prescriptive five-phase framework for CRM-integrated agentic AI, whose novelty lies in combining bounded transactional agency, middleware-mediated access to CRM/SIMRS tools, and staged governance. Its design assumptions are evaluated through a controlled proof of concept (PoC). The PoC implements an end-to-end transactional conversational workflow (WhatsApp/web chat) in which an LLM-based agent uses API middleware to call tools on a CRM/SIMRS sandbox, avoiding direct database access. The artefact structures are: preparation and alignment; analysis and detailed design; implementation and controlled testing; pilot and evaluation; and scaling and institutionalization, supported by governance mechanisms (clinical “green/red” boundaries, audit logging, and human-in-the-loop supervision). Empirical evaluation applied black-box testing across 15 positive and negative scenarios comprising 285 executions. Of these, 246 met the predefined scenario criteria, and 39 failed, yielding an overall controlled-scenario success rate of 86.32%. A separate message-level latency log contained 292 message-response pairs across 58 recorded conversation groups; median response time was 9 s (IQR 4–19 s), with 88.70% of responses returned in under 30 s and 97.26% in under 60 s. Selected persisted CRM records were additionally checked through authorized visual inspection, with no discrepancies observed. These findings support technical feasibility under controlled PoC conditions while identifying patient-centred evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, production load testing, economic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-site validation as requirements for broader deployment.
evidence_items.title: A Prescriptive Design Framework for CRM-Integrated Agentic AI in Hospital Patient Services: Design Science Development and Empirical Proof-of-Concept Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Municipalities increasingly delegate healthcare, social assistance, utilities, transit, and identity verification to semi-autonomous systems. Real-world failures, including Australia's Robodebt scheme and the Dutch childcare benefits scandal, show that automated administration can strip life-sustaining services from large populations whose formal entitlements never changed. Existing governance responses remain fragmented across sectoral silos, with none enforcing a computationally verified constraint at the individual level across multiple domains concurrently. We present \HSC{}, a multi-agent framework that operationalizes essential human functioning as a non-compensatory constraint on automated municipal allocation. The architecture establishes a per-resident capability floor over ten normalized dimensions, identifying deprivation via an Alkire--Foster dual cutoff so that surplus in one domain cannot offset deficits in another. A Human Sovereignty Gate evaluates candidate allocations by measured worst-case capability impact and reversibility, recording commitments in an auditable ledger for which we prove that no admissible sequence of automated decisions can cross the floor. A Basic Needs Assurance Engine coordinates sector agents over a cyclic dependency graph to block cross-sector cascades, backed by an offline resilience reserve during platform outages. We derive a feasibility bound showing that individual risk tolerance cannot be legislated to zero, and specify an agent-based evaluation protocol for 250{,}000 synthetic residents across six disruption scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Human Sovereignty in the Agentic City: Enforcing Multi-Sector Capability Floors Against Automated Deprivation

evidence_items.summary: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.
evidence_items.title: VoxProg: 3D Spatial Reasoning through Voxel Programming

evidence_items.summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
evidence_items.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate quantum programs, but reliable evaluation remains difficult because benchmarks differ in task composition, scoring, and failure handling. We evaluate 15 hosted frontier, open-weight, quantum-specialized, and retrieval-augmented models on five quantum code-generation suites (530 tasks), plus 10 models on our new QuantumBenchEval (QBE) benchmark (96 tasks across six topics). We report bootstrap confidence intervals, multiplicity-adjusted paired comparisons, and audits of output validity and evaluator behavior. QiskitHumanEval-Standard approaches saturation (98.7% pass@1), while its Hard variant retains headroom (63.8%). None of the five top-two comparisons across primary suites remains significant after multiple-comparison correction. Evaluator design substantially changes scores: removing checks for unspecified quantities raises GPT-6 Astra's QBE pass@1 from 0% to 94.1% (T1) and from 1.2% to 92.9% (T6), without changing model outputs. We identify 17 QuanBench-117 tasks with shared failures linked to benchmark-owned imports. Controlled probes also reveal unexecuted unit tests, leakage of canonical functions into candidate execution, and reference imports that block otherwise valid candidates. These defects can produce both false failures and false passes, so historical QuanBench results require revalidation under an isolated evaluator. Overall, leaderboard scores alone do not adequately characterize progress in quantum code generation. We release our harness, per-sample results, and audit artifacts and recommend validating evaluators, isolating candidate code, and reporting uncertainty and output validity.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking the Quantum Leap: Auditing LLM Evaluation for Quantum Code Generation

evidence_items.summary: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $\rho \approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($\rho \approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.
evidence_items.title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Dataset Description This dataset provides reference interpretation records and validation results for a remote-sensing assessment of agricultural land detection in Wadi Hadhramaut, Yemen, for the year 2021. The archive includes: Reference classifications for 250 sampled cells. Repeat interpretation records for 51 cells, including the predefined QA50 sample and one additional low-confidence cell. Researcher-approved adjudication records for 14 cases. A technically consolidated 250-cell reference dataset. Sampling information, evaluation weights, and 1,500 prediction records from six candidate classification rules. Recomputed accuracy statistics and supporting documentation for reproducibility. The evaluation demonstrates that high overall classification accuracy (approximately 95.46%) can coexist with low agricultural detection sensitivity (approximately 15.26%), highlighting the limitations of overall accuracy when agricultural areas are rare. Methodological limitations: The reference dataset underwent retrospective technical consolidation. Independent second-interpreter identity was not documented, and the dataset should not be described as independently verified field ground truth. The dataset is intended to support scientific transparency, methodological evaluation, and further research on agricultural remote sensing in hyper-arid environments.

evidence_items.summary: Poster of the paper titled "LinguaMark: Do Multimodal Models Speak Fairly? A Benchmark-Based Evaluation" presented at LLM-Eval Workshop NeurIPS 2025. Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) are typically trained on vast corpora of image-text data but are often limited in linguistic coverage, leading to biased and unfair outputs across languages. While prior work has explored multimodal evaluation, less emphasis has been placed on assessing multilingual capabilities. In this work, we introduce LinguaMark, a benchmark designed to evaluate state-of-the-art LMMs on a multilingual Visual Question Answering (VQA) task. Our dataset comprises 6,875 image-text pairs spanning 11 languages and five social attributes. We evaluate models using three key metrics: Bias, Answer Relevancy, and Faithfulness. Our findings reveal that closed-source models generally achieve the highest overall performance. Both closed-source (GPT-4o and Gemini2.5) and open-source models (Gemma3, Qwen2.5) perform competitively across social attributes, and Qwen2.5 demonstrates strong generalization across multiple languages. We release our benchmark and evaluation code to encourage reproducibility and further research.
evidence_items.title: LinguaMark: Do Multimodal Models Speak Fairly? A Benchmark-Based Evaluation - LLM-Eval Workshop NeurIPS 2025

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Benchmarking has been the cornerstone of progress in computer vision, natural language processing, and the broader deep learning domain, driving algorithmic innovation through standardized datasets and reproducible evaluation protocols. The growing availability of large-scale Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) datasets has opened new opportunities for applying machine learning to aerodynamic and engineering design. Yet, despite this progress, large-scale standardized benchmarks remain limited for high-resolution three-dimensional automotive aerodynamics, making it difficult to evaluate and compare models systematically. In this work, we introduce CarBench, a large-scale standardized benchmark dedicated to high-resolution 3D automotive aerodynamics, and perform a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art models on DrivAerNet++, the largest public dataset for automotive aerodynamics, containing over 8,000 high-fidelity car simulations. We assess eleven representative model configurations spanning multiple modeling paradigms: classical neural operator methods (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), geometric deep learning approaches (PointNet, RegDGCNN, PointMAE, PointTransformer), transformer-based neural solvers (Transolver, Transolver++, AB-UPT), and implicit field networks leveraging triplane representations (TripNet). Beyond standard interpolation tasks, we perform cross-category experiments in which representative transformer-based solvers trained on a single car archetype are evaluated on unseen categories to probe generalization. Our analysis covers predictive accuracy, pressure-field fidelity relative to the CFD reference, computational efficiency, and statistical uncertainty in evaluation metrics, providing a unified comparison across modeling families and quantifying the robustness of performance estimates under shifts in test geometry distributions.
evidence_items.title: CarBench: A comprehensive benchmark for neural surrogates on high-fidelity 3D car aerodynamics

organizations: Department of Engineering Technology, Fairmont State University
Department of Mechanical Engineering, Auburn University
evidence_items.summary: Hydrogels are highly tunable soft materials, but their analysis is challenging because researchers have to coordinate dataset cleaning, schema interpretation, predictive modeling, conditional generation, evaluation, and reporting through independent task-specific scripts. Here, we present Agentic Hydrogel, a lightweight, human-in-the-loop (HITL) agentic framework for hydrogel data analysis and conditional recipe generation. The system combines planning, analysis, generation, and reporting modules while retaining human control over dataset selection, target assignment, and scientific interpretation. Deterministic modules perform preprocessing, model training, evaluation, postprocessing, and artifact generation, whereas an optional large language model (LLM) is restricted to summarization and does not control scientific decisions. The framework is demonstrated using a polyacrylamide (PAA) hydrogel rheology dataset and a granular hydrogel dataset where it successfully executes regression, classification, and conditional hydrogel recipe generation tasks. The results establish the ability of the framework to execute and produce documentation for machine learning (ML) workflows. Agentic Hydrogel is therefore presented as a reproducible workflow system rather than a new predictive algorithm or a replacement for experimental validation.
evidence_items.title: Agentic hydrogel: a human-in-the-loop computational workflow for hydrogel analysis and conditional candidate generation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive emergent reasoning capabilities, yet they remain constrained by fixed model parameters and finite context windows. Even when augmented with static retrieval, they can produce statements that are unsupported by, or even contradictory to, retrieved evidence. This leads to hallucinations, difficulty incorporating up-to-date information, and failures to correctly interpret or reconcile sources. Recent work addresses these limitations by tightly coupling step-by-step reasoning with interactive search, treating retrieval as an action within an iterative agentic loop rather than a one-shot preprocessing step. This study reviews frameworks that implement such reasoning-search loops by interleaving planning, querying, retrieval, integration, verification, and stopping. We analyze these systems through four architectural axes: retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness. We separately treat the learning signal as a cross-cutting dimension because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can instantiate the same architecture while producing materially different search, stopping, and grounding behavior. We further distinguish benchmark difficulty from RSA-loop demand and synthesize controlled within-study ablations and quality-cost deltas, avoiding invalid pooling across heterogeneous model backbones, retrievers, corpora, and evaluation protocols. Our goal is to clarify the landscape of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs and outline a unified perspective on the design choices shaping future research.
evidence_items.title: Reasoning-Search-Augmented LLMs: An Operational Taxonomy, Benchmark Analysis and Controlled Evidence Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. evidence_items.summary: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
evidence_items.title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.
evidence_items.title: Omnilingual-MsASR: Benchmarking Multimodal, Multilingual, Long-Form Multi-Speaker ASR of Omni Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.
evidence_items.title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning (ML) for analog IC design is constrained by limited open data and the absence of standardized evaluation: results reported in different papers are typically obtained on bespoke, often closed, datasets and with ad-hoc metrics, leaving comparisons across methods unreliable. We address both gaps with a large opensource dataset and a suite of standardized benchmarks. The dataset contains more than 100 operational amplifier (opamp) topologies (1-, 2-, and 3-stage) in the SkyWater130 PDK, each shipped with structural and functional annotations, topology-specific sizing constraints (symmetry and sizing rules), an Ngspice testbench, and a multi-objective NSGA-II sizing run producing around 103 Pareto-optimal and 106 intermediate sizing-performance pairs per topology. On top of this data we define six benchmark tasks with precise protocols: inverse sizing, topology selection, sub-circuit classification, structural circuit generation, Pareto-membership prediction, and multi-objective optimization. Thus, the data presented here constitutes the most comprehensive dataset for ML development in over four decades of analog IC design automation. The dataset, ground-truth annotations, and reference implementations of the metric-defining routines are released under an open license, enabling reproducible and directly comparable evaluation across heterogeneous analog design automation methods.
evidence_items.title: LOADBench: A Large Open Analog Dataset and Benchmark for Machine Learning in IC Design

evidence_items.summary: Agent evaluation harnesses are software: they run a test suite, drive a test input generator, and decide outcomes with a test oracle. We audit them for defects a score table cannot show. First, a systematic oracle-integrity auditing approach - five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls - is measured by injecting seven oracle defect classes across two task domains and a synthetic domain. Every class is detected, and on the 57 separable variant-target combinations it detects 54; the repaired oracle yields no false positive. On a widely used agent benchmark, it exposes a reward function that resets the database to build a ground-truth hash and never restores it, so a harness scoring afterwards reads the reference solution's state: recorded labels report 4,194 database passes over 4,320 episodes, replay gives 2,883, and success falls from 94.3% to 65.5%. The correction is not a uniform offset; it removes 24 to 34 points from each agent and changes which agent this matrix measures as strongest. Second, more weakly, localising the apparatus is a property of the measurement: a 3,240-episode ablation associates the three documents with lower collapse in the tested configuration, without ordering them, and a second task domain reverses the language effect. Third, the method did not transfer to a second, independently implemented benchmark; we name the contract required. A replication package recomputes every analysis offline with no model calls.
evidence_items.title: When Agent Evaluation Becomes Unreliable: An Empirical Study of Oracle Failures and Configuration-Dependent Measurement in an LLM Agent Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown increasing potential for medical image understanding, yet their capabilities in ophthalmic imaging remain insufficiently characterized. Existing ophthalmic datasets are typically designed for individual diseases or specialized tasks, making it difficult to systematically evaluate whether VLMs can move beyond disease recognition toward comparative reasoning and fine-grained spatial grounding. We introduce EyeVQA, a unified visual question answering benchmark for comprehensive evaluation of ophthalmic VLMs. EyeVQA is constructed from 21 available ophthalmic datasets and contains 20,000 question-answer pairs spanning six disease groups and seven question types: Single-Choice, Multi-Select, Variable-Select, True-False, Ranking, Point Location, and Bounding Box. Gold answers are deterministically derived from source-provided diagnoses, severity grades, clinical findings, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and anatomical landmarks, enabling reproducible evaluation without relying on model-generated annotations. Notably, 44.5% of the questions require reasoning across multiple images, extending evaluation beyond conventional single-image medical VQA. We benchmark fourteen representative general-purpose, scientific, and medically specialized VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The best-performing model only achieves an overall score of 62.8, while substantial gaps remain in spatial grounding and cross-task generalization. These results highlight the limitations of current VLMs in comprehensive ophthalmic visual understanding and establish EyeVQA as a diagnostic benchmark for developing more reliable and spatially grounded ophthalmic multimodal models. The project page is available at https://github.com/PKUTHM/EyeVQA.
evidence_items.title: EyeVQA: Benchmarking Ophthalmic Vision-Language Models from Recognition to Spatial Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Medical concept extraction from electronic health records underpins many downstream applications, yet remains challenging because medically meaningful concepts are frequently implied rather than explicitly stated in medical narratives. Existing benchmarks with human-annotated evidence spans underscore the importance of grounding extracted concepts in medical text. However, they predominantly focus on explicitly stated concepts instead of implicit concepts. We present MedicalBench, a benchmark for medical concept extraction with evidence grounding that evaluates implicit medical reasoning. MedicalBench formulates medical concept extraction as a verification task over medical note-concept pairs, coupled with sentence-level evidence identification. Built from MIMIC-IV discharge summaries and human-verified ICD-10 codes, the dataset is curated through a multi-stage large language model (LLM) triage pipeline followed by medical annotation and expert review. It deliberately includes implicit positives, semantically confusable negatives, and cases where LLM judgments disagree with medical expert assessments. We define two complementary evaluation tasks: (1) medical concept extraction and (2) sentence-level evidence retrieval, enabling assessment of both correctness and interpretability. Benchmarking state-of-the-art LLMs reveals that performance remains modest, highlighting the difficulty of extracting implicitly expressed concepts. We further show that performance is largely invariant to note length, indicating that MedicalBench isolates reasoning difficulty rather than superficial confounders. MedicalBench provides the first systematic benchmark for implicit, evidence-grounded medical concept extraction, offering a foundation for developing medical language models that can both identify medically relevant concepts and justify their predictions in a transparent and medically faithful manner.
evidence_items.title: MedicalBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Toward Improved Medical Concept Extraction

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the data and Stata code required to reproduce the quantitative results of the impact evaluation of the Café Lumière project, a solar-powered micro-grid and energy-platform initiative implemented by the NGO Electriciens sans Frontière (ESF) and financed by the Agence Française de Développement (AFD) in six villages of the Vakinankaratra and Itasy regions of Madagascar between 2018 and 2021. The evaluation follows a randomized controlled trial (RCT) design at the village level, with twelve comparable localities identified through a common pre-feasibility study and treatment randomly assigned to half of them. Outcomes are measured using two waves of household and individual surveys collected in 2017–2018 and in 2023, complemented by locality-level data. The package is organised into two folders. The Data folder contains three Stata datasets: a panel of adults ( Panel adultes.dta ), a household-level panel ( Panel menages v2.dta ), and an unbalanced panel of children ( UnbalancePanel enfants.dta ). The Scripts folder contains five .do files intended to be run sequentially: household-level analysis ( 1 Reg Households.do ), individual-level analysis ( 2 Reg Individuals.do ), child-level analysis ( 3 Reg Children.do ), robustness checks ( 4 Robustness.do ), and Wild Bootstrap inference for cluster-robust p-values ( 5 Reg WildBootStrap.do ). Regression output is written to a RegTables subfolder. This package is released to support transparency and replication of the published findings on access to basic electricity services, secondary income-generating activities, household wealth, and social outcomes (health, education, public safety) attributable to the Café Lumière intervention. For questions, contact Vincent Nossek ( vincent.nossek@uca.fr ).
evidence_items.title: Replication package — Experimental impact study of the Café Lumière micro-grid project in rural Madagascar

The contract captures the bug if OpenJML verifies it on the fixed version and reports a violation on the buggy one.The package contains the benchmark-builder pipeline (Python; curation, generation, verification with OpenJML and evaluation), the 75 approved Defects4J instances with drafts and rejected candidates, every evaluation run with its prompt, model answer and OpenJML result (four models in the with-buggy variant, two in with-fixed and doc-only, five or three runs each, plus pilot runs), the summaries behind the tables of the thesis, and the scripts that recompute them without API keys. The entry point is 03 Code/benchmark-builder/README.md, which explains the setup, the data formats and how to replicate the results. The package is licensed under the MIT License; the bundled source files of open-source projects and the copied OpenJML specifications keep their own licenses, listed in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.
evidence_items.title: Replication Package: Building a Benchmark for LLM-assisted Formal Verification

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Public leaderboards and pricing catalogues offer complementary but hard-to-combine views of the large language model ecosystem. We analyse three linked public sources: an archived Open LLM Leaderboard v2 sample of 4,565 open-weight evaluation records with complete six-benchmark scores; an 89-snapshot human-preference panel of 279 models (June 2024–August 2025); and 2,685 priced chat endpoints (October 2026). Principal component analysis identifies a dominant common component (74% of benchmark variance), retained by parallel analysis and robust to family deduplication. Benchmark performance rises with parameter count (13.6 points per tenfold) and with submission date at constant size and type (10.5 points per year) under family-clustered inference. A documented change of the default rating on 20 May 2025 shifted all listed scores by about 18 points; within the stable period the preference frontier rose by about 187 points per year relative to a fixed reference set through 17 leaders with median spells of 12 days, top-20 slots concentrated among fewer organisations, and ratings did not drift within models. Among 201 models listed by three or more providers, the median maximum-to-minimum price ratio is 1.38 (1.27 under version-strict identifiers). A hedonic model adjusting for time since first listing attributes multipliers of about 3.1 to one standard deviation of arena score and 0.18 to open-weight status, robust to version-exact matching. Preference ratings and benchmark averages agree strongly for 69 matched models. Temporal mismatch, selective coverage, and related model families preclude causal interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Capability, ranking dynamics, and inference pricing in the large language model ecosystem: evidence from linked public data

evidence_items.summary: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
evidence_items.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence has recently been assessed through generative tasks such as spatially grounded image editing, yet language-guided generation of spatially consistent views from partial multi-view observations remains underexplored. We introduce MindView, a benchmark for generative multi-view spatial intelligence with 1,500 samples from 513 scenes across three indoor datasets. Its seven tasks form two families: geometry-dominant tasks specify changes in camera position and orientation, while semantics-dominant tasks require inferring target viewpoints by grounding referred objects and interpreting spatial relations and reference-frame cues. Evaluation of eleven generators reveals substantial room for improvement on MindView. A paired context analysis further shows that all eleven generators obtain lower overall scores under the expanded context setting. These findings motivate us to investigate whether task-specific supervision can improve target-view generation and whether models can use additional multi-view evidence effectively. We therefore fine-tune BAGEL on the MindView training dataset, improving its overall score by 24.3 points and yielding gains across all seven MindView tasks. Beyond these generation gains, the fine-tuned model also yields higher scores on three spatial-understanding benchmarks without training on their annotations, suggesting that learning to generate spatially grounded views may benefit spatial understanding. To improve evidence utilization under expanded context, we propose MindCue, a training-free spatial evidence selector guided by a target-view hypothesis. MindCue reverses the drop in overall score under expanded context and outperforms the standard-context baseline. Overall, MindView provides a concrete testbed for generative multi-view spatial intelligence.
evidence_items.title: MindView: Benchmarking Generative Multi-View Spatial Intelligence

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is widely used for language model post-training, but its performance depends strongly on the choice of its hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and the reference-policy regularisation parameter $\beta$. To better understand the DPO hyperparameter landscape, we conduct extensive experiments using a dense hyperparameter grid across different model scales from the same family. This allows us to analyse how the optimal DPO hyperparameters evolve with model size and the number of update steps, with intermediate checkpoints providing an inexpensive signal to accelerate the hyperparameter optimisation process. Furthermore, by evaluating our models on both static and dynamic benchmarks, we identify which benchmarks provide the strongest signal for hyperparameter selection. Finally, we investigate how different state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimisation strategies perform in this setting. Our experiments show that the optimal learning rate varies with model size and that hyperparameters are not transferable across training datasets. We also find that validation loss is a poor proxy for hyperparameter optimisation, as hyperparameters that minimize validation loss only weakly correlate with optimal hyperparameters for downstream benchmarks. Therefore, DPO hyperparameters need to be tuned specifically for the target model, dataset, and evaluation objective. We also show that short candidate training runs can substantially reduce the cost of this selection. We release all our training configurations and evaluation results to support reproducible analysis of selection quality and training cost.
evidence_items.title: The Shape of the DPO Hyperparameter Landscape: What to Measure, How It Moves with Scale, and When Not to Transfer It

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning benchmarks act as guideposts for model development and spur the creation of training datasets intended to improve benchmark scores. We introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive. Beyond preserving benign performance, BenchDoor requires benchmark gains that encourage adoption of data that also implants a backdoor. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data, creating an adversarial benchmark, or supplies an independent training dataset while leaving the benchmark unchanged. We formalize five attack scenarios, including training on rewritten test examples and applying similarity-based decontamination. Across multiple-choice Q&A, text classification, and open-ended Q&A with Qwen and Gemma models, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains for all 30 evaluated configurations, with held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10%. Both objectives remain achievable after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%. These findings show how benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that deliver improvements on them.
evidence_items.title: Adversarial Benchmarks and BenchDoor Attacks: Exploiting Benchmark Incentives for Backdoor Attacks

evidence_items.summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous Deep Search and Deep Research Agents capable of executing long-horizon, multi-step tasks, evaluating their reliability becomes increasingly critical. However, existing evaluation paradigms predominantly focus on final task outcomes, leaving a significant gap in understanding the intermediate execution traces, where agents are highly susceptible to various errors. To address this critical gap, we introduce a comprehensive methodology and analytical framework designed specifically to diagnose errors in intermediate workflows. Building upon this framework, we establish a structured taxonomy that categorizes these vulnerabilities into two primary dimensions: System-Level Errors and Task-Level Errors. Through a systematic examination of step-by-step execution traces and agent-environment interactions, we reveal how these underlying errors affect overall performance. Finally, through empirical experiments and systematic analysis of the identified error types, we provide actionable design guidelines, aiming to enhance the robustness, reasoning capabilities, and reliability of Deep Search and Deep Research agents.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking and Error Analysis of Deep Search and Deep Research LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Decision models support routing, guardrails, and output verification in LLM systems. However, item accuracy alone cannot establish whether models make correct decisions across controlled variations or assign reliable confidence to their predictions. We introduce DecisionPivot, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles. Its core track contains 7,800 items from 13 generated task families, organized into contrast groups with computed answers verified by independently implemented solvers. The complementary reference track contains 32,233 items from 35 public test sets, preserving their original evaluation metrics. We evaluate 40 decision models and 14 general models using documented, model-specific protocols, assessing item and contrast-group accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and empirical selective coverage. Our results reveal substantial differences obscured by aggregate scores: two 27B models separated by only 2.6 points on the reference track achieve contrast-group accuracies of 70.1% and 44.2%. Across 2,400 binary contrast pairs, Perplexity Decider correctly ranks the positive member above the negative member in 92.3% of pairs but answers both members correctly in only 74.1%, exposing a gap between probability ordering and decision correctness. Models with similar item accuracy also differ in the reliability of their high-confidence predictions. On a separate 1,296-item subset, GLM-5.3 achieves 93.5\% contrast-group accuracy at a higher reasoning setting, compared with 81.5% at its lowest effort. By linking errors to pivotal details and difficulty levels, DecisionPivot provides fine-grained diagnostics of decision failures that aggregate evaluation alone cannot reveal.
evidence_items.title: DecisionPivot: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Decision Models in LLM Systems

evidence_items.summary: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.
evidence_items.title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing; however, their direct application to food safety remains limited by insufficient domain knowledge, inadequate reasoning over regulatory documents, and the tendency to generate factual hallucinations. To address these challenges, this study proposes FSLLM, a domain-specific LLM designed for food safety applications. A high-quality domain corpus was constructed from diverse sources, including food safety incidents, regulatory documents, inspection reports, and industry-related materials. It initially comprised approximately 150 million tokens, of which 45,024 documents and approximately 121 million tokens were retained after decontamination. Based on the Qwen3-8B foundation model, FSLLM was developed through a two-stage training framework consisting of continual pre-training for domain knowledge adaptation and supervised fine-tuning for task alignment. Furthermore, a comprehensive benchmark covering 10 representative food safety tasks, including named entity recognition, text classification, text generation, factual verification, regulatory compliance analysis, and public health question answering, was established for systematic evaluation. Experimental results show that FSLLM outperforms the base model across multiple food safety tasks. Specifically, FSLLM achieved a Micro-F1 score of 0.5286 in named entity recognition and an accuracy of 85.21% in food safety event classification, demonstrating improvements over the base model. These findings indicate that domain-specific corpus and continual pre-training with fine-tuning enhance LLM expertise and reasoning, offering a viable solution for intelligent food safety supervision and risk analysis.
evidence_items.title: Data Engineering and Large Language Model Construction for the Food Safety Domain

evidence_items.summary: Organisations handling regulated or proprietary source code are frequently prohibited from transmitting it to third-party inference providers, which excludes commercial cloud large language models from their security-analysis pipelines regardless of the accuracy those models achieve. Whether self-hosted open-weight models can substitute for them on ordinary developer hardware has not been established. This study benchmarks five quantised open-weight models, from 1.5 to 8 billion parameters and executed entirely on a consumer laptop graphics processor with eight gigabytes of video memory, on 120 annotated web-application code snippets spanning five weakness categories. Each was evaluated under zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and compared against a rule-based static analyser and previously published cloud-model results on the identical corpus. The strongest local configuration reached an F1-score of 0.900, exceeding the previous-generation cloud flagship and trailing the current one by 4.7 points, while generating a remediation suggestion for every correct detection. The analysis further shows that F1 alone conceals degenerate behaviour: several configurations, including one cloud model, approach the score of a classifier labelling every input as vulnerable, so reporting specificity alongside F1 is proposed as a minimum requirement. Privacy-preserving on-premise vulnerability analysis is thus attainable without specialised infrastructure.
evidence_items.title: ON-PREMISE OPEN-WEIGHT LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FOR INTERPRETABLE WEB VULNERABILITY DETECTION: A BENCHMARK AGAINST CLOUD MODELS AND RULE-BASED STATIC ANALYSIS

evidence_items.summary: Forecasting the seasonal dynamics of Aedes albopictus, a highly invasive arbovirus vector now established across much of Europe, is a growing public health priority. Numerous mechanistic and correlative models have been developed over the last two decades, but largely in isolation, each calibrated and validated against its own data, which has prevented any assessment of where predictive capacity is genuinely limited. Rather than ranking models, which were built for different purposes and cannot be reduced to a single skill score, we establish common ground: a shared evaluation framework in which six mechanistic models, one correlative machine learning model, and two naive baseline predictors are driven by identical ERA5-Land forcing and assessed against the harmonised VectAbundance ovitrap dataset (Albania, Italy, Switzerland) using a single protocol, with robustness quantified by bootstrap resampling. We additionally combine the models into a weighted ensemble via approximate Bayesian computation. Both naive baselines outperformed every process-based and machine learning model, and the ensemble matched but did not exceed the best individual models. Predictive skill varied markedly in space, with all model classes, including the uncalibrated baselines, performing best in intensively monitored regions and worst at sparsely sampled sites. This pattern suggests that geographic variation in skill reflects the density and consistency of surveillance data more than differences in model complexity. We present this benchmark not as a league table but as shared infrastructure, common evaluation data, covariates, and protocol, on which comparable, policy-relevant forecasting tools can be built, and we argue that sustained, harmonised surveillance is the principal precondition for operational Ae. albopictus prediction.
evidence_items.title: A common benchmark for Aedes albopictus phenological models reveals surveillance data, not model complexity, as the limiting factor

evidence_items.summary: Object-detection benchmark scores are often transferred across settings without restating the evaluation target that gives a metric its meaning. This focused interpretive review examines how that target changes along a scale-centered path from regular-scale to small-object detection, with point-based targets treated as a representation-dependent branch. Orientation-aware and temporal evaluation are treated as selected extensions when geometric representation or sequence-level evaluation targets require criteria beyond scale alone. Across these settings, the review distinguishes reporting protocols, matching and localization measures, and loss-derived formulations used mainly for optimization. An intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold can determine whether a prediction is matched to a target, while precision and recall describe an operating point and average precision, mean average precision, and average recall summarize behavior under a specified benchmark protocol. The same metric label can therefore support different claims when thresholds, annotation granularity, prediction structure, or temporal targets differ. A four-slot evaluation contract makes the prediction target, matching primitive, reporting endpoint, and metric role explicit. A cross-setting guide links those slots to protocol selection. Reassessments of Common Objects in Context (COCO), Dataset for Object Detection in Aerial Images (DOTA), and multi-object tracking (MOT) predictions connect scale-conditioned reporting, geometric matching, and identity continuity to concrete interpretation decisions. The review synthesizes these findings into a practical guide for reading benchmark evidence and choosing evaluation protocols.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Protocols and Benchmark Interpretation for Deep Learning-Based Object Detection: A Scale-Centered Review

evidence_items.summary: Chinese short-form dramas (duanju) drive a growing demand for automated Japanese dubbing that preserves each character’s voice. The decisive component is zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning: synthesising Japanese speech from a short Chinese reference clip. We benchmark four neural text-to-speech systems—GPT-SoVITS v3, F5-TTS, CosyVoice2-0.5B, and the non-cloning commercial baseline EdgeTTS—on an annotated short-drama corpus (79 episodes, 3692 segments, 12 speakers) with native-speaker-verified Japanese references, combining automatic intelligibility (Whisper re-transcription) and speaker-embedding similarity with a blind listening study by five JLPT-N1 raters. Among cloning systems, only GPT-SoVITS attains usable intelligibility (character error rate 0.215, against 1.152 for F5-TTS and 4.603 for CosyVoice2), while EdgeTTS is most intelligible overall (0.030). Critically, the automatic and perceptual measures dissociate: F5-TTS scores marginally higher on embedding similarity (0.729 vs. 0.722), yet raters preferr GPT-SoVITS three to one. Naturalness shows no detectable gap between GPT-SoVITS and EdgeTTS (mean opinion score 3.08 versus 3.12, p=0.93), a null result at a resolution of about 0.6 points. In a single-speaker probe, speaker similarity rises from 0.64 to 0.71 as the reference lengthens from 3 to 10 s. Embedding similarity alone is therefore an unreliable proxy for perceived speaker identity.
evidence_items.title: Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Japanese Voice Cloning to Dub Chinese Short Dramas: A Four-System Benchmark with Human Evaluation
