evidence_items.summary: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affects social interaction and communication, and automatically recognizing emotions from the facial expressions of children with ASD remains challenging. A key barrier to facial emotion recognition (FER) in children with ASD is the absence of ASD-specific datasets with proper emotion-level annotations. To address this, we present ASD-FER , a benchmark of 2,779 facial images of children with ASD annotated across six emotion categories by three independent annotators using majority voting. We evaluate nine models — CNN, SVM, AlexNet, ResNet34, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, and three backbone configurations of our proposed task-specific architecture, EQFormer : ViT, Swin-T, and a compact Hybrid CNN-Transformer (HybridT) — under stratified 10-fold cross-validation and a held-out 90/10 evaluation. ResNet50 led conventional models at 84.89% mean cross-validation accuracy; among transformer-based models, ViT led with 88.27%, followed by Swin-T at 88.02% and HybridT at 86.58%. On the held-out set, ViT achieved the highest overall accuracy (91.01%), while Swin-T obtained the best balanced accuracy (74.47%) and macro-F1 (0.7078); HybridT remained competitive at 89.57% accuracy with a fraction of the parameters. To support explainability, Grad-CAM visualizations highlighted attention on emotion-relevant facial regions — eyes, eyebrows, and mouth — with Swin-T the most spatially focused and the HybridT the most parameter-efficient (2.66M). Class imbalance and cross-dataset generalization remain open challenges.
evidence_items.title: ASD-FER: An Annotated Multi-Class Benchmark and Comparative Study for Facial Emotion Recognition in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder

evidence_items.summary: Background Clinical trial data pipelines must follow Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) standards, including the study data tabulation model (SDTM) and analysis data model (ADaM). General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible artifacts that omit required variables, misuse terminology, or invent derivation logic. Curated context may reduce these errors, but the value of organizing that context by workflow topology has not been separated from corpus access alone. Objective This study aimed to examine when workflow topology–guided skill loading adds value beyond a domain prompt, nonrouted curated context, or lexical retrieval, and whether bounded scheduling retains quality with less injected context. Methods A 45-node, 7-layer directed acyclic workflow graph was linked to 59 modular rule files (SKILL.md). A sequential exploratory evaluation examined 4 evidence regimes spanning domain-context, component isolation, lexically reachable, and topology-dependent conditions (10 tasks, 90 runs; 10 tasks, 180 and 120 runs; 24 tasks, 288 runs; and 18 tasks, 324 runs; the task, not the agent run, was the inferential unit). End points included LLM rubric scores, deterministic atomic criteria, required-evidence recall, and manifest checks. A blinded practicing statistical programmer independently rescored 60 outputs. Task-level paired inference used bootstrap 95% CIs, exact sign-flip tests, and Holm adjustment. Results Routed context scored 4.63 versus 4.20 for prompt-only (difference 0.43 on a 1-5 scale; 95% CI 0.25-0.63; Holm-adjusted P=.01) but did not exceed flat or random loading. The lower-context scheduler used 28.82% less context while retaining quality; all 559 injected fragments had recorded sources, and all 120 manifests were reproduced exactly.
evidence_items.title: Workflow Topology–Guided Skill Loading for Agentic AI in Clinical Trial Data Pipelines: Sequential Exploratory Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Security operations centers increasingly rely on agentic artificial intelligence systems, which combine large language model reasoning with tool invocation and multi-step planning, to automate alert triage, investigation, and response. Independent research groups have proposed structurally distinct architectures for this purpose, ranging from single-agent reasoning loops to multi-agent systems with shared context or deterministic safety constraints, but no publication has systematically compared these designs against a common set of criteria. This review addresses that gap by constructing a five-dimension classification framework covering agent cardinality, coordination mechanism, autonomy boundary, safety enforcement layer, and validation maturity. A corpus of published systems relevant to security operations was retrieved from academic preprint archives and conference proceedings and coded against this framework. Five recurring design patterns were identified, together with the available quantitative evidence comparing them, including a controlled trial showing that multi-agent orchestration produced consistently reliable recommendations while single-agent approaches did not. The analysis found that claimed autonomy consistently outpaced empirical validation across the reviewed designs, with most systems evaluated no further than a single organizational deployment despite permitting autonomous action. These findings indicate that validation maturity should be assessed independently from architectural sophistication when organizations evaluate agentic artificial intelligence for security operations, and they identify calibration and human oversight effectiveness as priority areas for future empirical study.
evidence_items.title: Review of System Design Approaches in Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Security Operations Centers

organizations: Manipal University Jaipur
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed where tools fail, objectives change, and constraints tighten while a task is in progress. Prevailing benchmarks score only static end-task accuracy and therefore miss mid-episode responsiveness, which is the ability to adapt and recover after a controlled change. We present a responsiveness evaluation framework that pairs three agent architectures (ReAct, Reflexion, and Plan-and-Execute) with three deterministic synthetic environments (tool planning, debugging, and constraint planning) and injects tool denial, goal modification, or constraint injection at graded severity. Across two matched factorial grids of 4,320 episodes each—one with an explicit perturbation notice and one silent. ReAct attains the highest pooled reward (0.544), yet Plan-and-Execute leads on tool planning (0.711 vs. 0.532) while collapsing on constraint planning (0.114). Tool denial uniquely depresses behavioural recovery, and severity within [0.1, 0.9] yields no monotone dose–response. Explicit notices do not improve mean reward for any architecture. Code, logs, and analysis pipelines are released for extension.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking the responsiveness of LLM-based agentic systems under controlled mid-task perturbations

evidence_items.summary: AI-generated images linked to news events and online claims can mislead audiences, enable fraud, or cause public controversy. We introduce WildAIGC-Bench, built through recurring collection across news websites, fact-checking sources, and related social media content. The pipeline combines broad coverage, timely updates, and human-verified labels through scheduled discovery, automatic screening and preliminary annotation, and human review of image-specific evidence. The benchmark contains 407 verified AI-generated or edited images, each accompanied by a source webpage link and an evidence summary. Images retain the conditions encountered online, including compression, screenshots, and recapture. Evaluation of dedicated visual detectors, multimodal large language models, and a simple Perception Encoder baseline reveals substantial recall gaps relative to existing benchmarks. WildAIGC-Bench provides both a practical detection challenge and a basis for continued data expansion and source-based verification. The dataset is released at https://github.com/YuZijian/WildAIGC-Bench.
evidence_items.title: WildAIGC-Bench: Can AI Image Detectors Handle the Wild? A Benchmark of Generated and Edited Images in Online Circulation

evidence_items.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.
evidence_items.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift

evidence_items.summary: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut-off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut-offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single-shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self-assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single-shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense&sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman $\rho = +0.60$ with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR. (4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.
evidence_items.title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) of agent harnesses has emerged as an effective approach to enhancing the capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents. By searching the harness space for a specific LLM on a given dataset, RSI can discover a harness tailored to the capabilities and behavioral characteristics of that model. However, such optimization often creates a strong coupling between the learned harness and its target LLM, limiting generalization across models and requiring substantial computational resources to adapt to new LLMs. Moreover, existing RSI methods typically optimize a harness using feedback from a single model and evaluate its generalization to other models only after training. This paradigm treats model differences primarily as a criterion for evaluating generalization rather than as valuable evidence for optimization. In this paper, we introduce a new perspective that treats models as data and places the harness at the center of optimization. Building on this perspective, we propose \textsc{MaD-RSI}, a framework that directly optimizes a shared harness across multiple heterogeneous LLMs by incorporating their diverse failure trajectories into the training process. Rather than assessing model differences only after optimization, \textsc{MaD-RSI} leverages these differences as training evidence to guide the self-improvement of a shared harness. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation framework with two complementary metrics designed to assess the effectiveness of harness optimization across models. Experiments across multiple datasets and LLMs demonstrate that \textsc{MaD-RSI} improves generalization over existing approaches while reducing training costs.
evidence_items.title: MaD-RSI: Model-as-Data for Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.
evidence_items.title: Large Multimodal Models for Direct Robot Control: GPT-6 as a Beginning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can improve honeypot realism by generating dynamic, context-aware responses, but powerful cloud models incur substantial cost and latency, while lightweight models may provide weaker deception. This forces practitioners to choose between operational efficiency and interaction fidelity. In this work, we present HydraPoT, a configurable multi-agent honeypot framework that integrates traditional emulation, lightweight LLMs, and powerful cloud LLMs. HydraPoT routes each attacker command to an appropriate agent according to a configurable complexity-based policy, while maintaining shared session state to preserve consistency across agent transitions. We evaluate HydraPoT through an architectural-overhead analysis, a cross-agent context-preservation benchmark, and a three-agent case study. HydraPoT introduces less than 5% runtime overhead, preserves context across heterogeneous agents, and achieves fidelity close to a cloud-LLM-only honeypot. Under our case-study policy, it reduces cloud-processed tokens by 72.6% and operational cost by 3.7x. These results demonstrate that configurable multi-agent routing can make realistic LLM-assisted honeypots more practical under limited operational budgets.
evidence_items.title: HydraPoT: A Configurable Multi-Agent Framework for Cost-Aware LLM-Assisted Honeypots

evidence_items.summary: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer knowledge from large-scale pretraining into robot control, but their manipulation performance remains sensitive to changes in observation conditions, which recent work addresses by fine-tuning the visual module on target-domain data. However, it remains unclear how such adaptation affects robustness beyond the target condition, as existing robustness benchmarks only evaluate models without fine-tuning and adaptation studies only report the target gain. Measuring this cross-dimension effect requires separating target gains from off-target changes, isolating adaptation effects from architectural differences, ruling out generic forgetting, and comparing tuning choices. Therefore, we introduce VLA-Retain, a benchmark that compares five open VLA models, tuned on Camera-view or Sensor-noise data, with their own base checkpoints on LIBERO-Plus dataset spanning seven perturbation dimensions. Our study reveals four findings. First, targeted vision tuning is not local, and its target gain does not predict retention. Mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model--domain configurations. Under Camera-view tuning, X-VLA gains $69.4$ percentage points on the target but loses $4.6$ points on average elsewhere, whereas OpenVLA-OFT gains $39.3$ and $1.4$ points, respectively. Second, these regressions are not explained only by performance loss on the same tasks without perturbations. Third, broader training coverage raises overall gain over target-specific training but does not eliminate dimension-level regressions. Fourth, tuning strategies are model-dependent, as DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain to $+1.2$ points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's to $-23.1$. Overall, these findings show that target-domain success alone is insufficient and highlight cross-dimensional retention as a key criterion for targeted VLA adaptation.
evidence_items.title: VLA-Retain: Benchmarking Cross-Dimension Effects of Vision Tuning in VLAs

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language trackers (VLTs) accept descriptions intended to assist tracking, but accepting text does not establish that its content changes tracking decisions, particularly as visual evidence deteriorates. We introduce DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. We evaluate five VLTs on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching. Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use. Some effects contract under degradation, whereas others show no significant endpoint change after multiplicity correction. UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics, with no directed behavioral effect surviving FDR correction in the tested settings. Model-internal analyses reveal that at decision-near states, correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems. In the responsive models, decodability peaks at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change, whereas replacing selected earlier states redirects conflict-associated trajectories toward the target. Because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, these interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue. DISTRACT thus exposes when and where text affects tracking under degraded visual evidence.
evidence_items.title: DISTRACT: Degradation-Indexed Study of Textual Reference Across Competing Targets

evidence_items.summary: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 50 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
evidence_items.title: JARVIS: From Visual Manuals to Autonomous Robotic Assembly

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.
evidence_items.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with the dynamic evolution of real-world knowledge. Although RAG and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) provide practical ways to enhance LLMs, they remain insufficient for temporal reasoning. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. Meanwhile, conventional PEFT methods usually employ fixed and input-agnostic low-rank updates, making it difficult to capture time-dependent entity semantics and relation drift. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. TEPCA aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it introduces time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths, together with Mutual-Information (MI)-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. This design enables LLMs to better capture fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency. Experimental results on two TKG benchmarks demonstrate that TEPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets further verify its general input-adaptive capacity, scalability across LLM backbones, and interpretability.
evidence_items.title: Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment for LLM Reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.
evidence_items.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the dominant paradigm for grounding the outputs of large language models (LLM) in external knowledge. However, practitioners are faced with a vast configuration space comprising chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, prompting and generation models, and there is limited guidance on how these components interact. We present RAG-NIMBF, a modular benchmarking framework that attaches to existing RAG pipelines as a non-invasive evaluation layer. It evaluates the configuration space through controlled ablation with end-to-end experiment tracking. The evaluation combines LLM-based answer quality scores, retrieval correctness measures, and runtime indicators. This study validates the framework across multiple generation models on the SQuAD dataset. This process reveals non-obvious interactions and demonstrates how the experiments are tracked. The findings indicate that the retrieval balance of relevance and diversity substantially enhances the relevance and coverage of retrieved context in comparison to a conventional similarity search, with MMR raising nDCG@5 by +4 to +11 percentage points across the swept models. More detailed prompt instructions meaningfully increase how faithfully generated answers stick to the retrieved evidence, especially for capable and reasoning models (+10 to +13pp on Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.5-think, but negligible on the 20B generator). Overall, RAG-NIMBF transforms the configuration space of RAG into reproducible, comparable experiments. By attaching to existing production pipelines in a non-invasive way, it enables practitioners to systematically evaluate and improve deployed systems without disrupting existing workflows. This replaces ad hoc choices with evidence-based decisions.
evidence_items.title: RAG-NIMBF: A Non-Invasive, Modular Benchmarking Framework for Automated RAG Configuration Analysis

evidence_items.summary: The integration of Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning offers a promising direction for complex sequential decision-making tasks, such as multi-hop question answering over knowledge graphs. While LLMs provide strong semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities, they often struggle with precise, multi-step navigation in structured environments. Conversely, RL agents excel at learning navigation policies but are hindered by the difficulty of designing semantically meaningful reward functions. This paper introduces a novel hybrid approach in which an LLM serves as a mentor to an RL agent during training by providing dense, semantically informed reward signals. The RL agent, built on a Transformer-based policy and trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization, learns to navigate a knowledge graph to retrieve relevant information. The LLM evaluates the semantic relevance of the agent's traversed paths, generating reward signals that align the agent's behavior with the information needs expressed in a query. We integrate this Retrieval Agent for Navigating Graphs with Semantic Evaluation Rewards (RANGER) into a complete question-answering pipeline and evaluate it on the open question answering datasets. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms both a baseline retrieval-augmented system with classical graph search and one using an RL agent trained with heuristic rewards, achieving a significant increase in NLP metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge scores. Our findings demonstrate that deep integration of LLMs into the RL training loop yields more effective and semantically aligned retrieval policies for complex reasoning tasks.
evidence_items.title: RANGER: Retrieval Agent for Navigating Graphs with Semantic Evaluation Rewards

evidence_items.summary: Applications provide convenient features for users to complete daily tasks. However, different users may have different or even conflicting requirements for the same application, while the requirements of the same user may change over time. Personalizing applications produced by agent-to-app or UI-to-code approaches can require changes to the generated implementation. We propose Agent as App, a task in which users express their requirements in natural language and an agent creates a personalized application while continuing to supply its behavior during use. We implement LiveUIAgent, which generates a task-specific orchestration connecting the user interface, saved information, and service actions. A shared agent runtime renders and updates the interface while carrying out the requested operations. Revising the orchestration and interface while reusing that runtime provides a lightweight basis for personalization as requirements evolve. We introduce LiveUIBench, a benchmark with diverse requirements and ordered interactions across personal services. The empirical findings show that the evaluated models struggle to complete these workflows reliably. Applications can satisfy many local checks while leaving the overall task unfinished, and greater partial coverage can coincide with fewer completed workflows.
evidence_items.title: LiveUIBench: Evaluating Agent as App Workflows

evidence_items.summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
evidence_items.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning has become the default tool for medical image analysis, driven by the open-source movement. However, achieving the best performance on a given task remains difficult, with architecture selection and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) still considered"more of an art than a science". Automated machine learning (AutoML) automates parts of model training, yet helps little in medical imaging: general-purpose approaches lack medical architectures and preprocessing, and medical-focused ones demand engineering expertise and remain confined to narrow tasks such as 3D segmentation. We introduce MedicalMLOmni, a multi-agent AutoML framework that automates model training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks through a natural language interface. Specifically, MedicalMLOmni performs evidence-based planning by retrieving published results to guide model selection and configuration, and employs parallel HPO where multiple agents explore adjustment strategies concurrently. MedicalMLOmni achieves the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks; PMC-VQA is the exception, where a vision-language model with broader pre-training leads. Backbone-matched controls attribute the gains to the framework, not the backbone. By removing coding requirements, MedicalMLOmni lowers the barrier for domain experts with rich datasets but limited engineering expertise.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.
evidence_items.title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records

evidence_items.summary: The rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence has led to a significant increase in manipulated multimedia content, including synthetic faces, forged videos, AI-generated images, fake audio, and locally edited images. Existing detection approaches are typically designed for a single manipulation type, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios involving heterogeneous media sources. In this work, we present the Media Intelligence Platform (MIP), a unified web-based framework for multimodal media forensics integrating specialized modules for fake video detection, face morphing detection, AI-generated image detection, audio deepfake detection, localized image manipulation detection, and text analysis. Its modular architecture enables flexible integration of heterogeneous models and supports future extensions for emerging manipulation techniques. Experimental results on representative benchmark datasets demonstrate reliable detection performance across multiple media modalities while providing a practical and user-friendly interface for forensic investigations. The platform highlights the potential of unified multimodal systems for comprehensive deepfake detection in real-world environments, and is accompanied by a public demonstrator released with this workshop submission to support reproducibility and community evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Media Intelligence Platform: Multimodal Detection of Synthetic and Manipulated Content

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To compare the diagnostic performance of five contemporary vision-enabled large language models (LLMs) in mammography interpretation using a case–control benchmark design. Methods A total of 200 cases were analyzed using a quota-balanced case–control design (100 malignant, BI-RADS 4–5; 100 controls, BI-RADS 1–2). All models (ChatGPT-5T, ChatGPT-5I, ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) received standard mammography images. Models were evaluated for lesion detection, laterality, quadrant localization, lesion type, and malignant–benign discrimination. Performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, Cohen’s κ, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Breast density was recorded for all cases, while histopathological subtype and lesion size were documented for malignant cases. Results Lesion detection accuracy ranged from 79% to 91%, with high malignant sensitivity (92%–100%) but lower specificity in normal cases (24%–82%). ChatGPT-5T performed best in laterality (83%; κ = 0.70) and quadrant localization (73%; κ = 0.62). Lesion type classification was modest (74%–85%). In malignant–benign discrimination, ChatGPT-5T achieved the highest balanced accuracy (87%), while ChatGPT-4o showed poor specificity (28%). The study cohort was predominantly composed of lower-density breasts, larger lesions, and invasive ductal carcinoma as the most common subtype. Conclusion Vision-enabled LLMs demonstrated high sensitivity for breast lesion detection and classification tasks. More deliberative models, particularly ChatGPT-5T, consistently outperformed faster counterparts, especially in spatial reasoning tasks. However, reduced specificity in normal cases underscores that current LLM outputs should remain under radiologist supervision as supportive second-reader tools rather than standalone diagnostic systems.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Evaluation of Vision-Enabled Large Language Models in Mammography: A Case–Control Study

evidence_items.summary: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.
evidence_items.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains anonymized clinical and ultrasound-derived data collected from 111 pediatric patients (aged 0–19 years) evaluated for acute scrotum. It includes 65 patients diagnosed with testicular torsion and 46 patients with non-torsion conditions. For each patient, the dataset provides clinical examination findings, including pain onset, scrotal swelling, erythema, cremasteric reflex, testicular consistency, tenderness on palpation, and testicular retraction. Ultrasound-derived variables include increased testicular volume, tissue heterogeneity, absence of vascular signals, and the presence of the whirlpool sign. The dataset also includes the final diagnostic classification (torsion versus non-torsion), enabling its use in binary classification studies. Clinical and ultrasound variables are represented using numerical encodings, with missing or unavailable information identified through dedicated values. The dataset is intended to support research on pediatric acute scrotum diagnosis, clinical data analysis, and the development and evaluation of computational diagnostic methods.

evidence_items.summary: Dataset Description   This repository contains aggregate-level data summaries and supporting documentation from a retrospective longitudinal study investigating individual- and squad-level external-load dynamics in professional men's soccer during the 2024–2025 competitive season.   The study examines between-player differences, within-player variability, and match-to-match fluctuations in external-load measures, including total distance, relative distance, maximum speed, running distances across speed zones, and acceleration- and deceleration-related metrics.   The associated analyses investigate the stability of individual external-load profiles across repeated match observations, using longitudinal statistical approaches, including generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs), and sensitivity analyses based on different player inclusion and match-exposure criteria.   The repository includes aggregate statistical summaries and accompanying documentation to facilitate scientific transparency, interpretation, and secondary methodological evaluation.   Data availability and limitations: The deposited materials contain aggregate-level outputs only. Individual player-level observations and directly identifying personal information are not included. Consequently, the repository does not provide the complete underlying dataset required for independent reproduction of all statistical models.   These materials support an associated scientific manuscript on individual–squad external-load dynamics in professional soccer. The repository is independent of any particular journal or publication venue.
evidence_items.title: Aggregate External Load and Individual–Squad Variability in Professional Soccer: A Single-Team Longitudinal Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Short-term traffic speed prediction on the METR-LA benchmark is  commonly evaluated by collapsing all 207 sensor readings into a single mean speed  before prediction. This practice yields artificially low error metrics and produces  results structurally incomparable with graph-based methods — an artefact that  overstates the apparent advantage of graph architectures by a factor of approximately  2.83× at the 15-minute horizon. This paper makes two contributions: (1) a  reproducibility and benchmark-hygiene contribution — a per-sensor LSTM  architecture based on a shared-weight tensor-reshape strategy [B, N, T] → [B×N, T,  1], evaluated under the identical protocol used by DCRNN, Graph WaveNet, and  MSTGACN, achieving MAE = 3.03 mph and RMSE = 5.73 mph at 15 minutes with  52,611 parameters; and (2) a sparse-coverage contribution — three experimental  protocols applied to the trained baseline, revealing that block removal is the least  damaging missing-data pattern for a spatial-information-free model, while sensor-level  dropout is the most damaging — directly motivating a graph-convolutional successor  for cities where detector coverage falls below 50%.
evidence_items.title: PER-SENSOR LSTM BASELINE AND SPARSE-COVERAGE ANALYSIS  FOR SHORT-TERM URBAN TRAFFIC SPEED PREDICTION: A  REPRODUCIBLE EVALUATION ON METR-LA

evidence_items.summary: This record holds the code, data and results needed to check and reproduce the paper “Bats Could Learn Three-Dimensional Echolocation Using Echoacoustic Flow” (Jan Steckel, Cosys-Lab, University of Antwerp, and Flanders Make). In the paper, a simulated bat-like agent learns its echolocation-related transfer function (ERTF) in azimuth and elevation from its echoes and its own measured movements alone. It has no labeled echo directions and no external teacher. From a single call, the agent infers a three-dimensional scene. It moves that scene according to its self-motion and learns by predicting the echoes of the following calls. Learning runs online, with a short replay memory. The record contains: code.zip : the simulator, model, training, evaluation and figure code at the version used for the paper (the bat3d Python package, scripts, tests, paper sources and figures). worlds.zip : the simulated point-reflector worlds. These are the main training and validation worlds, the symmetric worlds, the sparse worlds, and the same sparse worlds inside a room of specular surfaces. runs/ : one folder per experiment (E1–E9, C1–C5, as listed in Supplementary Note 2 of the paper). Each holds the configuration, the final model, the training log, the evaluation metrics, the localization results and the learned transfer function over the drive. experiments.json : maps each experiment ID to its run folder. source data/ : the numbers behind the figures, including Supplementary Table 1 ( run table.json ). data/HRTF Phyllostomus Discolor azel.mat : the simulated head-related transfer function of Phyllostomus discolor (De Mey et al. 2008), which defines the ERTF of the simulated agent. It is included with the permission of its authors. video/hrtf ssl supplementary.mp4 : the supplementary video. The rendered echo datasets are not included. They are regenerated exactly from the seeds with the included code (see README.md ).
evidence_items.title: Bats Could Learn Three-Dimensional Echolocation Using Echoacoustic Flow: Code, Worlds, Runs and Video

evidence_items.summary: Contribution presented at the Second Pan African University (PAU) International Conference, held at the University of Tlemcen, Tlemcen, Algeria, on 1–2 December 2025. This contribution presents the development framework for the TRANS-SAHARA Agroforestry Intervention Design (AID) Tool, which combines Water–Energy–Food–Ecosystem (WEFE) Nexus modelling, agroforestry modelling, and interactive decision support. Developed within the EU-funded TRANS-SAHARA project, the tool aims to support nature-based solutions and integrated resource management in the Greater Northern African Region, drawing on Living Labs in Tunisia, Ghana, and Ethiopia. The tool is designed to assist researchers, policymakers, and other stakeholders in planning agroforestry interventions by integrating environmental, hydrological, socioeconomic, and governance data. Two complementary modelling streams underpin the approach: WEFE Nexus modelling to explore resource interdependencies, and optimization-based land-use allocation to compare baseline conditions and alternative intervention scenarios. The methodological framework comprises the classification of model families, data requirements, and knowledge gaps; harmonization of multi-source datasets and key performance indicators; development of Living Lab-specific WEFE models; optimization-based land-use allocation; and integration of climate and species-distribution projections. A reproducible data pipeline supports data ingestion, quality assurance and control, metadata management, and versioning. The decision-support interface combines dashboards, maps, time series, heatmaps, and scenario workflows. The framework also includes model calibration and validation using spatially explicit data, out-of-sample assessment, and spatial cross-validation. The modular system is designed for iterative stakeholder co-design and evaluation using real datasets and decision contexts.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Claims of quantum advantage in machine learning often rest on classical comparators that lack the same features, on simulation alone, and on unreported hardware cost. QBioBench is a benchmark of quantum machine learning on peripheral biosignals that holds quantum and classical models to the same features and reports calibration and hardware cost. It comprises three clinical tasks, 12-lead ECG diagnosis (PTB-XL), single-lead apnea detection (Apnea-ECG), and wearable stress detection (WESAD), each reduced to six to eight shared dimensions. A factorial grid of projected and fidelity quantum kernels and variational classifiers is screened in noisy simulation, and the promoted configurations are evaluated in an exploratory study on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor on the full test pools of 510 apnea minutes and 512 PTB-XL records. Every prediction is recovered from the device records, intervals resample recordings or patients, and classical baselines are trained on the same units and tested on the same executed inputs. No quantum model reaches its matched support vector machine in ROC-AUC on either primary task, and none is separably better in balanced accuracy. The angle-encoded fidelity and projected kernels reach ROC-AUC 0.697 and 0.693 on apnea, paired differences of $-0.127$ and $-0.119$ to the support vector machine, and both are classical by construction, since the entangling layer of the encoding cancels from the fidelity kernel and leaves closed-form local expectations in the projected kernel. A variational classifier comes closest, reaching 0.797 on apnea (difference $-0.012$, 95\% interval $[-0.052, +0.027]$), and falls to chance without its two-qubit gates. Test sets of the size that circuit budgets favour are unreliable, as random 80-minute subsets of the apnea pool give the fidelity kernel a central 95\% range of ROC-AUC from 0.589 to 0.797. Readout mitigation changed ROC-AUC by at most 0.015.
evidence_items.title: QBioBench: Benchmark of quantum machine learning for peripheral biosignals on real hardware

evidence_items.summary: Claims that hallucinations in learned world models are predictable and preventable require distinct assumptions about statistical identification, distribution shift, uncertainty measurement, and evaluation. This paper develops a framework for separating these questions, using a recent generative-world-model study and TD-MPC2 as case studies. A two-point argument identifies the limits of inference on unobserved contexts without implying that realized error is monotone in data density. A rollout bound separates estimation error on the sampling distribution, occupancy-ratio amplification, and deployment mass singular with respect to that distribution; complementary Wasserstein and pathwise formulations clarify geometric approximation and persistence of errors. We distinguish sampling-seed spread from calibrated epistemic uncertainty, establish the invariance of within-task AUROC to task-constant normalization, and characterize limitations of round-trip, flow-instability, and action-shuffle diagnostics. We provide explicit assumptions for importance-weighted validation and conformal false-alarm control, together with a separate certificate for accepted-prediction risk. For implicit models, corrected planning bounds, a scale-equivariant disagreement penalty, and local SimNorm gradient bounds delimit what short-horizon planning and latent normalization establish. Executed synthetic diagnostics illustrate aggregation effects, disappearing terminal discrepancies, and failure of calibration under unsupported shift. They are not replications of the benchmark studies. A controlled experimental protocol specifies the evidence still needed to distinguish coverage, representation, optimization, and capacity effects.
evidence_items.title: Coverage, Uncertainty, and Evaluation in Learned World Models Identification Limits and Validity Conditions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Multimodal large-language-model (LLM) evidence pipelines often attach rule-derived outcomes to candidate remediation actions even though only the executed action yields a factual production outcome. Treating those counterfactual rules as ground truth can miscalibrate routing, while discarding them wastes structured operational knowledge. We introduce EviRoute-DR, a disagreement-reliability routing method that learns when rule priors fail and combines corrected-rule experts with direct factual outcome experts through a reliability-conditioned meta-learner. The study uses 2,100 production cases, seven candidate actions per case (14,700 case-action records), and exactly one observed production outcome per case. Base models are trained on 600 factual cases, combined on 200, and evaluated on 1,300 held-out factual cases spanning main, temporal-labelled, hard, and workflow-shift cohorts. On factual outcomes, EviRoute-DR achieves AUC 0.926 and Brier score 0.0910, compared with 0.921/0.0971 for direct logistic regression and 0.924/0.0922 for a random-forest baseline. The paired bootstrap Brier improvement over logistic regression is 0.0060 (95\% CI 0.0021--0.0092). A separate production-derived counterfactual replay shows a stronger cost-resolution frontier at moderate operating costs, reaching approximately 0.815 resolution near 12 cost units. Because the logged action is always the argmax of the production score vector, we do not interpret those scores as stochastic propensities and make no inverse-propensity, doubly robust causal, or production-effect claim. The results support disagreement-aware reliability fusion as a practical methodology for evidence routing under partial factual feedback.
evidence_items.title: Disagreement reliability routing for multimodal large language model evidence pipelines with imperfect counterfactual priors

evidence_items.summary: The rapid ubiquity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical frameworks in engineering education, necessitating a critical examination of its impact on cognitive development and knowledge retention. This longitudinal study spans 30 years (1996–2025) to analyse shifts in student learning curves within an AI curriculum, testing the hypothesis that reliance on automated tools exacerbates a ‘J-curve’ learning style, characterised by delayed engagement and terminal production spikes, at the expense of fundamental understanding. By comparing weekly topic acquisition and final assessment data across cohorts, the research reveals a distinct morphological transformation from the classic sigmoidal progression (‘S-curve’) of the baseline 1996 class to an exponential ‘J-curve’ in the 2025 cohort. While modern students demonstrate high procedural efficiency in project delivery, this shift correlates strongly with a significant decline in independent examination performance, where mean scores fell from 9.50 to 7.75. Although a gradual decline in performance was observed prior to 2020, the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent ubiquity of generative AI tools may have intensified this trend (main finding). The data indicate that students utilise AI to bypass the cognitive friction necessary for deep learning, resulting in a failure to exit the assisted phase of skill acquisition. These findings suggest that current AI integration acts as a mechanism for cognitive offloading rather than scaffolding, creating a trade-off between immediate output and long-term declarative competence. The study concludes that engineering curricula must rigorously re-evaluate assessment strategies to ensure that the efficiency of automated generation does not erode the foundational logic required for sustainable innovation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence: Learning Flow in 30 Years

evidence_items.summary: Background. Knowledge-graph models can rank existing drugs for a disease, but their benchmarks mostly reward rediscovering known treatments, and their scores rarely come with evidence a researcher can check. We built OREVID, an open tool that shows a ranked candidate only when an evidence line supports it and reports how often each line was right on held-out data, and compared it with TxGNN on identical data. Methods. The graph combines PrimeKG, Open Targets, STRING and PubTator3 (157,822 nodes, 9.46 million edges). For each disease, 22 degree-weighted metapath features feed a LightGBM LambdaRank model trained with masked neighbourhoods. A candidate is shown only if it is indicated for an ontology-neighbour disease or for a disease sharing at least 3 associated genes (hypergeometric p &lt; 10⁻⁵ over the genes with at least one associated disease). The acceptance criteria for these rules were set in advance; the rules were revised on the hidden-treatment benchmarks and then measured on an external set of approvals not used to choose them. TxGNN was retrained with its official code on the same PrimeKG splits, and all tasks and predictions are released as OREVID-bench. Results. Zero-shot Recall@100 (mean ± SD over five splits) was 0.811 ± 0.042 for OREVID, 0.412 ± 0.042 for TxGNN and 0.358 ± 0.040 for a popularity baseline, with OREVID ahead on every split (paired difference with TxGNN 0.399, 95% CI 0.352–0.443, resampling diseases). On nine disease areas held out it was 0.617 against 0.237, ahead in all nine, although TxGNN had the higher AUPRC in five. Training OREVID without validation labels and excluding diseases where TxGNN outputs constant scores gave 0.809 against 0.421.
evidence_items.title: OREVID: Open, Evidence-Based Drug Repurposing with a Benchmark Against TxGNN

evidence_items.summary: We introduce a core–virtual-complete variant of mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory (MRSF-TDDFT), CV-MRSF, which completes the block of core-to-virtual (CV) excitations. For each CV excitation, the four determinants missing from MRSF-TDDFT are recovered by imposing exact spin adaptation, which makes every singlet and triplet spin pure and gives the proper singlet–triplet splitting of CV states without spin-pairing couplings. In addition, invariance under a rotation of the two singly occupied molecular orbitals (SOMOs) O1 and O2 adds the configurations C¹O₁²V¹ and C¹O₂²V¹. The number of CV configurations per excitation thus grows from one to four in the singlet and to five in the triplet configuration state function (CSF) response, and one quintet CSF also arises within the same CV block, instead of from a separate spin-flip-up calculation. As a result, the CV excitations properly couple to the complete set of open-to-open (OO) configurations, both singlet and triplet, as well as to the core-to-open (CO) and open-to-virtual (OV) configurations, which relaxes the excited states and accounts for most of the changes in excitation energy. For hybrid functionals, a spin-scalar one-body correction keeps the response matrix covariant under separate rotations of the core, open-shell, and virtual orbitals. For the Thiel benchmark set it lowers the mean absolute error of MRSF-TDDFT from 0.53 to 0.40 eV for the singlets and from 0.40 to 0.29 eV for the triplets. The largest gains are for n→π states by excitation character and nucleobase singlets by molecule class. The CV block also describes the spin-pure triplet-pair states ¹(TT), ³(TT), and ⁵(TT) of chromophore dimers on the same footing, the essential requirement for the description of singlet fission processes.
evidence_items.title: Eliminating the remaining spin contamination of MRSF-TDDFT by completing its core–virtual block

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations. However, the fast deployment of autonomous agents entails significant security issues, physical-layer attacks in cyber-physical systems, alignment problems, and advanced social engineering risks jeopardizing the stability of the modern sociotechnical infrastructures. This survey paper, which summarizes and analyses the literature, examines the duality of AI in cybersecurity, exploring its implications for strengthening digital defences and increasing the threat landscape for adversaries. We perform a thorough review of 36 cutting-edge research articles, which are organized into six important areas: self-evolving defensive paradigms, LLM-based intelligent agents, reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making, security of cyber-physical systems, human-machine co-teaming, and agent alignment. Our synthesis shows that multi-agent collaborations greatly shorten incident response times and automate discovery of vulnerabilities but are also highly vulnerable to prompt injection, training data poisoning, and physical-layer spoofing. Moreover, we identify a shift from model patches to model alignment and constitutional safety at runtime as a prerequisite for securing these systems. We believe that resilient digital defence must also be considered a sociotechnical problem, as there must be agents, autonomous systems, that are governed by other agents, aligned and constitutionally bound, and are able to collaborate, rather than operate completely separately, with human operators.
evidence_items.title: Cyber Defence, Agentic AI, and the Sociotechnical Paradigm: A Survey of AI-Driven Cybersecurity

evidence_items.summary: Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable-frame-rate codecs address this trade-off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold-based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable-frame-rate speech codec built on X-Codec-2 with an exact utterance-level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable-duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed-rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large-scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text-to-speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec's utterance-level event budget without an explicit generation-time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high-quality reconstruction and streaming text-to-speech generation. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec and https://huggingface.co/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec.
evidence_items.title: RubatoCodec: Budgeted Adaptive Speech Tokenization with Streaming Decoding

authors: Gabriel Wedson Mendon\c{c}a de Souza Veloso
evidence_items.summary: Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded-nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45-minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.
evidence_items.title: Speedrunning Relational Foundation Model Pretraining

evidence_items.summary: Semantic segmentation of 3D point cloud scenes is a crucial task for various applications. In real-world scenarios, training segmentation models often faces three concurrent forms of data insufficiency: scarcity of training scenes, scarcity of point-level annotations, and absence of 2D image sequences from which point clouds were reconstructed. Existing data-efficient algorithms typically address only one or two of these challenges, leaving the joint treatment of all three unexplored. This paper proposes a data-efficient training framework specifically designed to address the three forms of data insufficiency. Our proposed algorithm, called Point pseudo-Labeling via Open-Vocabulary Image Segmentation (PLOVIS), leverages an open-vocabulary image segmentation model as a pseudo label generator to compensate for the lack of training data. PLOVIS creates 2D images for pseudo-labeling directly from training 3D point clouds, eliminating the need for 2D image sequences. To mitigate the inherent noise and class imbalance in pseudo labels, we introduce a two-stage filtering of pseudo labels combined with a class-balanced memory bank for effective training. The two-stage filtering mechanism first removes low-confidence pseudo labels, then discards likely incorrect pseudo labels, thereby enhancing the quality of pseudo labels. Experiments on four benchmark datasets, i.e., ScanNet, S3DIS, Toronto3D, and Semantic3D, under realistic data-scarce conditions (a few tens of training 3D scenes, each annotated with only <100 3D points) demonstrate that PLOVIS consistently outperforms existing methods including standard fine-tuning strategies and state-of-the-art weakly supervised learning algorithms. Code will be made publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Data-Efficient Semantic Segmentation of 3D Point Clouds via Open-Vocabulary Image Segmentation-based Pseudo-Labeling

evidence_items.summary: Clinical metagenomic sequencing detects hundreds of organisms whose relevance to infection requires clinicians' manual interpretation. We retrospectively reviewed 4,855 specimens from 19 sampling sites, linked 1.33 million detected organisms to clinical culprit-pathogen determinations, and fine-tuned a large language model on these labels. The model recovered 92.44% of reference culprit calls in the held-out test set and 84.49% in a later cohort. In a blinded re-adjudication of 215 cases, the model matched 90.5% of culprit calls on which both expert reviewers agreed. Adjudication accuracy varied with organism identity and specimen types. mNGS-derived metrics such as read counts or genome coverage alone were insufficient to identify culprit pathogens, and organisms classified as common colonizers could still be judged causative. Certain organisms were frequently co-reported as causative in the same specimen. These findings support further evaluation of human and AI-assisted report review, particularly regarding missed pathogens, excess calls, and differences across specimen types.
evidence_items.title: Clinical pathogen adjudication in metagenomic sequencing using a large language model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Introduction Skin cancer is a growing global cause of morbidity and mortality. Rural populations are at an increased risk due to greater ultraviolet exposure and limited access to dermatology services. Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, their ability to accurately diagnose and triage skin lesions remains uncertain. Objectives To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy, triage safety and reproducibility of multimodal LLMs in interpreting skin lesions representative of rural clinical practice. Methods Seven multimodal LLMs from three developers (OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic) were evaluated using 34 histopathologically confirmed skin lesions from a rural Canadian practice. The dataset comprised paired macroscopic and dermoscopic images of both malignant and non-malignant lesions. Each image was assessed independently a total of five times by each model using a standardized prompt. Results A total of 2,380 model outputs were generated. Diagnostic accuracy varied widely across models (39.4%-72.1%). Claude Opus 4.8 achieved the highest accuracy (72.1%) and the best overall balance of sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility. GPT-5.5 Instant had the lowest specificity and highest over-triage rate, whereas Gemini 3.5 Flash had the lowest sensitivity and highest misclassification rate. Safe triage of malignant lesions ranged from 36% to 87%. Dermoscopic images significantly improved AI performance compared with macroscopic images (OR, 1.65; 95% Cl, 1.30–2.10; p < 0.001). Self-reported diagnostic confidence correlated poorly with model performance, and diagnostic reproducibility across repeated runs was moderate to almost perfect for most models. Conclusions Multimodal LLMs can interpret skin lesion images but are not yet accurate, consistent, or safe for independent diagnosis or triage.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language models for skin lesion diagnosis and triage in rural settings

authors: João Sergio dos Santos Soares Pereira
evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.
evidence_items.title: From Artificial Intelligence to Institutional Intelligence
