evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs).


OBJECTIVE
To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations.


DESIGN
Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective.


SETTING
Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026.


PARTICIPANTS
No human participants were involved.


MEASUREMENTS
Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action).


RESULTS
The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%).


LIMITATIONS
Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use.


CONCLUSION
The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations.


PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE
None.
evidence_items.title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
evidence_items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Chart reasoning requires multimodal models to interpret visual encodings, derive structured semantics, execute formal reasoning procedures, and generate evidence-grounded outputs. This survey reviews chart reasoning methodologies for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), categorizing them by their primary intervention points: data and supervision design, inference-time reasoning strategies, and model-integrated optimization. We examine how existing approaches extract chart semantics, use intermediate representations, execute reasoning workflows, ground predictions in visual evidence, and verify outputs. We also summarize major chart reasoning benchmarks and cross-paradigm empirical results, and examine limitations in current evaluation protocols and metrics. Finally, we discuss recurring challenges in synthetic-to-real generalization, semantic reconstruction, visual grounding, reasoning faithfulness, and diagnostic evaluation, outlining directions toward more reliable and generalizable chart reasoning systems.
evidence_items.title: Chart Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

organizations: Universitas Negeri Gorontalo
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced new possibilities for machine translation (MT) by allowing translation outputs to be shaped through natural-language instructions. However, evidence about how different prompt configurations affect translation quality relative to established neural machine translation (NMT) systems remains limited, particularly for Indonesian–English translation. This exploratory mixed-methods comparative study examines three prompt configurations applied to ChatGPT and compares the resulting outputs with DeepL and Google Translate across six tourism, promotional, and proverbial texts. Translation outputs were assessed computationally using cross-lingual cosine similarity from text-embedding-3-large as an exploratory indicator of semantic proximity and qualitatively through evaluations by three professional translators focusing on accuracy, appropriateness, naturalness, and discourse style. In the observed sample, DeepL and the baseline-prompt condition tended to obtain higher similarity scores for factual tourism texts, whereas contextual- and persona-prompt outputs received comparatively favorable expert evaluations in selected promotional and culturally embedded cases. Contextual prompting also produced additions beyond the wording shown in the source excerpts, indicating a trade-off between rhetorical adaptation and source fidelity. Because the corpus is small, the prompt conditions bundle several instructional features, repeated generations were not documented, and some reproducibility metadata were not archived, the findings are interpreted descriptively rather than as causal or statistically generalizable effects. The study therefore highlights a genre- and criterion-sensitive relationship among prompt configuration, semantic preservation, and functional translation quality, while underscoring the need for human verification of adaptive LLM translations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Prompt Engineering for Large Language Models-Based Translation

evidence_items.summary: Background The rapid growth of biomedical publishing in radiation oncology has created a need for automated methods to extract structured information from unstructured text. Large language models (LLMs) show promise in biomedical natural language processing, but their use for clinical trial data curation remains to be systematically evaluated. Methods We evaluated an LLM-based extraction system for radiation oncology trials on ClinicalTrials.gov. Forty-five classification questions spanning variables such as trial design, tumor type, stage, radiotherapy modality, systemic therapy, and outcomes were implemented using the data-element-extractor Python library with three open-source LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Qwen-3.6-27B). A manually curated ground-truth of 94 trials was used for performance evaluation based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Results Qwen-3.6-27B achieved the highest overall accuracy of 92.0% across all questions. For the 39 Boolean questions, it demonstrated 93.0% accuracy, 81.6% precision, 83.7% recall, and an F1-score of 82.6%, with 23 Boolean questions achieving an F1-score ≥80.0%. Three numerical questions reached accuracy ≥80.0%. Applied to the full dataset, the system characterized the clinical landscape of radiotherapy trials, detailing the prevalence of advanced techniques (e.g., 13.7% SBRT) and the integration of systemic agents, including chemotherapy (57.3%) and immunotherapy (26.1%). Conclusion LLM-based extraction can enable accurate, scalable curation of radiotherapy trial data. While challenges remain with complex categorical or numerical variables, open-source LLMs can serve as effective components of transparent, auditable clinical research pipelines.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the Automated Extraction of Radiation Oncology Trial Data at Scale from the ClinicalTrials.gov Database Using a Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Nowadays innovative technologies impact various aspects of the lives of people. The forefront of innovative technologies Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been among countries' strategic priorities in recent years in terms of economic development, transformation of public services, competitiveness, and social benefit. AI is now one of the primary powers behind both the global development race and technical innovation. Many countries think of AI as a means of competitive advantage and economic expansion, employing AI technology to analyze enormous volumes of public data. In this context, while governments establish national AI policies, international organizations offer shared principles and guidelines for the ethical, trustworthy, and human-centered application of AI, while also supporting standardization initiatives. Türkiye has published the transition process strategically and released the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) 2021–2025 document in 2021, describing its policy framework for AI. The article analyzes Türkiye's present status regarding the evolution of its AI policies, including global benchmarks, alongside the essential elements of the AI Strategy and its formulation and execution process. The strategy's multidisciplinary approach is given comprehensively, emphasizing the advancements and evaluations accomplished by NAIS.
evidence_items.title: Türkiye’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy

evidence_items.summary: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and quantum technologies are beginning to shape how countries design digital infrastructure, critical services and long-term security. However, technical work on models and architectures often evolves separately from national strategies on resilience, governance and capability building. This chapter brings these perspectives into a single structured view. We first position AGI within the evolution of artificial intelligence and explain how it differs from narrow, generative and agentic systems. The chapter groups AGI requirements into core capability areas and summarises the main architecture families that are emerging across model-centric, agentic, predictive, knowledge-integrated and system-integrated designs, together with current approaches to safety and evaluation. The second section focuses on emerging technologies that support AGI in practice. On the classical side, it describes computing and acceleration platforms, communication and 6G networks, digital twins, data and knowledge systems, and security foundations. On the quantum side, it explains how quantum computing and optimisation, quantum communication, quantum-enhanced simulation and quantum-safe security can strengthen optimisation, coordination, modelling and long-term protection for AGI-scale systems. Together, they show how AGI systems are trained, connected and protected in real environments. Building on this structure, the third section organises national AGI and quantum strategies into three layers: mission domains that guide where AGI creates public value, capability pillars that define the required technical foundations, and governance themes that link these technologies to safety and strategic readiness. Overall, the chapter provides a shared structure for researchers, engineers and policymakers who need to plan AGI as both a technical system and a national capability within a wider digital infrastructure.
evidence_items.title: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Emerging Technologies (Quantum Tech.)

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and smart technologies are transforming the way hotels function, but most studies have focused on a single application and do not quantify its operational value end to end. In this paper, we present and test five AI modules: using a common, simulated booking dataset for a resort hotel as well as for a city hotel (2015-2017) and a strict temporal train/test split, an integrated fourlayer framework (data and sensing, AI analytics, decision and automation, value) is proposed. For booking cancellation prediction, a gradient-boosting model yields well-calibrated results with an AUC of 0.845 [95% CI 0.841–0.848], with lead time, deposit policy, and distribution channel as the most important predictors. Classical methods, for forecasting occupancy from reservations made on the books, give the best results for periods up to 1 week before arrivals; by contrast, a gradient-boosting model produces accurate results at longer lead times, about 30 days prior to arrivals at the resort (MAPE 4.4% vs. 11.8% at 90 days prior). An ML risk-based overbooking policy can improve net room revenue by 0.55% and 0.32% (resort and city, respectively) compared with the historical policy and achieve 57–59% of the value of perfect information. The "K-means Segmentation" method shows 4 segments that guests can act on. Based on an hourly smartroom simulation, IoT based HVAC control saves 23.4% energy, while AI-based HVAC predictive pre-conditioning continues to save 21.2% energy without sacrificing guest comfort. Findings reveal that the value of AI within the hospitality sector depends on the horizon as well as context and integration, and offer practitioners and researchers benchmarks and open code.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Smart Technologies in the Hospitality Industry

organizations: Kocaeli University, Electronics and Telecom. Eng. Department, Kocaeli, Türkiye
evidence_items.summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has become a critical component in the deployment of deep learning-based object detection models, particularly in remote sensing applications where complex scenes, heterogeneous targets, and safety-critical decisions demand transparency and interpretability. Among XAI techniques, class activation mapping (CAM)-based methods are widely adopted; however, their relative effectiveness in object detection settings, particularly under varying scene complexity and target density, remains insufficiently explored. In this study, a systematic qualitative and quantitative evaluation of CAM-based XAI methods for target detection in optical remote sensing imagery is conducted, using the YOLOv5 architecture as the underlying detector. The evaluated methods are Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, XGrad-CAM, Eigen-CAM, Score-CAM, KPCA-CAM, Shapley-CAM, and Finer-CAM. Experiments are performed on the DIOR dataset, which provides a diverse set of object classes and scene configurations representative of real-world high-resolution remote sensing imagery. To quantitatively evaluate CAM-based explanations, a masking-based evaluation framework is employed, consisting of two primary strategies (M1 and M2), and complemented by an additional entropy-based analysis (M3). The M1 and M2 strategies evaluate the relevance and sufficiency of CAM-highlighted regions by selectively removing or preserving salient areas and analyzing the resulting changes in detection performance. In addition, an adapted M3 strategy based on Bernoulli entropy is introduced to analyze changes in the Bernoulli entropy derived from detector confidence scores under CAM-guided perturbations, providing a complementary assessment of the spatial concentration of CAM explanations around annotated targets.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of class activation mapping-based explainable artificial intelligence methods for target detection in optical remote sensing using YOLOv5

evidence_items.summary: Social behavior is a sensitive readout of brain state, but quantifying rodent social behavior at scale has relied on siloed, lab-specific tools. We assembled Days of our Mice (DooM), a benchmark of manually annotated video and pose tracking spanning 15 laboratories and 33 social and solitary behaviors, and hosted a community behavior classification challenge. We built on challenge solutions to develop the High-Dimensional Rodent Annotator (HiDRA), a behavior classification tool that generalizes to labs unseen during training and learns cross-lab movement features. Applied without retraining to experimental data, HiDRA resolves line-specific and state-dependent behavioral fingerprints with strong generalizability and reproducibility, establishing high-resolution, shareable social phenotyping as a scalable readout of brain and internal state. We release the DooM dataset and HiDRA classifiers as open resources.
evidence_items.title: A community benchmark enables high-resolution, cross-lab quantification of mouse social behavior

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Forecasting solar soft X-ray (SXR) and proton flux underpins space-weather operations, yet machine-learning work largely frames the task as flare classification, not continuous-flux prediction, and the few regression studies use one solar cycle, under-specified splits, and no baselines.We present a time-series benchmark for multi-step regression of two drivers, the GOES 1–8 ˚A SXR flux (2002–2026) and the ≥10 MeV proton flux (1999–2026), on a 5-minute cadence with historical horizons in days and forecast horizons in hours.A leakage-controlled, term-based rotating k-fold assigns half-year terms atomically, and event skill is graded against persistence and the operational National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) forecast with imbalance- and extreme-aware metrics.Across 36 settings a segment-recurrent model (SegRNN) attains the lowest root-mean-square error (RMSE) in 35, yet the aggregate ranking conceals an event-skill artefact: its SXR M-class per-day Heidke skill score (HSS) near 0.10 sits on the persistence floor, far below occurrence-persistence near 0.46, matched by the operational reference, and no model separates from the proton floor near 0.79.The impulsive SXR regime stays essentially unpredicted at 12–24 h, reaching parity only at 3–6 h despite low global error. We release the dataset and code.
evidence_items.title: A Leakage-Controlled Time-Series Forecasting Benchmark for GOES Soft X-ray and Proton Flux

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learning studies on the ann-thyroid benchmark routinely report near-perfect discrimination, yet the sources of that performance are rarely isolated and the benchmark’s own class labels are rarely questioned. We report a controlled audit of this benchmark, separating what a conventional pipeline contributes from what is inherited from the data. Ten classifiers were evaluated across ten stratified splits in a leakage-free pipeline. A 2 × 2 factorial ablation separated feature selection from class balancing; nine feature-selection methods and seven balancing strategies were compared; a parameter sweep tested the hybrid selector; and a simple threshold rule on TSH and TT4 served as a clinical baseline. Differences between methods were assessed by Friedman tests with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons and by two one-sided tests against equivalence margins fixed before the tests were run. Class labels were verified against the hormone panel and, at record level, against the diagnosis codes distributed with the same archive. The UCI files do not name their classes, and the accompanying documentation describes a hyperfunction class the data do not contain; matching against the diagnosis codes distributed in the same archive yields 3597 one-to-one correspondences with no discordance, establishing three hypothyroid-spectrum strata (overt hypothyroid, subclinical hypothyroid, euthyroid) instead, and locating 89 diagnosed hyperthyroid records inside the majority class. A majority-class baseline reaches 92.6% accuracy at macro-F1 0.320, so accuracy is uninformative. The principal clinical gain, macro-specificity rising from 0.905 to 0.987, is attributable predominantly to class balancing rather than feature selection.
evidence_items.title: Reported performance differences on the ann-thyroid benchmark reflect class labelling rather than method choice

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Actuator saturation forces two controller‐design choices: how to impose the force limit and how to represent post‐yield softening. We isolate the two choices on a reproducible OpenSeesPy reimplementation of the 3‐story and 9‐story Ohtori SAC steel‐frame benchmark structures, checked against published modal frequencies and selected uncontrolled response peaks. A matched finite‐horizon two‐by‐two factorial crosses elastic versus softened design models with post‐hoc clipping versus in‐QP actuator bounds. Across 44 3‐story evaluations using 22 FEMA P695 far‐field records at two intensity tiers, constraint handling accounts for 82% of the descriptive variance among four pooled cell‐mean costs, frequency tuning for 14%, and interaction for 4%; in the 9‐story 10‐case common‐finite‐score canonical subset the constraint‐handling share is 99.5%. Elastic in‐QP has the lowest mean under all five weight sets, yet under the primary score it loses to matched elastic clipping in 12 of 44 cases, with losses more frequent at larger uncontrolled drifts. Design‐frequency retuning stays small and inconsistent (elastic‐minus‐softened mean margin ); yield‐adaptive updating gives no consistent improvement, and a softening‐capable constitutive branch retains the principal ordering. In the transferred magnetorheological‐device comparison, powered operation reduces casewise peak drift by 19.9% on average but has a higher mean cost than zero‐current operation, and separate collapse‐limit analyses do not establish a consistent advantage for either allocation rule. For the primary score, the results prioritize actuator‐bound handling over the tested frequency retuning within the two planar frames, retaining clipping as a high‐demand comparator rather than a validated switching fallback.
evidence_items.title: Actuator‐Constraint Handling Versus Frequency Retuning in Active Seismic Control: A Two‐Height Yielding Steel‐Frame Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold3 (AF3), and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperones utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone.
evidence_items.title: Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing

evidence_items.summary: For public safety in crowded public places, less human detection is insufficient without interpretability and actionability of decision assistances. Although deep learning–based video surveillance systems have achieved accurate detection recently, the majority are restricted to passive perception and do not convert visual products into executive decisions for crowd status. This study presents an agentic AI-based decision support framework for interpretable real-time crowd status monitoring, to link vision-based perception and public safety decision. The proposed framework incorporates a YOLOv5-derived human detection module, an agentic state evaluation by considering persistability and a transparent rule-based decision making, which distinguishes scenes into crowd versus non-crowd. The human detections are temporally accumulated by counting and persistence measures to maintain stable and interpretable decision signals. The framework is tested on CCTV-style surveillance data and demonstrate consistent performance for detection, with a mean average precision of 95.3% (at IoU = 0.5) while achieving real-time processing speed of 25–30 fps on commodity hardware. The results interpretable decision logic explicitly into speech-and-video based monitoring of crowd status in safety-critical public facilities, which is practical, scalable, and explainable.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Decision-Support Framework for Interpretable Crowd Status Monitoring via YOLOv5

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) predict multiple token positions per forward pass, yet block-wise decoders serialize generation and repeatedly recompute stable predictions. We attribute this inefficiency to coupling a prediction's readiness for irreversible commitment with its utility as context. We introduce Tentative Context Pipelining (TeCoP), a training-free decoder that decouples these roles through staggered block-parallel pipelining and draft-and-verify. TeCoP reuses stable but uncommitted predictions as provisional cross-block context, with commitment governed by confidence and stability checks. Across four LLaDA and Dream dLLMs on GSM8K, Minerva MATH, and MBPP, TeCoP reduces number of forward evaluations by up to 87% and achieves up to 7.50-fold throughput without KV caching and 11.77-fold with caching over the uncached original decoder. It outperforms Fast-dLLM and DSB in throughput across all 12 model-benchmark settings, with and without caching, while keeping average cached accuracy within one percentage point of the original decoder.
evidence_items.title: TeCoP: Accelerating Diffusion Large Language Model Decoding via Tentative Context Pipelining

evidence_items.summary: Ensuring the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) with diverse cultural values is critical for their safe global deployment. However, existing alignment benchmarks are predominantly English-centric or confined to simple discriminative tasks. Moreover, they often fail to effectively evaluate model robustness against complex, adversarial inductions within specific cultural contexts. To address these limitations, we propose ABench, a fine-grained, handcrafted benchmark specifically tailored to taxonomized values in Chinese. Grounded in a rigorous hierarchical taxonomy comprising 158 derived value subcategories, ABench consists of 2,895 open-ended questions. These questions employ techniques such as role-playing and logical traps to probe the stability of models'stances in adversarially induced contexts. Furthermore, we propose a weighted automated evaluation framework that utilizes question-specific scoring criteria for nuanced assessment. Extensive experiments on 16 mainstream LLMs reveal that most models exhibit significant vulnerabilities when subjected to sophisticated adversary attacks on values (scoring below 60). This underscores the need for more robust, culturally specific alignment strategies. Our data will be publicly released to promote further research on taxonomized value alignment.
evidence_items.title: ABench: Adversarily Benchmarking Large Language Models across Taxonomized Values

evidence_items.summary: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians'ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors'internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.
evidence_items.title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI

evidence_items.summary: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.
evidence_items.title: PI-MLLM: Psychophysics-Inspired Multimodal Large Language Model for Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Code translation converts source code from one programming language to another while preserving its functionality. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved code translation, their outputs still contain hallucinations: generated code that conflicts with the source program, violates target-language facts, or introduces contextually inconsistent dependencies. These failures are especially harmful in translation because small semantic deviations can silently change program behavior. Existing hallucination studies mainly focus on natural-language generation or code generation, leaving the forms, distribution, and mitigation of hallucinations in cross-language code translation insufficiently characterized. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of LLM hallucinations in code translation. Across three benchmark datasets, six language pairs, and seven LLMs, we construct a taxonomy with three major categories: Semantic Consistency Conflicts, Factual Knowledge Conflicts, and Project Context Deviations. We manually annotate 13,919 hallucination cases and analyze how hallucination types vary across models, datasets, and language directions. Guided by the taxonomy, we further propose HaluCodeTran, a mitigation framework that combines BM25-based retrieval of relevant translation examples with taxonomy-aware reflective refinement. The study provides an execution-tested characterization of code-translation hallucinations and a practical baseline for building more reliable LLM-based code migration tools.
evidence_items.title: Hallucinations of Large Language Models in Cross-Language Code Translation: Phenomena and Mitigation

evidence_items.summary: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only"does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask"which of its core abilities remain intact?"Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.
evidence_items.title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Recent work reports that the distribution verbalized directly in the output text aligns far better with human opinion distributions than the next-token log-probability distribution of LLMs. However, the verbalized distribution reflects what LLMs know about a group's opinions (knowledge distribution), while what they actually output at deployment is governed by their log-probability distribution (behavior distribution). We find that when prompting LLMs to predict the opinion of a specific group, the most likely answer under the verbalized distribution differs from that under the log-probability distribution for 37% of World Values Survey questions, averaged over three LLMs. Thus, LLMs'knowledge does not match their behavior. This matters for evaluation: a verbalized distribution can score well against a group while its most likely answer is one the model never outputs, so the score no longer describes the model. The alignment scores for these two distributions reflect only the model's behavior or its knowledge, separately. We therefore propose a learnable combination of the two distributions that follows the most likely answer of the behavior distribution while preserving the shape of the knowledge distribution, with a single hyperparameter trading off behavioral fidelity against distribution quality. Our experiments on three opinion survey datasets and six models show that the balanced distribution improves behavioral consistency over the verbalized distribution from 71.6% to 95.6% on average, while the total variation distance to the human opinion distributions rises only slightly from 28.8% to 33.8%, and it remains effective under temperature scaling and cross-dataset settings.
evidence_items.title: Speak vs. Know: Balancing Behavior and Knowledge Distributions of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Reasoning about fine-grained placement constraints, such as support and containment, is essential for realistic 3D scene creation. It remains a significant challenge for existing methods that rely on simplified object representations like oriented bounding box (OBB), which are blind to the detailed geometry. To address this limitation, we introduce GALA, a geometry-aware language model with explicit point cloud perception for controllable object placement. Our model performs autoregressively by predicting the 6D pose of one target object at a time conditioned on the scene context and placement instruction. We utilize a two-stage training strategy: the first stage aligns geometric and textual modalities through pretraining tasks, and the second stage fine-tunes the model for placement. To facilitate this task, we also curate a multi-source scene dataset covering diverse room types and fine-grained furniture arrangements, which will be open-sourced for community benefit. Experiments on our benchmark show our model significantly outperforms baselines without explicit geometric reasoning. We further develop a multi-stage plan-place-verify agent pipeline that uses the model for text-driven scene generation. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/
evidence_items.title: GALA: Geometry-Aware Language Model for Controllable Object Arrangement

evidence_items.summary: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
evidence_items.title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have shown increasing potential in audio understanding and reasoning by generating intermediate reasoning steps before answering. However, directly eliciting long-form reasoning from audio does not always lead to more reliable predictions. Even reasoning-oriented LALMs may gradually shift from acoustic evidence to language-continuation patterns during generation. A natural solution is to use contrastive decoding with an audio-masked branch, but directly applying this strategy to plain chain-of-thought reasoning is often ineffective, since the masked branch lacks sufficient audio-related context and provides an unstable reference. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SKAD} (\textbf{Sk}etch-Guided \textbf{A}udio-Contrastive \textbf{D}ecoding), a training-free inference-time method for audio reasoning. SKAD first constructs an acoustic evidence sketch that summarizes question-relevant auditory information. It then performs contrastive decoding between an audio-conditioned reasoning branch and a sketch-only branch. By using the sketch as a shared semantic scaffold, SKAD makes the masked branch more informative and encourages decoding decisions that are more dependent on the original audio. We evaluate SKAD on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and Step-Audio-R1 across three audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks: MMAR, MMAU, and MMSU. Experimental results show that SKAD consistently improves the average accuracy of both models across all benchmarks. Further ablations show that direct contrastive decoding without the acoustic evidence sketch provides limited or negative gains, confirming the importance of constructing a reliable contrastive reference before audio-contrastive decoding.
evidence_items.title: SKAD: Sketch-Guided Audio-Contrastive Decoding for Reasoning in Large Audio-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Persuasive writing exploits cognitive biases, recruiting a reader's mental shortcuts to shape belief, often without the reader noticing. We call the linguistic features exploiting such mental shortcuts cognitive bias triggers. As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people encounter news, summarizing it, ranking it, and answering questions over it, a natural question is whether they can recognize the features of a text that bias a human reader. We introduce BAIT (Bias Annotation In Text), a resource for detecting cognitive bias triggers in news. BAIT pairs a schema of nine triggers, each specified in an annotator codebook, with 50 English news articles annotated by trained annotators at the article and span levels and adjudicated into a gold standard. On this data we define two tasks, detecting which triggers a text contains and locating the spans that carry them. We then benchmark six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three or ten in-context examples. The models approach human agreement on which triggers an article contains, but rarely recover its full set of triggers, and they reach less than half of human agreement in locating the passages that carry them. Moreover, they over-predict triggers that come with easy surface cues, and most of the passages they mark for these triggers are not triggers, yet carry the trigger's surface cue far more often than random text. These findings suggest that the evaluated LLMs respond to surface cues rather than to the mechanisms that make a passage manipulative. We release the schema, the codebook, standoff annotations, and the evaluation pipeline.
evidence_items.title: BAIT: Can LLMs Find What Biases a Reader? A Benchmark for Cognitive Bias Triggers in News

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.
evidence_items.title: TriGeoBench: A Multimodal Mathematical Geometry Benchmark with Figures and TikZ

evidence_items.summary: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
evidence_items.title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V

evidence_items.summary: Instruction-based image editing models can now add, remove a specified number of objects or change their category while preserving the scene. Yet these models often fail to produce the correct number, and these failures grow sharply as scenes become more complex and the requested count increases. Current benchmarks largely miss this problem: they score edits with holistic similarity metrics or with vision-language model (VLM) judges that are themselves poor at counting, so numerical errors go unnoticed or are graded incorrectly. As a result, the true numerical ability of today's editing models has never been accurately measured. We address this issue with ABACUS, a new benchmark, evaluation protocol and dedicated scoring metric for numerical image editing. Our protocol is judge-free: no VLM or MLLM scores an edit or counts objects (a VLM only confirms the category of rare ambiguous crops). Instead, it verifies each edit at the instance level against panoptic ground truth confirmed by detector consensus, checking both that the exact requested count was achieved and that the rest of the scene was preserved, across the add, remove and change operations. By evaluating leading image editors, our method reveals substantial numerical editing failures that worsen with increasing scene complexity and object count; failures that prior benchmarks often overlooked or misjudged.
evidence_items.title: ABACUS: A Benchmark for Image Editing Models to Assess Object Category and Counting Under Scene Conservation

evidence_items.summary: Despite advances in photorealism, semantic fidelity, and aesthetics, text-to-image generation and image editing remain understudied in a human-centered dimension: whether their outputs feel psychologically comforting. Grounded in cognitive evaluation theory, we define psychological comfort as an affective response shaped by viewers'appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive visual cues. We introduce HealBench, a fine-grained benchmark of 30,000 high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 categories and 92 subcategories, selected from 100,000 candidates through a human- and expert-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language model matching, human preference models, expert filtering, and exemplar-guided augmentation. We also construct HealBench-Eval, a feature-clustered evaluation set of 1,095 instances. Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies. Results reveal a gap between conventional visual quality and perceived comfort: strong semantic alignment and aesthetics do not guarantee emotionally restorative images. Reinforcement learning experiments further show that HealScorer can serve as a reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings establish psychological comfort as a distinct dimension of human-centered image generation and position HealBench as a foundation for affect-aware generative models.
evidence_items.title: HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Existing reasoning evaluations typically provide task-relevant information to models as available premises, rarely examining concurrently how models discover evidence autonomously and how information presentation within narratives guides or obscures judgment. This paper proposes the WORTH Benchmark: models read original mystery narratives without clue annotations, autonomously select key clue sentences, identify case participants, and explain their reasoning process. The narrative materials are designed by professional authors such that evidence facilitating reasoning coexists with narrative arrangements that delay the revelation of truth. We report a pilot experiment under full-story conditions across two episodes, conducting a total of 70 formal runs on models, of which 67 runs are content-scorable. Scoring separately records hits on author-designated key clue sentences and participant selections; natural language explanations are used for case diagnosis and are not scored independently. The results show that clue hits and participant judgments are not synchronized; across 37 content-scorable runs in Episode 02, 31 runs simultaneously selected the same set of incorrect participants, while adjacent suspicion-oriented and exoneration-oriented sentences were selected 25 times and 0 times, respectively. These phenomena illustrate the diagnostic value of component-wise analysis and suggest that not-fully-cooperative informational relationships may influence evidence selection and judgment. This study only implements full-story conditions for two episodes, and does not establish stable model rankings or infer general mechanisms on this basis; human player records have not yet been cleaned, and this version does not report human-model comparisons.
evidence_items.title: WORTH Benchmark: Evidence Discovery under Not-Fully-Cooperative Information -- A Two-Episode Pilot

evidence_items.summary: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
evidence_items.title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as research collaborators for hypothesis refinement, methodological planning, and technical analysis across multi-turn interactions. In this setting, a useful assistant must be accurate, methodologically justified, logically consistent, and token-efficient. Current alignment approaches rarely achieve all of these together. Instruction-tuned models gain conversational quality through verbosity, and we show that science-agnostic general collaborative rewards compress responses at the expense of scientific rigor. We propose CollabSciReM, a goal-conditioned reward framework that decomposes the session-level reward into conversational quality, scientific rigor, and structural efficiency. We also introduce SciQuality, a pairwise evaluation of multi-turn research conversations grounded in 300 held-out scientific papers and scored on six dimensions: methodological soundness, justification, logical consistency, factual correctness, novelty, and responsiveness. Fine-tuned on 8.62K synthetic research conversations, CollabSciReM is preferred on SciQuality over a science-agnostic reward baseline trained on the same data for all four Llama and Qwen models, including a 65.3% win rate at matched response length. For the 7B and 8B models, CollabSciReM outperforms the science-agnostic reward baseline on the primary metric in 8 of 10 single- and multi-turn benchmark settings. In a blind study, domain experts rated CollabSciReM significantly higher on novelty than the general-reward variant and reported fewer hallucinated responses than both the general-reward variant and the base model.
evidence_items.title: CollabSciReM: Aligning Language Models for Scientific Conversations via Science-Aware Reward Decomposition

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVES
To evaluate whether increasing agentic architectural complexity via self-reflection or multiagent design improves clinical code status extraction (Do Not Resuscitate [DNR], Do Not Intubate [DNI], Comfort Measures Only [CMO]) across open-source large language models (LLMs) of varying capabilities.


MATERIALS AND METHODS
We conducted a controlled cross-model comparison evaluating 3 architectures: (1) single extractor agent, (2) single agent with self-reflection, and (3) sequential multiagent extractor-reviewer system. Four open-source LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B) were evaluated on 1000 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV-Note discharge summaries. Ground truth labels were established through a physician-AI dual review with adjudication (Cohen's κ = 0.98-0.99). Models were evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Cohen's κ, token consumption, and processing latency. McNemar's test was used for paired comparisons.


RESULTS
For capable larger models (GPT-OSS-20B, MedGemma-27B-IT, Qwen3.5-27B), single-agent architectures achieved comparable or superior performance for explicit code status (DNR, DNI) relative to complex systems, whereas multiagent review doubled token consumption and latency without accuracy gains. Reflective self-review significantly impaired MedGemma-27B-IT on DNI extraction (P = .047). For the smaller DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, multiagent review provided statistically significant corrective benefits for DNR (P = .017) and CMO (P < .001), demonstrating a capability-threshold effect, though performance remained below clinically acceptable levels.


DISCUSSION
Architectural complexity does not enhance extraction performance for capable LLMs, and reflective self-review may cause conservative overcorrection. Multiagent verification value is inversely related to model capability.


CONCLUSION
Single-agent LLMs provide optimal accuracy and efficiency for explicit clinical extraction in capable models. Agentic complexity must be matched to both task characteristics and model capability rather than adopted by default.
evidence_items.title: Agentic artificial intelligence for code status extraction from clinical notes: a cross-model comparison of single agent, reflective agent, and multiagent extractor-reviewer system.

evidence_items.summary: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings

evidence_items.summary: Visual anomaly detection aims to detect abnormal objects, while anomaly samples are often scarce during model training. Assembling multiple pretrained detectors can help by leveraging their transferable image scores and anomaly maps. However, most existing ensemble methods apply fixed fusion rules over saved predictions which struggle when pretrained detectors clearly disagree due to different training objectives, priors, and visual representations. To this end, we design AnomalyAgent, a post-training fusion framework for accurate visual anomaly detection. AnomalyAgent aligns heterogeneous scores and maps, summarizes score- and region-level disagreement, and treats fusion as a finite action-selection problem. It implements two types of actions: 1) score actions that determine how to fuse image-level detector confidence via consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, or score-map consistency; 2) map actions that fuse dense anomaly responses via consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, or disagreement correction. A constrained vision-language model (VLM) is introduced to inspect high-conflict samples and select valid score action and map action to produce the final prediction. We evaluate AnomalyAgent on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks, together with seven additional public anomaly benchmarks and Real-IAD for large-scale score-level evaluation. Across these benchmarks, AnomalyAgent consistently improves over equal-weight fusion and achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among the compared fusion methods on MVTec AD and VisA, while demonstrating robust transfer across additional anomaly domains.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Ensemble with Vision-Language Models for Visual Anomaly Detection

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents UvA-MT's submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation shared task, competing in the unconstrained track across all 23 translation directions. This year, we fully leverage the test-time methods of Large Language Models (LLMs) for machine translation. Specifically, (1) we use sequential sampling with a refinement prompt to generate a pool of translation candidates for each source segment, a strategy shown to outperform traditional parallel sampling; and (2) we employ LLMs as pairwise judges to select the best candidate via a round-robin voting mechanism, with offline evaluation on the WMT25 benchmark showing a very clear improvement over point-wise best-of-N selection. Combined, these two strategies form our WMT26 submission.
evidence_items.title: UvA-MT's Participation in the WMT26 General Translation Shared Task

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are expected to estimate their own uncertainty, with confidence signals used to guide retrieval, adaptive compute allocation, routing, and selective abstention. We investigate whether confidence signals measured at different temporal stages of problem solving encode distinct forms of epistemic information and remain reliable beyond English-centric settings. Inspired by classical meta-memory theory, we distinguish anticipatory pre-solve confidence (Feeling-of-Knowing, FOK) from retrospective post-solve confidence (Judgement-of-Learning, JOL). We evaluate these signals across two frontier LLMs, multiple reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and a newly constructed benchmark of genuinely local Marathi factual questions. Across settings, the cheaper pre-solve signal remains weakly calibrated, while post-solve confidence generally provides stronger epistemic alignment despite its additional inference cost. Confidence behaviour transfers surprisingly well under direct language translation, with calibration trends largely preserved between English and Marathi, but degrades substantially on local Marathi knowledge, suggesting that linguistic transfer alone is insufficient for region-specific information needs. Finally, hallucinated responses maintain persistently elevated confidence after answer generation, highlighting important limitations of current LLM self-assessment mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Calibration: Temporal LLM Confidence Assessment Across Languages and Local Settings

evidence_items.summary: Large language models can achieve strong Text-to-SQL benchmark performance while still producing schema and query-logic errors. Most evaluations characterize such failures only in the final generated query, making it difficult to determine whether a related error was also observed in an earlier, simpler step or appears only at the final stage. We present a drill-down evaluation framework that decomposes Text-to-SQL queries into progressively more complex executable sub-queries and corresponding natural-language questions, allowing rule-based hallucination categories to be examined across a generation path. We distinguish recurrent hallucinations, in which the same rule-based category is observed in an earlier step and again in the final query, from emergent hallucinations, in which the category is observed at the final step without an earlier detection in the same path. Across five LLMs evaluated on an expanded BIRD-mini benchmark, several categories show appreciable recurrence probabilities, while clause abuse shows comparatively higher conditional emergence. Under the conversational-history condition, recurrence probabilities are generally higher and emergence probabilities are generally lower. These observations indicate that the two conditional measures do not move uniformly in the same direction under additional context and motivate trajectory-level analysis in addition to final-output evaluation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available in the project repository. https://github.com/HaydenMM/bird-mini-drilldown
evidence_items.title: Tracing Recurrent and Emergent Hallucination Patterns in Decomposed Text-to-SQL Generation

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.
evidence_items.title: DIVE: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Interaction with Visual Engagement in Continuous Streams

evidence_items.summary: Mathematical reasoning remains underexplored for low-resource languages, including Dialectal Arabic. To bridge this gap, we introduce the DAR-MGSM (Dialectal Arabic Multilingual Grade School Math) Benchmark, the first manually curated benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in Dialectal Arabic. DAR-MGSM consists of math word problems (MWPs) requiring multi-step reasoning and covers five major Arabic dialects alongside Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The benchmark comprises two parallel versions: translated-only and translated&culturally localized. The latter version adapts entities and references to regional varieties. We evaluate eleven Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models on DAR-MGSM. The results show that the performance generally declines on the localized version, highlighting the challenges introduced by culturally grounded adaptations. However, the magnitude of this effect varies across models, with Arabic-centric models exhibiting different levels of sensitivity to localization. A mechanistic interpretability analysis shows that translated and localized variants of the same MWPs often induce distinct internal reasoning trajectories, even when aggregate accuracy remains similar. Overall, our results show that mathematical reasoning performance depends on both linguistic variety and cultural context.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Arabic Dialects for Math Problems

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon language agents requires identifying whether intermediate actions make eventual task success more or less likely when supervision is available only at trajectory level. The main difficulty is that a critic with aggregate return-prediction accuracy may still fail to resolve the local value differences needed to assign credit to actions, especially under sparse feedback and function approximation. Conventional critics estimate future return, but policy improvement also depends on knowing whether each intermediate decision makes task success more or less likely. We introduce SCALE, an actor-critic framework that augments conventional return estimation with explicit prediction of eventual task success. At each interaction prefix, the critic predicts a return value and a Success Value, defined as the probability that the task will eventually be completed from that prefix. SCALE converts changes in Success Value into multi-step action credit through Success-GAE and modulates its contribution according to the estimated reliability of the predictor, while retaining the token-level PPO objective. Across five agent benchmarks and three model backbones, SCALE improves task performance over the compared RL baselines in most settings, with gains of up to 4.1 percentage points in success rate. Separate critic-learning analyses show that SCALE also improves critic estimation and training stability.
evidence_items.title: From Outcomes to Steps: Reliable Success-Aware Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Agents

evidence_items.summary: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others'expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.
evidence_items.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents are often given an inference budget and asked to maximise success within it. A multi-turn agent has to allocate this budget across many environment interactions. An external harness can enforce the budget, but it remains unclear whether the agent itself can learn when and how much to spend. We ask whether agents can learn this allocation across dynamically specified budgets and which rewards best teach this behaviour. We adapt existing length penalties to budget constraints spanning multiple resource types, introduce new reward formulations, and compare eleven objectives in a shared training pipeline. We train Qwen3.5 models at 4B and 9B on AppWorld with budgets over tokens, API calls, and environment steps, and on the BabyAI gridworld with turn budgets. We train a separate policy for each environment and resource type, with each policy trained across budget values. Training with rewards that penalise overspending substantially improves within-budget success and natural compliance over untrained models and over training on task success alone, with agents learning to adapt their resource use to stated budgets and task difficulty. These gains extend to unseen budgets and, zero-shot, to a shifted task distribution and a new benchmark. Reward objectives trade off success within budget and natural compliance. A sigmoid penalty for overspending most often achieves the highest within-budget success at an individual budget, while a fixed negative reward for overspending generally yields the strongest natural compliance. Combining penalties for overspend frequency and magnitude gives the smallest average gap to the best method at each budget. Overall, we show that a single agent can learn to allocate resources across turns and adapt its behaviour to user-specified budgets using budget feedback without external budget-allocation controllers.
evidence_items.title: Rewards for Budget-Aware Multi-Turn Agents That Adapt to Arbitrary Test-Time Constraints

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute business operations through tools and interact directly with application data and services. Beyond completing user requests, these agents must obey domain-specific business rules that constrain when actions are permitted and what data or resources may be affected. Violating such rules can lead to business logic bugs, even when a task appears successful. Detecting these bugs is difficult because the rules are rarely available as explicit, testable specifications. They are distributed across system prompts and tool definitions, while others remain implicit in domain knowledge. Existing agent testing approaches typically evaluate task success, predefined policies, or known attack scenarios. This limits their ability to systematically uncover previously unspecified business-rule violations. We present AgenTest, which mines business rules from system prompts, tool definitions, and domain knowledge, refines them into Given-When-Then specifications, and systematically tests each specification. For each extracted specification, AgenTest instantiates its Given conditions by constructing a satisfying environment state and simulated user, exercises the agent through multi-turn interactions, and checks its Then conditions over messages, tool calls, and state changes using a hybrid oracle. On the airline, retail, and telecom agents of tau2-bench with two underlying models, AgenTest produces 551 refined specifications, and detects violations of 89 and 121 distinct specifications, respectively -- 3.4X and 2.5X as many as all baselines combined. Only AgenTest detects cases where an agent improperly accesses or modifies another user's data. Moreover, about 60% of bug-triggering runs cannot be detected from the final state alone, highlighting the need to check the full interaction against explicit business rules.
evidence_items.title: AgenTest: Mining Business Rules to Test LLM Agents for Business Logic Bugs

evidence_items.summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
