evidence_items.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

evidence_items.summary: We present our solution to the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, where we achieved a score of 0.6836 on the official leaderboard, more than double the baseline of 0.2964. This task requires generating all possible objects for subject-relation pairs using a language model with up to 32 billion parameters, with no retrieval or fine-tuning involved. We show that the prompting methodology is as important as the model architecture: while the instruction-tuned model version achieves 0.5681 with its chat interface, the base model achieves 0.6836 when prompted using text completion. Thus, instruction tuning decreases factual recall; we refer to this effect as the instruction tax, which is caused by the model's weights rather than the prompting method. Our final solution is fairly straightforward: we prompt the base model with some examples from the training data, generate 64--256 outputs, and retain only the repeated ones. Two specialized methods are then applied for each relation: one improves the recall of large answer sets, and the other verifies a person's vitality before predicting their place of death.
evidence_items.title: The Instruction Tax on Factual Recall: Base Models Can Beat Their Instruction-Tuned Counterparts

evidence_items.summary: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
evidence_items.title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning

organizations: University of Zurich
evidence_items.summary: Speech act classification aims to assign communicative functions to utterances, a task that is central to understanding pragmatic aspects of language. Automating this process can substantially reduce the need for manual annotation, enabling large-scale pragmatic analysis. In this study, we evaluate different automatic classification approaches on the SPICE Ireland dataset. This dataset has been pragmatically annotated according to Searle’s taxonomy of illocutionary acts. We compare traditional machine learning models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models), a fine-tuned RoBERTa language model, and GPT-4o using zero- and few-shot prompting. Finally, by fine-tuning GPT-4o, we achieve the best performance with an accuracy of 87% and a macro average F1-score of 66%. A qualitative analysis of disagreement cases further indicates that fine-tuned GPT-4o often produces predictions that align with expert judgments, suggesting that some disagreements between model predictions and reference labels may reflect annotation ambiguity or context sensitivity rather than clear model errors.
evidence_items.title: Empirical Evaluation of Automatic Speech Act Classification: From Logistic Regression to GPT-4o

evidence_items.summary: Examining existing benchmarks for grounding in 3D VLMs reveals a pervasive"semantic leakage"in the evaluation and prompting protocols: a heavy reliance on bounding boxes as spatial prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes are highly informative of object categories, they introduce a shortcut for the models to neglect visual information during 3D VLM training. We demonstrate this with a"blind"LLM that, prompted only with the box coordinates, can perform surprisingly well. To further analyze this shortcut, we propose point-based grounding prompting - querying models with a single 3D point instead of a box. Under this protocol, the accuracy of the blind LLM drops from 36.4% to 18.0% on ScanNet's Nr3D, and similarly degrades for 3D VLMs (e.g. LL3DA). Building on this insight, we introduce P$^3$-VLM, a novel tri-pathway 3D VLM that supports point-based prompts and achieves 52.1% state-of-the-art accuracy on location-grounded captioning under this setting. To achieve this, we redesign the architecture while keeping it detector-free, scene-centric, and suitable for 3D GS inputs. P$^3$-VLM utilizes three complementary pathways (location-, task-, and context-aware), enabling strong reasoning about scenes without any bounding box dependencies. The key benefit of point-based learning is a consistent improvement across settings: P$^3$-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance under point-based grounding while also improving robustness, OOD generalization, and performance on ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA benchmarks, reflecting its reduced reliance on bounding-box shortcuts and resulting stronger visual-spatial reasoning.
evidence_items.title: P$^3$-VLM: A Point-based Alternative for Grounded 3D Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0-5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language- or grammar-specific failure.
evidence_items.title: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing

evidence_items.summary: Common instruction following (IF) benchmarks, such as IFEval, evaluate the ability of language models (LMs) to follow simple constraints that can easily be verified programmatically. These same constraints, in turn, are used as reward signals for reinforcement learning. This design may lead to reward hacking of constraints, pushing models away from the main task. Recent attempts to address this resulted in benchmarks with richer constraints, but required expert labor, remained closed-access, and cannot be easily extended. We present Lift-Bench, an IF benchmark that asks a model to draft a document given a topic and a structured outline. Constraints are scoped to certain document sections, providing finer control over constraint density. Lift-Bench includes both verifiable and judged constraints, as well as a training counterpart, Lift-Train. Importantly, Lift-Bench provides both main task and instruction-following constraints, mitigating shallow reward hacking. On experiments with multiple models, we find that frontier models struggle with the harder subsets of our benchmark and analyze model performance along multiple axes. We also find that training on Lift-Train is much less susceptible to reward hacking than training on the common IFTrain. Lift-Bench and Lift-Train are publicly available, as well as the data generating pipeline.
evidence_items.title: LIFT: Scoped Constraints for Evaluating and Training Instruction Following

evidence_items.summary: Generative reward models (GenRMs) generate natural language rationales to justify preference judgments, yet a correct verdict does not guarantee a sound justification. Existing approaches often rely on reference explanations to supervise rationales, but obtaining such references can be costly and does not necessarily establish whether generated rationales support the resulting verdict. To address these limitations, we propose DeCert, a framework that evaluates the validity and verdict consistency of generated rationales without requiring reference explanations. Crucially, DeCert translates these assessments into preference supervision that accounts for both verdict correctness and justification quality. In particular, when multiple sampled judgments share the same correct verdict, differences in certificate quality enable DeCert to construct rationale preference pairs that distinguish stronger from weaker justifications. Extensive empirical studies across two model families and multiple in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that DeCert consistently outperforms strong generative judge baselines while improving rationale quality. Moreover, DeCert effectively mitigates positional bias, improving position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.8 points. These results highlight the importance of supervising not only which verdict is correct, but also how that verdict is justified.
evidence_items.title: Judging the Justification: Decision Certificate Supervision for Generative Reward Models

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built from language models are deployed on the premise that collaboration beats a single-agent system (SAS), yet when it pays is unclear. The most systematic study to date gives a capability-saturation rule: coordination helps while the SAS is weak and hurts once it is strong, with the crossing near 45% single-agent accuracy. That rule was derived on autonomous benchmarks, where no user takes part. We test it where agents now work: in conversation with a user under a written policy, on $\tau^2$-bench, the dual-control benchmark. On its airline, retail and telecom domains we compare the stock SAS with a centralized MAS built from the same model for six models from three families, over about 7,950 simulated conversations, with one completion-token ledger per episode per system. The study was pre-registered with a public change log; the MAS is reported as built, with one validity bar unmet (its planner never saw the tool schemas). Under a fixed simulated user no cell shows a MAS benefit: the MAS is worse in 12 of the 13 valid cells and tied in the thirteenth, and the fitted gain is negative across the observed capability range (weighted mean -28 points, 95% CI [-44, -12]). On the two cells where the rule predicts a benefit, the MAS loses by 13 and 22 points, and without a budget ceiling it at best draws level at 5.5 times the SAS's token spend. The one gain appears on the cell nearest 45%, under a second simulator. Whether the gain declines with capability is unresolved (slope -0.41, 95% CI [-1.51, +0.68]), because model-by-domain effects dominate. The MAS does not detectably reduce wrongful database writes; it converts other failures into budget exhaustion and inaction. For agents that serve people, the SAS is the default; a multi-agent design must show compute-matched evidence from the setting itself. We release all trajectories, ledgers, prompts and code.
evidence_items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? Testing Agent Scaling in Dual-Control Settings

evidence_items.summary: VLMs for medical image interpretation are typically evaluated on clean inputs, despite the progressive evidence loss that can occur in high stakes clinical settings. Existing robustness studies show that performance can degrade while confidence remains high, but do not establish when a previously reliable model-case pair ceases to behave reliably. We introduce a baseline-anchored framework that traces baseline-correct cases through progressive image degradation to identify an empirical evidence boundary, and define mirage as continued commitment at this boundary, regardless of correctness. Across three VLMs on three medical datasets, only MedGemma provides a sufficiently large baseline-correct pool for trajectory analysis. On VQA-RAD, the only dataset in which the question text varies, language-only answerability is associated with baseline correctness (AUROC 0.677) and with commitment at the boundary (AUROC 0.653 to 0.670). MedGemma's post-boundary behavior is heterogeneous, including direct mirage, correct recovery, mirage dissolution, consistent abstention, and oscillation, with mirage rates of 16.0 to 100.0% across dataset-modality pairs. Despite this behavioral heterogeneity, residual-stream probes decode commit-versus-abstain behavior at the boundary with AUROC of 0.895 to 0.994 under nested cross-validation. These results show that progressive evidence loss can produce persistent commitment that output entropy and abstention behavior do not consistently reflect, motivating boundary-aware evaluation, option-order controls, and improved abstention mechanisms for reliable medical foundation models operating under partial observation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Evidence Boundary: Behavioral Mirage Under Progressive Degradation in Medical VLMs

evidence_items.summary: We investigate associative creativity in descriptions of abstract visual stimuli by humans and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). While conceptual association is central to human communication, it remains unclear how humans and models adapt when visual stimuli become increasingly difficult to map onto familiar semantic concepts. We evaluate several state-of-the-art MLLMs and human participants along two dimensions of creativity, originality and effectiveness, using two datasets with controlled manipulations of difficulty. SilCC varies naming difficulty through progressively more complex combinations of abstract shapes, and PixCC varies difficulty through increasing levels of random visual noise. Results show that humans produce more diverse associative descriptions than MLLMs, including greater semantic distance, higher entropy, and more novel expressions relative to reference lexica. As difficulty increases, effectiveness declines in SilCC, and humans increasingly shift from holistic associations to descriptions of low-level visual properties in PixCC.
evidence_items.title: Testing Associative Creativity in Humans and Multimodal LLMs with Difficult-to-Name Visual Stimuli

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models have shown strong code generation capabilities, yet their outputs often contain subtle bugs. Automatically repairing such code requires informative tests: inputs that expose faulty behavior, paired with correct expected outputs. Recent RL-based test generation methods apply the same outcome reward to all reasoning steps, which can discourage useful reasoning and reinforce flawed steps. They also fail to effectively learn from trajectories that find bug-triggering inputs but predict incorrect outputs, leaving their verified bug-triggering progress insufficiently exploited. To address these limitations, we propose SCALF, a process-supervised RL approach that combines Step-level Credit Assignment with targeted Learning from valuable Failed trajectories. SCALF derives step-specific advantages from process rewards, allowing each reasoning stage to receive its own learning signal. It further routes trajectories that expose bugs but predict incorrect outputs to on-policy self-distillation, using execution feedback to learn from their valuable bug-triggering progress. Across three benchmarks, SCALF outperforms strong prompting and post-training baselines by up to 2.97, 5.26, and 3.53 percentage points in joint success rate, output correctness rate, and bug-triggering rate, respectively. Our code and datasets are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALF-F4D1.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing Bug-Exposing Test Generation via Step-Level Credit Assignment and Self-Distillation from Valuable Failures

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can leverage semantic feature names alongside summary statistics for tabular feature selection, yet it remains unclear when such information improves subset selection relative to established statistical methods. We investigate this question within an 18-dataset framework comprising 10 datasets for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training, 2 for checkpoint validation, and 6 held-out evaluation datasets. We compare five classical baselines, frozen Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.3-70B selectors, and two GRPO-adapted Qwen2.5-7B models, reporting classification ROC-AUC and regression R^2 separately and using dataset-wise ranks for cross-task comparison. Across five seeded evaluation partitions, classical selectors generally achieve higher predictive performance than the tested 7B LLM/RL selectors, including under a pre-specified ~33% feature budget with strict train-only classical fitting, while the 7B selectors retain compact subsets. A cardinality-matched semantic sensitivity experiment shows that, for Zero-shot Qwen-7B, informative feature names improve regression performance over anonymized and shuffled alternatives (+0.1964 and +0.1606 mean R^2), whereas aggregate classification differences are smaller (+0.0159 and +0.0084 ROC-AUC) and dataset-dependent. These results characterize when semantic information benefits LLM-based feature selection and show that classical selectors remain strong baselines for predictive tabular feature selection.
evidence_items.title: When Do LLMs Help with Feature Selection? A Systematic Empirical Study

evidence_items.summary: With increasing autonomy, Large Language Models (LLMs) may engage in deceptive behaviors, such as scheming to pursue misaligned goals or sandbagging to escape oversight. Monitoring outputs alone is insufficient, as models can produce seemingly benign responses while harboring misaligned internal objectives. While mechanistic approaches like linear probing are promising, they rely on the assumption that deception corresponds to a single direction in representation space. We demonstrate that such single-direction probes fail to generalize across diverse deception scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose representing deception as a multi-dimensional subspace rather than a single direction. Our method utilizes iterative orthogonal decomposition to identify complementary directions that capture distinct facets of deceptive intent. To effectively leverage these directions for detection, we find that static combinations prove brittle due to strong domain dependence across different scenarios. We therefore introduce a domain-adaptive gating mechanism that dynamically composes the extracted directions through few-shot adaptation at test time. With only 10 examples, our approach achieves an average AUROC of 0.97 and 94% recall at 5% FPR across all evaluated datasets, substantially outperforming existing methods.
evidence_items.title: Why Static Probes Fail: Context Determines Deception Feature Composition

evidence_items.summary: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: Gaze2HOI: Gaze-Aware Intention Disambiguation for Egocentric Hand-Object Interaction Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and recent work shows that such associations can be implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the description that a prompt omits. Existing prompt optimizers are not well suited to this task. Gradient-based methods require backward access to the scoring encoder. Discrete evolutionary search treats semantically unrelated tokens as equally close. Language-model-guided search requires one inference call per candidate, which limits exploration. This paper presents EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers concepts present in a set of images but absent from the prompt that generated them. EmbGA keeps the population structure of genetic search but applies its operators in the token embedding space. Crossover interpolates between parent embeddings, and mutation moves an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is then projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, so every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence. We evaluate EmbGA on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets. EmbGA achieves the highest alignment when the exploration budget is large, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than language-model-guided search.
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Prompt: Recovering Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation over visually rich documents requires evidence at a finer granularity than entire pages. Existing visual retrievers typically index or return full pages, whereas training region-level retrievers often requires costly query-to-region annotations or noisy model-generated labels. We introduce GARRET, a region-retrieval framework trained from (page, question, answer) triplets through differentiable generative feedback. A shared context-preserving retriever produces page and region multi-vector representations. During training, their retrieval scores define a soft routing distribution over candidate region crops. An auxiliary vision-language model attends to each crop separately, aggregates crop-specific contexts using the routing weights, and predicts the question followed by the answer under a next-token prediction objective. Gradients through the routing distribution assign query-conditioned credit to the indexed region representations, without requiring query-to-region annotations. At inference, the auxiliary model is removed. GARRET also reuses the contextualized region representations, together with page summary tokens, to construct a compact page representation. We introduce ViDoRe-V3-Region, a corpus-wide benchmark containing 200,682 fixed candidate regions across eight domains. GARRET achieves a macro nDCG@10 of 0.4126, outperforming the strongest visual baseline by 2.94 points. On page retrieval, it remains comparable to ColQwen2.5-v0.2 while indexing 47.8% fewer vectors per page.
evidence_items.title: GARRET: Generative Feedback for Region Retrieval in Visual Documents

evidence_items.summary: Agent harnesses are executable code that specifies the prompts, tools, and control flow around a language model. A single global harness can struggle with heterogeneous tasks that require different execution strategies. In this work, we introduce Object-Oriented Harness (OO-Harness), a harness optimization framework that evolves a hierarchy of executable harness classes using object-oriented design. During training, an evolution agent uses execution records to create a family of specialized harnesses, each implemented as a subclass of the base or an existing specialized harness via inheritance. At test time, a harness router uses routing lessons accumulated during training to select a specific harness for each task. Across three long-horizon benchmarks spanning business workflows, workspace tasks, and tool use, OO-Harness achieves the best performance among the compared methods, with an absolute improvement of up to 15% over the base. Extensive ablation studies examine the contributions of its core components.
evidence_items.title: Object-Oriented Harness: Evolving Agent Harnesses through Object-Oriented Design

evidence_items.summary: Identifying recipe entities and linking them to ontology concepts is fundamental for semantic recipe understanding. However, food mentions in recipes are often ambiguous, context-dependent, and lexically diverse, making ontology entity linking (EL) challenging. We propose SCODEL, a streamlined, model-agnostic approach based on a central idea: contextual food mentions and ontology concepts that refer to the same entity should learn the same canonical ontology-oriented definition. SCODEL uses these shared definitions as a semantic normalisation layer, providing complementary semantic information to existing EL models without requiring a new linking architecture. We further introduce ReciLinkD, the first benchmark for contextual food ontology entity linking in recipes. Experiments show that SCODEL consistently improves three modular EL models (ReFinED, GSM-EL, and BLINK): SCODEL x BLINK achieves the highest Hit@1 on seen concepts (88.33%), while SCODEL x GSM-EL achieves the highest Hit@1 on unseen concepts (83.15%), outperforming the strongest large language model (LLM) based EL baseline in each setting. Experiments on a biomedical ontology benchmark further demonstrate that SCODEL generalises beyond the food domain. Finally, we use SCODEL to ground food mentions at scale and construct an ontology-grounded recipe knowledge graph, demonstrating its utility for ontology-aware recipe retrieval and corpus-level food analysis.
evidence_items.title: SCODEL: Shared Canonical Ontology Definitions for Food Entity Linking and Ontology-Grounded Recipe Knowledge Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.
evidence_items.title: Staged Continual Adaptation of Multimodal Foundation Models for Japanese Financial Documents

evidence_items.summary: Accurate and efficient document layout analysis is critical for modern document parsing systems. However, although the YOLO framework represents a leading paradigm for the real-time detector, its adaptation to heterogeneous documents remains underexplored. To address this gap, we propose DocLayout-YOLO, a document-specialized real-time detector that integrates diverse synthetic document pretraining and page-axis context modeling. From the data perspective, we introduce MeshLayout-1M, a synthetic pretraining corpus generated by the proposed Mesh-candidate BestFit algorithm, which provides large-scale and diverse document layouts for pretraining and improves adaptation to heterogeneous document scenarios. From the model perspective, we propose Page-Axis Layout Attention (PALA), which captures long-range dependencies along the horizontal and vertical page axes while remaining computationally efficient. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DocLayout-YOLO achieves state-of-the-art performance on four heterogeneous document benchmarks, obtaining 72.4%/75.5%/96.0%/73.1% mAP50:95 on D4LA, M6Doc, HJDataset, and PRIMA-LAD, respectively. Compared with existing real-time detectors, DocLayout-YOLO establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off in document layout analysis. Code, model, and data are available at https://github.com/opendatalab/DocLayout-YOLO/tree/release-v2.
evidence_items.title: DocLayout-YOLO: Axis-Attentive Document Layout Detector with Mesh-Guided Synthetic Pretraining

evidence_items.summary: Generative-prior-based super-resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large-scale models to enhance low-resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high-fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real-world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large-scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi-step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi-reference super-resolution model, which provides fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real-world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super-resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity-level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model-bound generative priors.
evidence_items.title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution

evidence_items.summary: Visual tool use enables vision-language models (VLMs) to acquire task-relevant evidence, but its effectiveness can be limited by predefined visual operations and the tool-use strategies learned during training. Representing these operations and strategies as reusable external skills allows them to be refined through self-evolution without updating model parameters. However, skill refinement can introduce performance regressions. Meanwhile, inspecting accumulated task execution trajectories together with skill evolution history may lead to evolution evidence overload. To address these challenges, we propose VisualEvolve, a self-evolving framework that evolves executable visual operations and tool-use strategies for VLMs through a Select--Execute--Evolve--Evaluate cycle. Skill-Library Snapshot Selection uses performance on a fixed validation set disjoint from execution tasks to select an effective historical snapshot for subsequent evolution, limiting the propagation of performance regressions. Progressive Evidence Access (PEA) guides capability-gap diagnosis through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy comprising the Skill-Performance Report, Evolution Log, Trajectory Summaries, and relevant raw trajectory segments. Across four VLM backbones and six evaluation sets from three benchmarks, VisualEvolve improves over the Initial Skill Library in 23 of 24 settings, with a maximum gain of 15.1 percentage points on VisualProbe Hard using Qwen3.5-Plus. Ablation studies support the contributions of Snapshot Selection and PEA, while further experiments show that skills can be improved using experience from different data settings and directly reused across backbones. Moreover, VisualEvolve enables effective skill self-evolution with over an order of magnitude fewer task-solving trajectories than estimated for representative RL-based methods.
evidence_items.title: VisualEvolve: A Skill Self-Evolution Framework for Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Systems for code-mixed (CM) text and speech rarely start from scratch. CM data is scarce, so most work borrows from the languages being mixed, which we call native languages. This transfer can also run in reverse, when CM data is used to improve models for the native languages. Existing surveys focus on processing CM itself, and none brings the two directions together. This paper fills that gap with a systematic survey of transfer in both directions, across text and speech. We organise the surveyed work in a taxonomy of transfer direction, route and modality. Through this taxonomy, we find that most transfer runs from native languages into the CM setting. The reverse direction is younger, and in it code-switching mainly helps by aligning the two languages. Text and speech work share methods but rarely cite each other. On a shared speech benchmark, native data helps more than new architectures. These findings point to open challenges, such as how much native and CM data to mix in training, and how to evaluate CM text written in different scripts.
evidence_items.title: A Two-Way Street: Surveying the Interplay between Code-Mixing and Native Languages in Text and Speech

evidence_items.summary: Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability, an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, it bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building on this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We show conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. We also specify an open-source validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper on exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking.
evidence_items.title: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics

evidence_items.summary: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students'use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.
evidence_items.title: AI Security Literacy: Ecosystem-based Competency Framework and K-12 Learning Platform

evidence_items.summary: Recommender Systems (RSs) can be evaluated for many aspects, two of them being recommendation relevance and fairness. These two aspects can be evaluated either in isolation, using a measure for each aspect; or jointly with a single`relevance-aware'fairness measure that quantifies fairness with respect to relevance. Yet, neither approach provides a simultaneous evaluation of both relevance and fairness: the first approach may result in two different rankings of models, each corresponding to an evaluation aspect; the second approach often provides an imbalanced evaluation of the two aspects. To address this gap, we propose Distance to Pareto Frontier (DPFR), a new approach to jointly evaluate RS fairness and relevance. DPFR is based on a Pareto frontier of relevance and fairness scores from existing measures. The frontier is generated from user-item interaction data and represents various Pareto-optimal trade-offs between the two aspects. Thus, the distance from a point in the frontier provides a joint score of fairness and relevance. As DPFR can be used with existing measures, it is modular and intuitive. Our experiments with 4 recommenders and 3 fairness-aware re-rankers on 6 real-world datasets reveal inconsistent associations between existing measures and DPFR, showing that they are not reliable proxies for evaluations based on Pareto optimality. We further examine the robustness of DPFR as a joint evaluation approach for fairness and relevance by conducting experiments with artificial recommendations and with various fairness-relevance trade-offs, as well as by analysing DPFR's agreement to simple measures of fairness and relevance. These analyses show that DPFR is more robust than existing joint evaluation approaches. Finally, we provide guidelines for evaluating fairness and relevance jointly with DPFR. Our code: https://github.com/theresiavr/robustness-DPFR-recsys-evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Robustness Analysis of Pareto-based Joint Evaluation of Fairness and Relevance in Recommender Systems

evidence_items.summary: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.
evidence_items.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Cytology artificial intelligence (AI) systems often depend on whole-slide images (WSIs) or high-magnification cell images and are commonly optimized for a single specimen type. We developed CYTOLONE-v2, a contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP)-based hierarchical classification framework for cervical and urinary cytology that is designed for individual-field inference without WSI input.


METHODS
CYTOLONE-v1.1, previously trained for cervical cytology, was further trained by low-rank adaptation using WSI-derived urinary cytology fields equivalent to ×10 magnification. The 90-case source cohort was divided at the case level into training (72 cases; 360 fields) and validation (18 cases; 90 fields) subsets. Five diagnosis-representative fields were manually selected from each case. Field-level performance was evaluated in an independent urinary test cohort of 40 cases (20 Reactive change and 20 Urothelial carcinoma; 200 fields), and retention was assessed using an independent cervical cytology test set.


RESULTS
In urinary cytology, CYTOLONE-v2 achieved field-level accuracies of 64.0% for Anomaly and Malignancy and 72.5% for Diagnosis. At the Diagnosis level, sensitivity for urothelial carcinoma was 99.0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 96.7%-100%), whereas specificity against Reactive change was 46.0% (95% CI, 30.0%-62.0%). Cervical cytology accuracy was retained at the Anomaly level (94.8% vs. 94.7% with CYTOLONE-v1.1), decreased modestly at the Malignancy level (91.2% vs. 93.5%), and decreased more at the Bethesda and Diagnosis levels.


CONCLUSIONS
CYTOLONE-v2 demonstrates the technical feasibility of extending a hierarchical cytology classification framework from cervical to urinary cytology. The findings are limited to selected WSI-derived fields and a Reactive change-versus-Urothelial carcinoma test cohort; external, case-level, direct-microscopy and prospective workflow validation is required before clinical utility can be established.
evidence_items.title: A WSI-Independent Inference Framework for Cervical and Urinary Cytology Using Hierarchical Labels.

evidence_items.summary:
The purpose of this research study was set to address the problem of cyberattacks, such as phishing delivered via short message service (SMS) or SMiShing, targeted towards senior citizens. In 2023, they lost over $36m to such attacks. Phishing success increases when attackers use persuasion principles that bypass logical decision-making and rely on heuristics. Security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programs can reduce susceptibility, yet little research investigated SETA programs that incorporate these principles.
 
 
 
 This research was conducted in three phases, beginning with Subject Matter Experts’ evaluation of SMiShing messages operationalizing these persuasion principles for use in this study’s instrument. The next phase was a pilot study. The third phase was the main data collection and analysis phase. This research employed a pretest-posttest design to evaluate the efficacy of its novel SETA program. The SETA program used Behavioral Skills Training methodology with 118 senior citizens from South Florida and Central Massachusetts.
 
 
 
 The experimental results indicated a statistically significant mean difference between pretest and posttest group scores (F = 6.604, df = 5, p = 0.011) in identifying SMiShing messages that operationalize the principles of persuasion used in social engineering. Specifically, the pretest group’s mean score was 73.62, and the posttest group’s mean score was 79.28. The calculated effect size (η2 = 0.054) nears the threshold for a medium effect (η2 = 0.06).
 
 
 
 Recognizing persuasion in SMiShing messages helped senior citizens better detect these cyberattacks. Practical implications include incorporating persuasion principles into the SETA framework to address evolving cyberattacks (e.g. deepfakes, vishing) that are being enhanced by generative artificial intelligence.
 
 
 
 As a group, senior citizens have lost millions to cyberattacks. SETA programs that incorporate principles of persuasion appear to help reduce the financial losses this group incurs from cyberattacks and may also improve senior citizens’ confidence and reduce fear when using communication technology.
 
 
 
 This research’s original contribution is the integration of persuasion principles into cybersecurity training programs, helping senior citizens quickly recognize the malicious intent of SMiShing messages, which apply psychological pressures to achieve the attacker’s goals.
evidence_items.title: An empirical study on how social engineering and persuasion principles training affects senior citizens’ responses to SMiShing attacks

evidence_items.summary: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.
evidence_items.title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution
Involvement of general dental practitioners in epidemiologic data collection: insights from the Belgian Oral Health Dental Registration and Evaluation Survey.

evidence_items.summary:
Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term.
  We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates.
  We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.
evidence_items.title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking

evidence_items.summary: WP3 Docduck OCR evaluation inputs Private evaluation inputs for the WP3 multilingual OCR study, across 31 languages. The collection contains page images, the PDFs submitted to the OCR pipelines, generated reference text, text-block coordinates and the saved sample selections. It contains inputs and references, not model predictions or human-certified transcriptions. Archive Contents full-pages.tar.gz 3,100 original canonical PNG pages, 31 original 100-page image-only… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/RfKnowledge/wp3-docduck-ocr-evaluation.
evidence_items.title: RfKnowledge/wp3-docduck-ocr-evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Uncensored model leaderboard Public "uncensored" and abliterated models make the same claim: the refusals are gone and nothing else broke. This table measures both halves on one setup: how often each model still refuses harmful and harmless prompts, how far its outputs moved from the stock model, and what it scores on two task sets next to stock. One table per base model. Every row is pinned to a repo revision. Only scores are published here: no weights, model outputs or prompt… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/spicysharkco/uncensored-leaderboard.
evidence_items.title: spicysharkco/uncensored-leaderboard

evidence_items.summary: This master’s thesis designs, implements, and evaluates a map-based Intervention Design Tool within the EU Horizon Europe TRANS-SAHARA project. Piloted in the Tunisia Living Lab, the tool supports exploration of three WEFE Nexus-aligned interventions: agroforestry, water harvesting, and solar-powered irrigation. Stakeholder surveys inform interface requirements. Suitability is modelled using Weighted Linear Combination, with criterion weights derived from an Analytic Hierarchy Process survey of domain experts. Uncertainty is calculated as the coefficient of variation across expert-derived suitability surfaces and visualized separately from suitability. Practitioners from the project’s African Living Labs participate in a summative evaluation. Participants favour explanatory information accompanying suitability scores and quantile classification over continuous gradients. Most identify suitable locations and understand the reasoning behind their scores, while interpreting confidence remains more difficult. The thesis contributes an integrated suitability and uncertainty visualization workflow, complementary absolute and relative classification schemes, and eight empirically informed cartographic and interaction design principles.
evidence_items.title: From Data to Interventions: A Visual Analytics Framework for Agroforestry Management. Case study: Tunisia Living Lab
Do Sentinel-2 vegetation indices improve forecasts of Phenacoccus solenopsis on okra? A two-season retrospective benchmark study

evidence_items.summary: France's long history of mining, with more than 4,000 mining permits, led to the development of a specific risk management policy in the late 1990s. To date, more than 250 risk assessment studies have been conducted to evaluate the impact of abandoned mines on infrastructure and land use planning. 80% of identified risk areas are affected by sinkholes, with over 4,000 cases reported and around ten new cases appearing each year. The assessment of the predisposition to sinkhole formation on former mining sites is based on expert judgement taking into account various criteria and data on previous sinkholes. Discussions have been underway to improve and modernise these methods in France. The European SIRIMA project focuses on the development of quantitative prediction tools, in particular probabilistic models and machine learning. A comprehensive database and a web map to document sinkholes in the project's partner countries: France, Germany and Poland. This work has revealed that it is difficult to complete all the data due to the age and loss of information. The information collected will be used to analyse the conditions under which sinkholes occur in order to better manage this risk in the future in coal-mining regions in transition, particularly in France .
evidence_items.title: Post-mining Sinkhole Hazard and Risk Management in France: Feedback and Outlook

evidence_items.summary: Automatic identification of a script in a given document image facilitates many important applications such as automatic archiving of multilingual documents, searching online archives of document images and for the selection of script specific OCR in a multilingual environment. This paper provides a comparison study of three dimension reduction techniques, namely partial least squares (PLS), sliced inverse regression (SIR) and principal component analysis (PCA), and evaluates the relative performance of classification procedures incorporating those methods. For given script we extracted different features like Gray Level Co-occurrence Method (GLCM) and Scale invariant feature transform (SIFT) features. The features are extracted globally from a given text block which does not require any complex and reliable segmentation of the document image into lines and characters. Extracted features are reduced using various dimension reduction techniques. The reduced features are fed into Nearest Neighbor classifier. Thus the proposed scheme is efficient and can be used for many practical applications which require processing large volumes of data. The scheme has been tested on 10 Indian scripts and found to be robust in the process of scanning and relatively insensitive to change in font size. This proposed system achieves good classification accuracy on a large testing data set.
evidence_items.title: Dimension Reduction for Script Classification - Printed Indian Documents

evidence_items.summary: This master’s thesis develops a gender-responsive geovisual analytics framework for shea agroforestry in Burkina Faso and Ghana. It combines the Water–Energy–Food–Ecosystem (WEFE) Nexus with spatial analysis, multi-criteria evaluation, gender statistics, and cartographic design to support integrated and inclusive planning. The framework harmonizes environmental, geospatial, and gender-disaggregated socioeconomic data. GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation identifies land suitability for shea agroforestry, while the Women’s Empowerment and Agroforestry Resilience (WEFE–WEAR) Index combines resource-system indicators with measures of women’s agency. An interactive dashboard presents opportunity zones where biophysical suitability and conditions for empowerment align. The findings highlight both promising areas and constraints associated with accessibility, resource availability, and burdens such as water and fuelwood collection. evidence_items.summary: The purpose of this report is to offer the technical specifications for the interoperability protocol (hereafter referred to as “the protocol”) developed within the SURIMI project. These specifications guide the development of the modelling framework that interlinks the various models participating in SURIMI. The deliverable is relevant to modellers and software developers engaged in the coupling of scientific models for real-world applications in the marine domain. SURIMI’s mission is to demonstrate that previously disconnected scientific models can operate together to address policy and end-user questions. The models participating in SURIMI span fisheries, fisheries management, ecology and market dynamics and include analytical modules such as CMSY++, Value Chain, and Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE) procedures. These components are driven by fisheries management policy questions and climate scenarios. The resulting SURIMI modelling complex will be deployed on the EDITO infrastructure, while remaining system-agnostic and adaptable to future case studies. To enable interoperability, the protocol separates concerns, allowing foundational technical mechanisms to be engineered independently from evolving scientific and policy use cases, and from specific computing infrastructures. This architecture ensures: Clear separation between transport, data structure, meaning, and control logic. Controlled extensibility toward future, more complex real-world scenarios. Formalisation of what models can and cannot exchange. Deterministic and reproducible coupled model execution. The SURIMI interoperability protocol is structured across four layers: (1) technical interoperability, (2) syntactic interoperability, (3) semantic interoperability, and (4) coupling and control logic. These layers operate within a broader business context, which defines the purpose, configuration, and use of the modelling complex but is not part of the protocol itself.
evidence_items.title: D4.3 Interoperability protocol

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains environmental, biological, and molecular data collected from Laizhou Bay, Bohai Sea, China, to investigate the responses of marine  Synechococcus populations to environmental variability, eutrophication, and warming. Field surveys Field surveys were conducted during four cruises in November 2021, May 2022, August–September 2022, and April 2023. All samples were collected from surface seawater (sampling depth: 0 m). The dataset contains 135 sampling records, including sampling dates, geographic coordinates, hydrographic parameters, nutrient concentrations, chlorophyll a , and other biogeochemical variables. Flow cytometry was used to quantify Synechococcus abundance and distinguish phycoerythrin-rich (SYN-PE) and phycocyanin-rich (SYN-PC) populations. The dataset also includes station classifications based on salinity gradients and shellfish aquaculture activities. Incubation experiments A 14-day bottle incubation experiment was conducted from 13 to 27 July 2024 to investigate the effects of warming and nutrient enrichment on Synechococcus populations. Four treatments were established: control (CK, 27°C), warming (HT, 30°C), nutrient enrichment (HN, 27°C), and combined nutrient enrichment and warming (HN-HT, 30°C). The dataset contains measurements of nutrient concentrations, chlorophyll a , and the abundances of Synechococcus and other small-sized phytoplankton groups at eight sampling time points. rpoC1 assemblage composition The genetic composition of Synechococcus assemblages was characterized using rpoC1 amplicon sequencing at 12 stations during the summer survey. The dataset includes the taxonomic classification and sequencing read counts of 58 operational taxonomic units (OTUs), together with the read counts and relative proportions of 11 identified clades or taxonomic groups. The processed data contain 32,564 assigned reads per sample.

evidence_items.summary: Tool-using artificial intelligence agents increasingly act on evidence that can change between verification and execution. Existing output-focused assurance and permission gates do not by themselves establish that previously checked preconditions remain valid at action time. This paper develops the assurance freshness gap, a temporal assurance framework combining signed evidence receipts, private and shared-source change hazards, probabilistic revalidation, queue-sensitive risk and conditional atomic commit. Under independent baseline-error and generating-shock assumptions, the paper derives an exact invalid-execution probability and evidence lifetime; a conservative union-bound certificate applies to enumerated dependent events with defensible marginal bounds. A stationary M/M/1 authorization queue yields a 5%-budget utilization ceiling of 85.93% under explicit illustrative parameters. The revision extends the analysis to nonstationary hazards and general M/G/1 service-time distributions. At identical 85% utilization and mean service capacity, theoretical invalid-execution risk is 2.99% with deterministic service, 4.73% with exponential service and 9.48% with high-variance hyperexponential service. Independently replicated synthetic queue simulations corroborate these transform predictions; age-dependent hazard and uncertain-hazard calculations further show how nominally acceptable mean risk can breach the target. The paper provides executable controller pseudocode, formal proofs, sensitivity results and reproducible scripts, while distinguishing conditional probabilistic guarantees from atomic state-transition protection. The evaluation is entirely synthetic and does not establish real-world safety effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: The Assurance Freshness Gap: Risk-Bounded Revalidation and Queue-Aware Execution Control for Tool-Using AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Designing molecules with prescribed properties is central to pharmaceutical and materials innovation, but vast chemical design spaces make development lengthy and costly. Generative artificial intelligence can accelerate molecular discovery, but its deployment in many real-world domains remains limited by the need for large task-specific training datasets. To enable generative design when property-labeled data are scarce, we present a data-efficient foundation-model adaptation strategy combining complementary positive and negative property prompts with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Generated molecules are then ranked by molecular graph-kernel Gaussian process regression for structure-aware prioritization. In a controlled computational setting, the platform generated candidates with novel scaffolds satisfying multiple design objectives, including predicted target binding, synthesizability, and drug-likeness. Although only a few hundred training molecules per target met all three criteria, the model generated thousands of new molecules matching the desired profiles. For prospective validation, we applied the model to nanoparticle design, a domain of high clinical potential but limited excipient diversity. Fine-tuning on only 1,521 labeled drug-excipient pairs - including just 139 nanoparticle-forming examples identified new nanoparticle-forming excipients for the anticancer drug sorafenib. The model proposed lithocholic acid and the sorafenib metabolite M6, and experiments confirmed that both form stable sorafenib nanoparticles with high encapsulation efficiency and increased in vitro potency. These findings show that foundation-model fine-tuning with complementary prompts and graph-based prioritization enables data-efficient molecular design in low-data chemical domains.
evidence_items.title: Data-efficient molecular and nanoparticle design via fine-tuned large language models

evidence_items.summary: The security of multi-turn autonomous agent architectures is fundamentally compromised by context-steering vulnerabilities, specifically Salami attacks, where adversarial intent is incrementally dispersed across sequential interaction turns. Conventional probabilistic filters and static language guardrails fail under such trajectory-based manipulation due to the lack of dynamic state memory and the presence of model-vs-payload space mismatch. To resolve this challenge at its mathematical core, we formulate multi-turn intent containment as a data-driven, state-space control problem governed by Unfalsified Control Theory and Koopman Operator dynamics. By lifting discrete token interaction streams into an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the nonlinear evolution of multi-turn dialogue trajectories is linearized into observable subspace projections. We define a dual-subspace energy framework that continuously evaluates the instantaneous directional momentum of user intent relative to an immutable, zero-calibration energy density hyperplane boundary. To eliminate subspace saturation and contextual information decay during extended multi-turn sessions, we introduce a session-isolated adaptive dual-loop learner augmented with a sliding-window forgetting operator. This mechanism guarantees bounded memory dissipation while preserving short-term intent trajectory momentum. Upon falsification—defined strictly by a negative Lyapunov-like energy density derivative—the system executes an immediate, deterministic state-transition into a closed-loop containment sandbox, accompanied by a zero-remanence memory sanitization protocol that destroys volatile trajectory information.
evidence_items.title: Session-Isolated Unfalsified Adaptive Control for Multi-Turn Intent Containment in Autonomous Agent Architectures

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.
evidence_items.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
evidence_items.title: RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use

evidence_items.summary: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.
evidence_items.title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles

evidence_items.summary: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.
evidence_items.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Privacy concerns represent a primary barrier to the adoption of large language model (LLM) applications, particularly in sensitive domains such as health care. Although a growing body of survey-based research has examined user privacy concerns with LLMs, no standardized instrument exists for measuring this construct. Objective This study aimed to develop and validate a concise, standardized questionnaire for assessing user privacy concerns with LLM-based systems, suitable for use by researchers and practitioners such as AI application developers and health care professionals. Methods A literature review was conducted to identify privacy-related domains relevant to LLM use. A draft questionnaire was developed and subjected to content validity review by 8 experts. The finalized instrument was administered via Qualtrics to adults aged 18 years or older who were aware of LLM-based applications, recruited through the University of Pittsburgh, LinkedIn, and the Pitt+Me research participant registry between April 2025 and July 2026. Internal consistency reliability and factor structure were assessed, with factor structure examined in a split-sample design, in which exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted on a random one-third of the sample and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) on the holdout two-thirds. Results All questionnaire items achieved acceptable content validity (item-level content validity index >0.80; average scale-level content validity index=0.964). A total of 603 responses were collected. After preprocessing, the final sample comprised 361 participants. Most participants were younger than 35 years of age (198/361, 54.8%), female (230/361, 63.7%), and White (285/361, 78.9%); 88.1% (318/361) held at least a bachelor’s degree. The 6-item questionnaire showed high internal consistency (Cronbach α=0.90; McDonald ω=0.90). EFA (n=121) supported a single dominant factor with all standardized loadings ≥0.70.
evidence_items.title: Development and Validation of the Large Language Model Privacy Concern Assessment Questionnaire: Psychometric Evaluation Study on a Brief Instrument for Assessing User Privacy Concerns With Large Language Model Applications

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The massive volume of paired microbiome and metabolome measurementsgenerated through high-throughput sequencing and mass spectrometryhas created an urgent need for dedicated, integrative analytical pipelines. Existing tools lack the capacity to simultaneously support sample clustering, multi-omics visualization, disease risk stratification, and biological age quantification using matched dual-modal datasets. To overcome this analytical bottleneck, we introduce the matrix factorization with shared and specific graph learning (MFSSG) toolkit: an unsupervised matrix factorization framework that jointly learns both shared and modality-specific graph structures. MFSSG preserves cross-omics spatial consistency by leveraging shared nearest-neighbor graphs derived from analytical profiles and incorporates two complementary regularization termsentropy regularization to enhance cluster discriminability and a pre-trained microbial graph Laplacianto mitigate measurement bias inherent in microbiome sequencing versus metabolomic mass spectrometry data. Validated across three independent multi-omics cohorts derived from gastric and gut biospecimensincluding gastric cancer, end-stage renal disease, and type 1 diabetesMFSSG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art integration methods in disease classification. Furthermore, a novel pairwise learning module enables parallel and accurate quantification of the metabolic age and microbial age, facilitating refined patient risk stratification. This versatile toolkit provides a robust chemometric strategy for uncovering latent biological patterns embedded within heterogeneous multi-omics analytical data.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Enhanced MFSSG Enables Effective and Accurate Integration Analysis for Microbiome−Metabolome Data
