evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) may support healthcare workforce allocation, but their decisions can be sensitive to demographic cues and decision architecture. This study examined gender–task congruity, Candidate-A dependence under the tested decision architecture, and patient-gender-conditioned nursing allocation. Methods: Three provider-specific LLM configurations were audited across 24 nursing tasks. Male and female nurses were professionally equivalent and counterbalanced across Candidate A/B; patient gender was varied in six intimate-care tasks. Sixty conditions were repeated three times per model, yielding 540 valid outputs. Results: Male nurses were selected in 50.0% of Technical/Procedural and Relational/Educational allocations. Candidate A was selected in all 288 observations, although 285 (99.0%) assigned identical suitability scores. Because A/B assignment was bundled with labeling, presentation order, evaluation order, and response-template anchoring, this pattern indicates Candidate-A dependence under the tested decision architecture rather than an isolated position effect. Changing patient gender from female to male produced 57 female-to-male nurse switches and no reverse switches (p < 0.001). Conclusions: The audited configurations showed no generalized gender–task pattern but demonstrated decision-architecture dependence and patient-gender-conditioned allocation. Fairness audits should assess equivalent-candidate handling, patient preference, and counterfactual stability.
evidence_items.title: Decision-Architecture Dependence and Patient-Gender-Conditioned Allocation in Large-Language-Model-Assisted Nursing Allocation: A Multi-Model Counterfactual Audit

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background Retrieving MRI safety conditions for implanted devices is increasingly complex and time‐consuming. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of internet‐enabled large language model (LLM) chatbots in retrieving implant‐specific MRI safety conditions, using manufacturer documentation as the reference standard. Study Type Prospective comparative evaluation in a constructed device cohort, followed by a retrospective clinical pilot. Population Fifty purposively selected device configurations and 20 patients (10 with cardiac and 10 with noncardiac devices) referred to the MRI Safety Committee. Field Strength No field‐strength or sequence restrictions. Assessment Standardized single‐shot prompts requested eight parameters from ChatGPT‐5.0, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5: MRI safety label, field strengths, eligible regions/centering, transmit‐coil restrictions, RF exposure limits, maximum spatial gradient, maximum gradient slew rate, and scan duration. Two radiologists (10 and 25 years' experience) and an MRI technologist (32 years) independently scored 1200 parameter‐level outputs against manufacturer Instructions for use and technical manuals using a 5‐point scale (5, fully correct; 1, substantively incorrect or fabricated); scores of 4–5 indicated accuracy. In the pilot, 160 outputs from ChatGPT‐5.6, a newer version of the best‐performing chatbot, were scored identically. Statistical Tests Intraclass correlation coefficient; Gwet's first‐order agreement coefficient (AC1); Friedman test; Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests; device‐clustered bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs); two‐sided significance threshold, p < 0.05. Results Mean ordinal scores were 4.76 (ChatGPT), 4.20 (Gemini), and 4.17 (Claude); ChatGPT scored significantly higher. Respective pooled parameter‐level accuracies were 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89–0.98), 0.79 (0.71–0.86), and 0.78 (0.69–0.87). Pilot accuracy with ChatGPT‐5.6 was 0.98 (95% CI, 0.94–1.00).

evidence_items.summary: Safety-aligned language models often encode that a request is harmful yet still comply with it. We turn this gap between internal recognition and observable behavior into an inference-time defense. The proposed activation-steering method uses a multiplicative operator that amplifies the residual-stream component along a harm-recognition direction. Intervention strength scales with the model’s own assessment of the request. A second additive term steers activations along the refusal direction when harm is not internally recognized. Two linear probes computed from the model’s activations gate both components. The model weights remain unchanged, and inference requires neither fine-tuning nor calls to an external model. An external safety classifier is used only before deployment to provide training targets for the second probe. We evaluate five models from three families, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Mistral-7B-Instruct, in BF16 and NF4. Successful attacks on SORRY-Bench decrease by 40 to 68%. Without hyperparameter retuning, the method removes 67 to 79% of the harmful responses on HarmBench. MMLU accuracy decreases by at most 0.7 percentage points, while over-refusal on lexically hazardous benign prompts increases by 4 to 8 points. Steered NF4 models produce 36 to 62% fewer harmful responses than their unmodified BF16 counterparts.
evidence_items.title: Amplifying Latent Safety in Large Language Models via Gated Activation Steering

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Simulation-based controller comparisons can report a single winner even when score differences are too small to justify a unique engineering preference. We assessed preference reliability for five fixed controllers on a numerically verified nonlinear rotary inverted pendulum model using two independent Latin-hypercube realizations across matched ± 10%, ± 15%, and ± 20% uncertainty bands (30,000 closed-loop simulations). A four-metric score and a prespecified 5% practical margin quantified controller separation. Under the common uncertainty score, PID had the lowest controller robustness index in every band, but the four leading indices remained within 3.87%. In the pooled ± 15% domain, all ten paired comparisons were detectable after Holm correction, yet 69.40% of 2,000 scenario blocks lacked a unique practical preference. PID retained rank one in 99.95% of paired-bootstrap replicates but only 63.16% and 43.06% under two weight-variation analyses. Post-review sensitivity analyses showed that the principal practical-separation conclusion was robust to the tested CRI coefficient, realization-specific median normalization, and heavier-tail dependence models, while command delay altered separation among near-tied controllers. These findings are specific to the fixed controller portfolio, score definition, RIP model, and simulated uncertainty domain.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying controller preference reliability under uncertainty in a rotary inverted pendulum benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Published database comparisons typically cover engine pairs, conflate the engine effect with the schema effect, and compare queries that do not compute the same result. We present StreamCart, a benchmark built on a realistic e-commerce workload, and use it to decompose performance across six systems, PostgreSQL as an optimized relational baseline and five specialized engines (MongoDB, Cassandra, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, TimescaleDB), each implemented at a naive migration level and at an engine-optimized level, eleven configurations in all. Result equivalence for the claim-bearing analytics queries is verified row by row against the relational reference. Across seven read query classes, no naive implementation outperforms the baseline on any query, and no single engine dominates, with the classes splitting between PostgreSQL, optimized Elasticsearch, and optimized MongoDB. Schema design emerges as a factor on par with engine choice, improving performance by up to 3892 times on Cassandra and 137 times on Elasticsearch, where load-time denormalization lets the optimized form outperform PostgreSQL by 15.8 and 6.3 times on identical results, while a single omitted uniqueness constraint reduced Neo4j write throughput a hundredfold. Concurrent write throughput spans roughly two orders of magnitude (165 to 12,603 events per second). All code, data, and raw timings are public.
evidence_items.title: Decomposing Engine and Schema Effects in Database Performance: A Result-Equivalent E-Commerce Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Modern technological society is highly vulnerable to extreme geomagnetic storms, yet the terrestrial upper limit of such events remains poorly constrained because continuous instrumental geomagnetic records cover only a relatively short historical period. To extend this baseline, we quantitatively reconstruct the geomagnetic superstorm of September 1770 (termed Qianlong XXXV storm) using systematically documented auroral observations preserved in Chinese regional chronicles. These historical records indicate that the auroral oval expanded to a magnetic latitude as low as 20.40°N at the ionospheric height, implying an exceptionally intense magnetospheric disturbance. From this equatorward auroral boundary, we derive a best-estimate Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) index of −1,319 nT (95% Confidence Interval (CI): [−1,832, −1,066]), exceeding the reconstructed Dst intensity of the 1859 Carrington event ( ≈ −1,025 nT, 95% CI of [−1367, −853]) by approximately 30%. An extreme value statistical model suggests an order-of-magnitude recurrence interval of approximately 14,000 years for the Qianlong XXXV event, compared with approximately 1,400 years for Carrington-class storms. These results suggest that the Qianlong XXXV geomagnetic storm represent an important low-latitude benchmark for extreme solar–terrestrial disturbances. This potential benchmark provides a quantitatively constrained reference for testing the physical limits of modern infrastructure and the atmosphere of the Earth under the impact of catastrophic space weather.
evidence_items.title: The Qianlong XXXV event: a potential benchmark for extreme geomagnetic storms based on historical Chinese auroral archives

evidence_items.summary: By disrupting soil ecosystem functioning, cadmium threatens food safety. Therefore, a significant research imperative is to develop effective remediation strategies and understand the relationships between cadmium content in soil and plants and the content of other metals. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of calcium carbonate, sepiolite, expanded clay, zeolite, and molecular sieve on the growth and physiological response of Zea mays grown in cadmium-contaminated soil. Plant growth and development were assessed together with the translocation and bioaccumulation of cadmium and other metals (Pb, Cr, Cu, Zn, Fe, Ni, and Mn) and changes in soil physicochemical properties. The study was conducted as a pot experiment using uncontaminated soil and soil contaminated with 15 and 30 mg Cd kg−1. Depending on the contamination level, cadmium reduced the leaf greenness index of Zea mays by 10–16%, the yield of the aboveground parts by 60–76%, and root yield by 60–69%. The tested sorbents modified these responses mainly by altering the soil physicochemical properties. The molecular sieve was the most effective, reducing the negative effect of cadmium on the yield of the aboveground parts and roots by an average of 31% while not significantly affecting the leaf greenness index. Cadmium increased the translocation factor of all analyzed elements except cadmium itself, indicating its potential to affect the homeostasis of other elements in the plant. Heavy metal bioaccumulation in the roots of Zea mays was significantly greater than in the aboveground parts. Cadmium altered the bioaccumulation of individual elements to different extents, but these effects could be modified through the appropriate selection of mineral sorbents. These findings make an important contribution to the development of effective methods for remediating cadmium-contaminated soils.
evidence_items.title: Interactions Between Cadmium Contamination and Mineral Sorbents in Shaping Heavy Metal Bioaccumulation in Soil and Plant Biomass

organizations: Department of Electronic and Electrical Engineering, University College London, Torrington Place, London WC1E 7JE, UK
evidence_items.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative Agentic AI) models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs), and agentic AI have recently gained widespread attention in both research and industry. They have rapidly emerged as a concept that elevates Generative Agentic AI from passive text generators to the next generation of agentic AI as autonomous, goal-driven agents capable of perception, planning, and dynamic action execution—Coherent Generative Agentic AI (CGA). In addition, CGA provides supervisory intelligence by maintaining persistent, evolving internal world models of the environment, networks, resources, agents, user intents, and policies. CGA reasons over time, runs long-horizon plans, checks consequences against its internal models, and coherently orchestrates lower-level controllers. It sits above network controllers, providing a global, semantic, model-driven brain. The paper starts with a review of CGA functional and non-functional characteristics in the context of key research and development results of agentic AI. It introduces a coherence-first architectural construct and system variable across all future 6G/7G networking planes (data-, transport-, management and operations,- orchestration,- autonomicity-, programmability-, and AI as a Service-plane). It proposes a new deterministic CGA mathematical (CGAM) model that provides a new abstraction and theoretical foundation for analyzing the systemic consequences of different structural design and optimization options. It defines the relation between coherence and intelligence. The CGAM model represents the compute–communications continuum as a partially observable, intent-driven, contract-governed, multi-agent dynamical system with persistent memory and coherence constraints. We also included detailed CGAM validation and evaluation measures. This paper explores and details the CGAM’s role in 6G and 7G networking, as well as the challenges and opportunities for future work they present.
evidence_items.title: Coherent Generative Agentic AI Enabled 6G/7G Networking

evidence_items.summary: Agentic coding tools, such as OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor, are changing how software is developed. These AI-powered systems function as autonomous teammates capable of planning and executing complex development tasks. Agents have become active participants in refactoring, a key practice for improving internal code quality without altering observable behavior. Despite their increasing adoption, there is little empirical understanding of how agentic refactoring is used in practice, how it compares to human-driven refactoring, and what impact it has on code quality. To address this empirical gap, we present a large-scale study of AI agent-generated refactorings in real-world open-source Java projects, analyzing 51,412 refactoring instances across 12,256 pull requests and 14,998 commits based on the AIDev dataset. Our empirical analysis shows that refactoring is a common and intentional activity in this development paradigm, with agents explicitly targeting refactoring in 26.1% of commits. The subsequent analyses of refactoring types, purposes, and code quality focus on the 3,907 commits (32,611 instances) with explicit refactoring intent. Analysis of refactoring types reveals that high-level refactorings form the largest category overall. However, agentic refactoring contains a slightly larger share of lowlevel, consistency-oriented edits than human refactoring (27.6% vs. 24.4%), and its two most frequent operations are Rename Variable (7.6%) and Change Variable Type (6.8%). Additionally, the stated motivations behind agentic refactoring focus overwhelmingly on internal quality concerns (with 52.5% in maintainability and 28.1% in readability), although the measured metric improvements from these frequently occurring low-level refactorings remain limited.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Refactoring: An Empirical Study of AI Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: The high rate at which telecommunication services are changing has yielded a volume of heterogeneous data never seen before such as call detail records, signaling data, and subscriber activity traces. These datasets are crucial in relation to optimization and business intelligence, but effective use of such datasets requires quality metadata. Traditional metadata management is mostly manual and centralized, which cannot support the pace and scale of the new telecom big data systems. As a solution to these shortcomings, the present article suggests a scalable metadata mining strategy that is founded on agentic intelligence. In comparison to more traditional machine learning pipelines, agentic intelligence enables the use of autonomous goal-oriented AI agents, capable of reasoning in a hard data space and relevant to new network topologies and network schemas. The proposed architecture will include a multiagent architecture at a distributed level, having specialized agents: (1) schema drifting ingestion and monitoring agents of data flows; (2) semantic mining actors based on natural language processing to infer contextual metadata; (3) process-aware agents for process mining to determine lineage and dependencies between data; and (4) compliance with policy and metadata retrospect: government agents. A major effect of the work is the integration of agentic intelligence and scalable infrastructures of big data such as cloud-native analytics platforms and distributed data lakes. These agents coordinate themselves using lightweight coordination mechanisms to provide a persistent metadata knowledge layer that facilitates system interoperability and robust downstream analytics. The design concepts are geared toward horizontal scalability and fault tolerance, enabling the distribution of the agents at dynamically evolving manner regarding the workload peak. Besides, agents also enhance their strategies upon continuous feedback to handle concept drift as well.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Intelligence for Scalable Metadata Mining in Telecom Big Data Systems

evidence_items.summary: Bringing a new drug to market can exceed $1 billion, and integrated commercial computational-chemistry platforms cost $200,000–$5,000,000 per year, placing them beyond most resource-constrained research groups. We demonstrate that open-source tools with large language model (LLM) orchestration can democratize early-stage New Chemical Entity (NCE) prioritisation. Three computational case studies (Case A: proprietary target, class withheld, public experimental co-crystal structure; Case B: kinase with co-crystal structure; Case C: protein–protein-interaction interface, apo) each ran Tier 1 (target-enriched ZINC20 library) and Tier 2 (GNINA v1.1 docking with CNN rescoring, plus SwissADME and ADMETlab 2.0 profiling). Tiers 3–4 are proposed future work. A tiered Claude Opus 4/Sonnet 4 agent orchestrated the workflow. Each library (~154,000–400,000 compounds) was reduced to 200 or fewer docked and 10 prioritised candidates per case, with Case C treated as an exploratory PPI stress test. LLM citation accuracy on independent PubMed verification was 88%, 78%, and 90% (pooled 85%, 23/27). No experimental assays were performed. Incurred LLM API cost was $1,450–$1,800; projected discovery-phase cost $3,450–$10,800 (lower bound). A retrospective public-target benchmark (acetylcholinesterase, PDB 4EY7) reproduced the crystallographic pose to 0.31 A but showed that the docking score alone did not enrich known actives (ROC-AUC 0.23); mechanism-based interaction filtering restored above-random early recognition (BEDROC 0.02 to 0.44), supporting the multi-evidence, human-gated design rather than docking-based ranking alone. This provides a reproducible, low-cost blueprint for computational NCE prioritisation in resource-constrained settings, not a validated drug-discovery platform; prioritised compounds are computational predictions requiring subsequent Tier 3 experimental confirmation.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI-Orchestrated Computational Drug Discovery: A Case-Study-Demonstrated Open-Source Workflow Blueprint

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Design for Additive Manufacturing tools apply predefined geometric checks, while dimensional limits require experimental validation for specific alloys, machines, and process settings. Engineers often interpret their applicability and manually coordinate assessment, redesign, and simulation. Large language models alone cannot reliably provide precise geometric measurements. This paper introduces AgenticDfAM, which coordinates reasoning agents and tools to revise designs and their assessment and construction procedures. Tools retain authority over numerical evidence. The feature-recognition and measurement tools were developed and benchmarked against reference geometries. Scripted agent replies were used to test validation of communication between agentic stages, error handling, and recovery. Invalid inter-agent messages were rejected by semantic validators. Across computational case studies, three redesign strategies remove all reference violations while exposing material and distortion tradeoffs. Thermal feedback lowers a part’s predicted layer-scale peak temperature by 160 °C. In a support design experiment, support above an intended contact surface was identified by a reviewer and corrected by the agent after diagnosis of the construction code. The correction was verified on curved and flat targets and reused in four autonomous clamp runs, with returns to support construction reduced from ten to five. The workflow investigates issues beyond prescribed checks while retaining verifiable engineering evidence.
evidence_items.title: AgenticDfAM: An agentic workﬂow automates design for additive manufacturing through traceable adaptive assessment and multicriteria redesigns

evidence_items.summary: The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes posttreatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. An end-to-end multiagent large language model and convolutional neural network system for automated BTRADS classification was developed and evaluated. Five hundred nine consecutive posttreatment glioma MRI examinations (March 2017-July 2021) from a single center were retrospectively evaluated. An extractor agent identified clinical variables from notes using gpt-oss (OpenAI, 20-billion parameters). A scorer agent applied BTRADS decision logic integrating these with quantitative volumetrics. System accuracy was compared against initial assessments, using expert annotation as the reference standard. Four hundred ninety-two examinations were evaluable. Overall system accuracy was 76.0% (374/492) versus 57.5% (283/492) for initial assessments, an absolute difference of +18.5 percentage points ( P < .001). Cohen kappa between the system and the reference standard was 0.71. The system achieved high sensitivity in context-dependent categories (BT-1b; 100%; BT-1a, 92.7%; BT-3a, 87.5%) and moderate sensitivity for threshold-dependent categories (BT-3c, 74.8%; BT-2, 69.2%; BT-4, 69.3%; BT-3b, 57.1%). The BT-4 positive predictive value was 92.9%. These results support further evaluation of this system as a clinical decision-support tool, with local open-weight inference preserving data privacy. ©RSNA, 2026
evidence_items.title: Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring Using an End-to-End System for                     Standardized Glioma Follow-up Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.
evidence_items.title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
evidence_items.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model

evidence_items.summary: norregel asks language models for numeric values in Norwegian statutes, regulations and parliamentary decisions (NOK amounts, percentages, multiples of the National Insurance basic amount (G) and age limits), each at a stated date. The 916 items were extracted mechanically from Lovdata's open data, and each carries the dated history of its provision, so an answer can be classed as correct, outdated, wrong or uninterpretable. We report a first and a second preregistered run on the same items. In the first run (five models, listed publicly only after local analysis), H1, that outdated answers are more frequent for values that took effect after a model's cutoff, could not be tested in substance, and H2 and H3 were inconclusive; Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 4.6 answered 46.7% and 40.2% of the 880 primary items correctly. The second run was preregistered and published before any of its calls, and eight models were analysed. Its pooled primary test supported H1 under the preregistered decision rule (d = 17.8 percentage points, 95% interval [7.7, 28.9], p = 0.0001). In the preregistered sensitivity analysis S8, which counts as outdated only the most recent value that differs from the key, d was 3.9 [-3.6, 12.7] (p = 0.1754), an interval that contains 0. H1 was supported in every other preregistered sensitivity analysis, but S8 is the only one that gives both groups one target value, so we do not regard the support for H1 as robust. The share of outdated answers equal to that most recent value (H2) was 56.1% [46.6, 65.0], an interval that contains 0.5, and the pooled test of a lower share correct in Nynorsk than in Bokm{\aa}l (H3) was inconclusive. Several models, among them Haiku 4.5, gave mostly uninterpretable answers. Items and keys are withheld; item IDs, per-answer classes, code and results are on Zenodo.
evidence_items.title: norregel: a preregistered benchmark of dated numeric values in Norwegian law

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
evidence_items.title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling

evidence_items.summary: The Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) is widely used to assess clinical communication skills in medical education, requiring trainees to take histories and reason clinically with standardized patients (SPs). Large language model (LLM)-based virtual standardized patients (VSPs), typically built by persona-injected prompting, offer a practical alternative. However, existing evaluations rely on a single backbone LLM, small human rater panels, or LLM-as-a-judge scoring without an utterance-aligned human-expert reference, and so cannot identify the specific shortcomings of individual models. We evaluated four LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3.1 70B, and HyperCLOVA X), spanning commercial, open-source and Korean-developed models, against a human-expert reference across three Korean OSCE cases (hematuria, fever in pregnancy, and chronic cough). In a double-blind, fully crossed design, 17 senior medical-student raters scored every model utterance on three sentence-level and six encounter-level Likert metrics, yielding 7,480 data points. We analyzed the scores using a stratified linear mixed-effects model based on an 11-category history-taking and 3-level linguistic-form taxonomy. At the encounter level, three of the four LLMs fell 0.08 to 0.47 Likert points below the human-expert reference on Comprehensibility, Consistency and Hallucination-freeness. The difference was not statistically significant for Hallucination-freeness in Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, Consistency in GPT-4o, and Engagement in HyperCLOVA X. Llama-3.1 70B fell significantly below the reference on all six metrics. We also introduce a web-based OSCE platform that supports virtual practice across diverse clinical cases and continuously collects student-VSP dialogues under research and privacy consent.
evidence_items.title: A Stratified Multi-Rater Evaluation of LLM-Based Virtual Standardized Patients with a Deployed Data-Generation Platform

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we present 5uGUE, a large language model (LLM)-driven hardware-in-the-loop agent, which enables the wireless fuzzing of 5G-enabled devices (such as mobile phones). 5uGUE combines multi-step reasoning with tool-assisted interaction and integrates into the fuzzing pipeline by leveraging specialized tools for internet search, 5G protocol analysis, memory management, and test-case execution. The agent iteratively generates test cases, executes them on targets, collects runtime feedback, and adaptively refines the fuzzing strategy. We evaluate 5uGUE on five commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) 5G devices across six LLMs. The best performing runs for 5uGUE trigger 167 crashes in total (141 novel and 31 unique) within 60 interaction turns (49 to 133 minutes total runtime). In contrast, the best runs for the state-of-the-art baseline (5GHOUL) discovers only 13 crashes in total (10 novel and 6 unique) within 150 minutes. Overall, by integrating LLM-driven agents, 5uGUE demonstrates significantly better crash discovery performance (12.8x total, 5.2x unique improvement). Notably, among the crashes discovered by 5uGUE, MediaTek has confirmed two new high-severity vulnerabilities, with one CVE assigned (CVE-2026-20525), while UNISOC confirmed seven crashes. Finally, to demonstrate that 5uGUE is agnostic to wireless protocols, we also extend it to Bluetooth Classic with only minimal code changes. In our evaluations, 5uGUE finds an average of 6.4 novel crashes and 1.6 unique crashes. In a nutshell, 5uGUE highlights that LLM agents are capable to operate effectively beyond software-in-the-loop settings, extending autonomous vulnerability discovery to the proprietary, hardware-bound systems that affect billions of end-user devices across multiple wireless protocols.
evidence_items.title: 5uGUE: Agentic Hardware-in-the-Loop Fuzzing for 5G Devices and beyond

evidence_items.summary: Managed and wild bees sustain roughly a third of the global food products, yet colonies face mounting stress from climate-change including extreme weather patterns, altered parasite and disease patterns. Timely assessment of colony condition such as understanding colony strength, brood area, honey and pollen storage, comb usage, is essential to adaptive management. However, manual hive frame inspection is slow, costly, and quality depends on scarce expertise. We present an artificial targeted intelligent system framework focusing on edge deployable pipeline that turns hive frame photographs into interpretable and action-oriented inspection report. The pipeline includes an object detector to detect biologically-meaningful comb-cell classes; detections are distilled into structured fact schema; facts are converted into constrained factual text; the text triggers a grounded knowledge-base for interpretations and recommendations. Knowledge-base entries are required to be triggerable by evidence expressed in the fact schema. We built our system based on open source FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset and favour reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general purpose frontier models. We additionally release FAIRHiveText-1K dataset that turns FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset into interchangeable facts and text interpretation of the facts, making it easy for further LLM-based research into this area. We also propose a pathway to develop the grounded knowledge-base that will be helpful in providing interpretable and actionable reports from the facts.
evidence_items.title: Computer Vision and Knowledge-Grounded Language Models for Intelligent Beekeeper Assistance

evidence_items.summary:
Why large language models trained via log-loss minimization over massive and diverse datasets exhibit broad capabilities and generalizable skills is not yet fully understood. Grau-Moya et al. (ICML 2024) offer a conceptual explanation through the lens of meta-learning: if sequence-generating environments $
u$ are drawn from a prior $w_{
u}$, minimizing population log-loss recovers the corresponding Bayesian mixture predictor $\xi=\sum_
u w_
u
u$. In the idealized limit in which $w$ is a universal prior, the optimal predictor corresponds to Solomonoff universal induction. Practical machine learning algorithms, however, generally produce only \emph{approximately} optimal predictors. This raises a natural question: \emph{Does the prediction performance remain robust under approximation}? In this paper, we first provide a tight bound on the worst-case effect of approximation on prediction error. We show any predictor $ho$ satisfying $D_{KL}(\xi \|ho)\leq \eta$ retains bounded cumulative-expected-squared prediction error. However, while the Bayesian mixture predictor $\xi$ has error $O(\log(1/w_\mu))$ in an environment $\mu$, we establish a tight $\Theta(\eta/w_\mu)$ bound on the excess error of $ho$ relative to $\xi$. Thus, approximation can substantially degrade performance in environments assigned small prior probability. In sharp contrast, when environments are averaged according to prior $w$, we prove that the excess prediction error is only $O(\eta)$. Furthermore, we establish a distribution-shift theorem for dominated shifts from a training prior $w$ to a test prior $w'$, interpolating our average-case and worst-case guarantees. Finally, we extend our robustness analysis to a finite-sampling setting relevant to learning universal predictors with neural networks and Transformers, where $D_{KL}(\xi\|ho)$ could be unbounded. [For the full abstract, see the paper.]
evidence_items.title: Approximate Solomonoff Induction: On the Robustness of Learned Universal Predictors

evidence_items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel. New draft-training objectives are usually credited with the acceptance they add over cross-entropy on externally written responses, yet many pipelines let the target rewrite them. We ask how much of that gain survives. With a vision-language target and a block drafter, we train three objectives on four versions of one corpus: cross-entropy on corpus tokens, token-level distillation from the target, and distillation gated to positions that would survive verification. Distillation and the gate add large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation adds a smaller gain and the gate little or none. The shrinkage persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures and, for distillation, initializations and learning rates. Most of it remains at matched supervised length and at each objective's best measured training length. A second vision corpus shows the shrinkage, as does a text-only replication, for distillation also with an autoregressive drafter. Objective gains should therefore be measured against a target-regenerated baseline and across training lengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRegeneration.
evidence_items.title: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding

evidence_items.summary: Federated learning (FL) keeps data at its source, but locality alone does not make a federation trustworthy. Without sufficient observability, an aggregator cannot determine whether the client service was healthy, the local data pipeline was trustworthy, or contractual constraints were properly monitored during training. We take the position that trustworthy FL needs an evidence plane in addition to its model-update process. Each participant continuously summarizes local infrastructure, data into minimal, signed trust evidence associated with each FL round, while raw data, logs remain local. A local TinyLLM may assist in interpreting observability signals, deriving contextual evidence, and providing natural-language explanations to operators. We instantiate this vision through FAIR-O, an observability extension of FAIR principle. Rather than benchmarking FL accuracy, a three-level trust model has been proposed and a two-participant Python prototype demonstrates evidence generation and trust assessment. We further discuss future integration of FAIR-O Trust Evidence into participant selection, evidence weighting, and federated aggregation.
evidence_items.title: Extending FAIR Principles with Observability for Trustworthy Federated Learning

evidence_items.summary: We present a Bayesian framework, Two-stage Inference for Light curve DEcomposition (TILDE), for mapping the accretion disk and the broad line region (BLR) from active galactic nuclei (AGN) multi-band light curves. By inferring delayed BLR contamination from the underlying disk variability, TILDE provides the delay measurements of the disk as well as the BLR. We validate TILDE using synthetic data, finding that TILDE recovers the known time delays of the disk and BLR. By applying TILDE to the Seoul National University AGN Monitoring Project sample, we find that the inferred BLR light curves match the observed H$\beta$ emission light curves, providing consistent BLR lags compared to the reported H$\beta$ lags. Using the lag spectrum, effectively corrected for the BLR contamination, we find that the disk size is broadly consistent with the standard thin-disk model, suggesting that BLR contamination can significantly bias the disk size derived from the cross-correlation analysis of the broad-band photometry. These results demonstrate that the new inference method is a powerful tool for determining both disk and BLR sizes from broad-band photometry in the era of time-domain surveys.
evidence_items.title: Unveiling Accretion-Disk Reverberation Beneath BLR Contamination with TILDE

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents now complete tasks autonomously, modifying real-world state such as artifacts, software environments, and configurations along the way. Yet they show limited backup awareness: recognizing that an action will modify state that may later be needed, and preserving it beforehand. To evaluate backup awareness, we introduce RegretBench, a benchmark of 205 executable tasks grounded in regret moments reported on platforms such as X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow, where users explicitly regretted not preserving state they later needed. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average yet back up before these moments in only 15.2%, showing that task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. Because it is hard to predict which changes will be regretted, we propose BackUpper, a harness plug-in backup layer that checks every tool call and preserves affected state before modification. It combines rule-based strategies for common operations with a lightweight subagent for complex cases, and its rule table can expand with subagent decisions over time. On RegretBench, BackUpper covers every regret moment action and restores states with 92.2% average similarity to the original. Achieving this costs only $0.014 per task, with 7x fewer tokens than the main-agent self-backup baseline. When users have preferences on what to back up, BackUpper can also narrow its scope accordingly, matching human annotations on whether an action is worth preserving with an 84.5% F1 score. These results suggest that agents can keep actions reversible at low cost while respecting users' preferences.
evidence_items.title: Back Up Before You Regret: Measuring Backup Awareness and Automating Backup in Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Step-by-step painting tutorials are used for learning artistic techniques, but existing video resources lack interactivity and personalization. While recent generative models have advanced artistic image synthesis, they still struggle to generate temporally and structurally consistent videos. Video models excel in consistent frame generation, yet fine-tuning an image-to-video model on forward painting sequences creates a long-range dependency on the first-frame reference, disrupting its pretrained attention pattern and hindering reconstruction. We address this issue by training on reversed sequences that better preserve the reference-attention behavior. Building on this, we present Loomis Painter, a framework for reconstructing coherent painting processes. We further introduce a media-transfer training strategy that decouples input appearance from the target process, enabling generation across different artistic media. Trained on a curated dataset of real-world painting processes, our method outperforms existing baselines across LPIPS, DINO, and CLIP metrics and is consistently preferred in expert and non-expert user studies. Code available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/wlp.

evidence_items.summary: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.
evidence_items.title: Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds

evidence_items.summary: Aiming to modify textual content while preserving the original style, Scene Text Editing (STE) has significant practical value in many applications. STE typically requires paired images before and after editing for training. However, recent approaches rely heavily on synthetic paired data and complex disentanglement strategies. They struggle to faithfully capture the diversity and complexity of natural scenes, often producing artifacts or hallucinations. In this work, we challenge the common practice and investigate whether STE can be driven by turning each real sample into its own paired supervision. Concretely, we explore multiple ways to disrupt the original image (e.g., Crop, Shuffle, Mask) to construct self-paired training data, and build a strong baseline (TextRIRO}) upon a conditional diffusion architecture. Our experiments show that combining character-column shuffling with image cropping (Shuffle&Crop) effectively destroys text semantics while preserving key style cues, enabling the model to learn editing behaviors directly from the real text image. With this concise yet real-oriented design, TextRIRO achieves promising performance in both accuracy and visual realism across real-world benchmarks, substantially mitigating the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Furthermore, we leverage TextRIRO to build TextRIRO-3M, a large-scale realistic dataset for long-text recognition by concatenating edited and original images. Experimental results show that training recognition models with TextRIRO-3M significantly improves recognition accuracy, demonstrating that TextRIRO provides highly useful training resources for downstream tasks. Overall, TextRIRO lifts STE to realistic, reliable, and widely applicable new levels. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextRIRO.
evidence_items.title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?

evidence_items.summary: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai
evidence_items.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models

evidence_items.summary: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.
evidence_items.title: SolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering

evidence_items.summary: Electromyography (EMG) provides a non-invasive means of decoding silently articulated speech into text, but accurate decoding remains challenging due to limited availability of paired EMG-text data. We introduce PhonoBridge, a two-stage framework comprising a channel-aware EMG-to-phoneme frontend and a large language model (LLM) backend for text reconstruction. The frontend is trained on paired EMG-text data that consists of channel-wise feature extraction, cross-channel fusion, and electrode embeddings. With phonemes as the intermediate representation, we expand the backend's training data by converting LibriSpeech transcripts into phoneme-text pairs without additional EMG recordings. To adapt the LLM to frontend noise, we introduce Error-Profile-Guided Augmentation (EPGA), which perturbs transcript-derived phoneme sequences according to error patterns estimated from frontend predictions, generating additional training pairs for the LLM. On the Open Vocabulary silent-speech dataset, PhonoBridge achieves 24.77% WER, outperforming the previously reported best of 28.27% on the same test split.
evidence_items.title: PhonoBridge: Error-Aware Phoneme-Mediated EMG-to-Text Reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: The increasing use of large language models for code generation calls for methods that distinguish purely human-written code from AI-involved code: files in which any part, however small, was generated or substantially modified by a model. Beyond flagging such files, we aim to localize the lines or blocks attributable to AI. Existing approaches compress a file into a single score, from surface stylistic features or a global code representation, which averages away the evidence when only a few blocks are AI-involved. We propose a framework that models AI authorship at the token level and predicts at the line, block, and file levels. A frozen code language model is equipped with two low-rank adapters, trained separately on machine-written and human-written files; their per-token log-likelihood ratio provides local evidence of AI authorship. Lightweight heads aggregate this evidence within lines and blocks, using the surrounding code context, and their local predictions are aggregated into a file-level decision. We train on mixed-authorship files built from human originals and their AI-generated or AI-modified counterparts, including continuation and fill-in-the-middle scenarios. On an internal test set of 11,773 AI-involved files across six generation regimes against 2,541 human files, our method reaches 72.4 macro F1 at a 1% FPR operating point. With no adaptation, it reaches 62.5 line-level F1 on HybridCodeAuthorship, an external human-AI co-writing benchmark with no training split, above the 56 its own paper reports as the best line-level result. On 19,445 human-written files from repositories created before 2022, the false-positive rate stays between 0.55% and 0.81% under the transported 1% threshold, so the operating point holds on real human code.
evidence_items.title: From Tokens to Files: Multi-Granularity Detection and Localization of AI-Involved Code

evidence_items.summary: Picture-description dementia classification uses a shared visual scene, but a transcript-level prediction alone does not identify the scene evidence underlying its inputs. NarraSpace links words and speech times to named picture elements and retrieves utterances for predefined scene events. Narrative-spatial descriptors summarize coverage and temporal organization. A frozen language model contrasts each event's text under examples from Alzheimer's disease and healthy-control training participants, alongside transcript surprisal and coverage measurements. Retained source records link event scores to their source utterances, speech intervals, and lexical matches. On the official 48-participant test set of the Alzheimer's Dementia Recognition through Spontaneous Speech benchmark, a fixed support vector classifier achieves $80.88\%\pm2.56\%$ mean accuracy over fifty seeds; averaged probabilities yield $81.25\%$ accuracy and $91.32\%$ area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. NarraSpace makes the construction of scene-linked classification inputs explicit and inspectable by connecting event-indexed language-model measurements to their source utterances, speech timing, and extraction records. Such source-linked measurements could support clinician review of picture descriptions by presenting quantitative summaries alongside the original speech evidence.
evidence_items.title: NarraSpace: Multimodal Scene-Grounded Evidence for Picture-Description Dementia Classification

evidence_items.summary: This editorial discusses how health misinformation and disinformation combine long-established narratives with new technologies that substantially increase the speed, reach, personalization, and apparent credibility of misleading content. The novelty of the contemporary information environment lies less in entirely new false narratives than in digital infrastructures that allow misleading content to be created, tailored, disseminated, and monetized at unprecedented scale. Online social media platforms and generative artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed these conditions, enabling misleading health information to be created and disseminated at previously impossible scale and speed. Health misinformation and disinformation can influence behavior, undermine trust in scientific and public health institutions, delay appropriate care, promote ineffective or harmful interventions, and weaken responses to disease outbreaks. Their effects may be particularly pronounced among populations with limited access to reliable information, healthcare, and trusted institutions. This editorial also examines how engagement-driven platform design, commercial and political incentives, synthetic media, and inconsistent safeguards amplify the problem. It argues that fact-checking and individual media literacy, while necessary, are insufficient on their own. A more effective response requires timely, transparent public health communication; institutional support for healthcare professionals; greater platform accountability; systematic safety evaluation of generative AI; independent access to relevant data; and policies that address the incentives sustaining the production and circulation of false and misleading health information.
evidence_items.title: Health misinformation and disinformation: Old narratives, new technologies.
